Certain catered events are considered low risk and the requests will be approved automatically. Events considered
higher risk require review by the local liquor inspector for approval.

Catered events will be considered low risk if the following circumstances apply:
• Events under 500 people
• Indoor events (other than community events) under 500 people
Any event (other than a community event) where the duration of liquor service does not exceed two hours

All other events, as well as catered events with extended hours, will require the liquor inspector’s approval. For
these higher risk events, the request must be submitted 21 calendar days prior to the event.

In some circumstances, the Branch may require that all catered events from a certain caterer be approved by a
liquor inspector.

For example, cases where the caterer or business location is deemed high risk or the caterer has a
poor compliance history.

The Branch may cancel an event authorization if the information for an event was inaccurate or has changed. The
Branch may amend an event authorization upon request. The general manager may limit the frequency of catered
events at specific locations. You must notify police, via fax or email, of all catered events.

Local Government/First Nation Approvals
You must keep copies of local government/First Nation approval on file for all community events and for events
with extended hours (outdoor events after 10 p.m., or indoor events after 2 a.m. on New Year’s Eve). In addition,
you must keep copies of approvals from the Tsawwassen First Nation or Nisga’a Nation for all events on their
land.

If a local government or First Nation issued their approval subject to conditions, you must provide a copy of the
conditions to the liquor inspector.

Security Plans
For certain events, the liquor inspector will ask you to submit a security plan through the online Liquor and
Cannabis Licensing portal. The security plan must describe the event in some detail, including staffing levels and
security, if required, liquor service areas and venue capacity.

It must describe how key safety and security risks will
be addressed, such as service to minors, overcrowding, intoxication and control and safety of guests, including
entering and exiting the venue.

Someone other than you may prepare the plan, but you are responsible for submitting it to the inspector.

Terms and Conditions that Apply to Your Catering Endorsement
• All staff that are serving or managing events must have Serving It Right certification.
• Catered events must be primarily held offsite.
• Minors may serve food or work as entertainers at events, but they cannot serve liquor.
• Only you or your employees may sell liquor at an event, and you or your employees must be at the event
at all times liquor is being sold or served.
• You must remove any unused liquor at the end of the event and return it to the inventory at your
establishment. With the exception of re-sealed bottles of wine, you can’t leave unfinished bottles of spirits
or unopened bottles of liquor at the event.

Food Primary 36
Terms & Conditions

• There are no restrictions on liquor pricing at catered events. Minimum drink pricing requirements do not
apply.
• The price list and the quantity of liquor in each drink must be made available to guests upon request. For
events with a hosted bar, you only need to state that the liquor is provided complimentary of the host.
• You cannot promote or invite guests to events you are catering.

Exceptions to this are infrequent client
appreciation and staff appreciation events where you provide the liquor at no cost to your invited guests.
• You must not cater a series of events for the same person if it appears that you are operating an ongoing
business with that person. Universities and colleges with a catering endorsement may cater a series of
events hosted by the university or college (or events hosted by groups associated with the university or
college) as long as the events are held on-campus.
• You must retain all revenue from liquor sales at an event. You must not give any portion of the revenue
from liquor sales to the event host.
Terms and Conditions that Apply to Catered Events
The term “catered event” refers to any event that is not held in a residence and where liquor is sold by a licensed
caterer.
Authorization: You must obtain a catering authorization prior to each catered event.
Licence: You must post a copy of your liquor licence and catering authorization and have available any local
government/First Nation approvals or security plans at a catered event.
Venue:
• The site of a catered event must be adequately separated from adjacent areas and supervised. Outdoor
events must be surrounded by a barrier. The type of barrier required will vary – stanchions may be
sufficient for a small corporate event, whereas a community event requires more substantial fencing.
• You must ensure that all catered events comply with local bylaws and health and fire regulations.

Catered
events on land within the Agricultural Land Reserve must comply with Agricultural Land Commission
requirements.
• The number of guests at a catered event must not exceed the venue’s occupant load or the number of
guests specified in the catering authorization. You must have controls at each entry point to the venue
and you must be able to count the number of people entering and leaving.
Minors: Minors are permitted at catered events unless restricted by the Branch or the host. Minors are not
permitted at events with adult entertainment or gambling, except for ticket raffles and BC Lottery products.
Hours: Liquor may be served at indoor events between 9 a.m. and 2 a.m. and at outdoor events between 9 a.m.
and 10 p.m. With local government and branch approval, liquor service for outdoor events may be extended until
2 a.m. on New Year’s Eve. You may serve liquor until 4 a.m. on January 1, as long as local government has given
approval and food is available to customers.

Food: Food and non-alcoholic beverages must be provided at all catered events. While food does not need to be
served at all times during events, liquor service must be secondary to food service over the course of the event. At
a minimum, appetizers must be served and more food may be required depending on the length and type of
event. Packaged snacks do not meet the minimum food requirement.
Liquor Service:
• Patrons may only consume liquor in the areas noted on the catering authorization.
• The host or guests are not allowed to bring their own wine or other liquor to a catered event.

All liquor
purchased from you must be consumed at the event, with the exception of unfinished bottles of wine,
which may be re-sealed for guests to take home.

Food Primary 37
Terms & Conditions

• You may sell or serve liquor only during the hours indicated on the catering authorization for a particular
catered event. You must ensure that liquor is taken from guests within half an hour after the time stated
on the catering authorization for liquor service.
Gaming: In most cases, all types of gaming licensed by the Gaming Policy and Enforcement Branch are permitted
at catered events. However, if minors are allowed at a catered event, you must not permit any gaming, except for
ticket raffles and BC Lottery products.
Entertainment:
• The entertainment offered at a catered event must be compatible with the nature of the event and must
not interfere with your ability to maintain effective care and control.

For example, if the entertainment
uses part of an event area, you must ensure that guests will not be so crowded together that staff will be
unable to observe and control their conduct.
• Entertainment must conform to local bylaws, and must not create excessive noise or otherwise negatively
impact nearby residents and businesses.
• Entertainment, games and activities that may jeopardize patron or public safety are not permitted.
• You cannot hold a contest or tournament at a catered event, but the host may do so.
• If a catered event features adult entertainment, you must post a sign at the entrance and not allow minors
at the event.

Terms and Conditions that Apply to Residential Events
A residential event is an event for the client and their invited guests held at a residence.
• Catering authorizations are not required.
• Minors may be permitted at residential events.
• You may only sell liquor to the host; you cannot sell drinks directly to the patrons at a residential event.
• You may only sell liquor that has been purchased from the Liquor Distribution Branch. However, you may
serve liquor provided by the host or the host’s guests. This includes commercially made and UBrew/UVin
(Ferment-on-Premises) product.
• All liquor you sell to the host must be consumed at the event.

At the end of the event, all unused liquor
purchased under your licence must be returned to your establishment, with the exception of unfinished
bottles of wine, which the host may keep or guests may take home, as long as staff have re-sealed the
bottle.

Food Primary 38
Terms & Conditions

Temporary Use Area Endorsements

A Temporary Use Area Endorsement enables a licensee at a golf course or ski hill to hold up to 26 events per year
at outdoor areas on the property. Licensees must apply for a Temporary Use Area Endorsement.

Apply online
through the Liquor and Cannabis Licensing portal.

Temporary Use Area Terms and Conditions
To hold an event in your Temporary Use Area, you must have a Temporary Use Area authorization.

The terms and conditions of the authorization are only in effect during the times indicated on the authorization.
Authorizations are generally subject to the same terms and conditions as your primary licence; however, they may
also have specific rules or restrictions for each event site.

Terms and conditions that apply to a TUA authorization:
• You must post the authorization and a copy of your licence onsite during the event
• Patrons are not required to leave the event site within 30 minutes of the end of liquor service; however,
you must ensure that all liquor is removed from patrons within this time period
• Events must end no later than 10 p.m.
• The number of people in attendance at the event site must not exceed the attendance listed on the
authorization, and must not exceed the occupant load, if one exists
• The event site must be appropriately bounded and staffed (as set out in the terms and conditions of your
endorsement, authorization and/or security plan), so that the liquor service and consumption area is
clearly visible

Requesting a Temporary Use Area Authorization
Requests for a Temporary Use Area authorization are submitted to the Branch online through the Liquor and
Cannabis Licensing portal.

You may request an authorization to hold multi-day events.

Multi-day events must be for consecutive days, on the
same event sites and have the same maximum attendance, but they may have different hours for each day. Each
day of a multi-day event counts towards the 26 day annual maximum.

Authorizations may permit liquor service at different event sites at different times during the day. This counts as
only one day towards the 26-day total, but attendance numbers for all locations are calculated in the total daily
attendance for the authorization.

Certain authorization requests are considered low risk and are approved automatically; others will require the
liquor inspector’s approval. The distinction is based on the total daily attendance or capacity of all the activated
locations.

Small event requests (under 500 people) require submission at least seven days in advance. When the total
attendance for all event sites exceeds 500 people per day, an event is considered large and the authorization will
require approval.

Food Primary 39
Terms & Conditions

Large event requests must be submitted at least 21 days in advance and you must submit a security plan to
your liquor inspector by email, and send copies of your authorization request notification and security plan to
your local police.

The Branch may cancel a Temporary Use Area authorization if the information provided for an event was
inaccurate or has changed. The Branch may also amend an authorization upon request, as long as the same
advance notice is given i.e.

seven days for small events and 21 days for large events.

If you wish to cancel your own event, you may do so by contacting your liquor inspector at least 24 hours before
the start time listed on the authorization. Doing so will ensure the event will not count against your annual limit of
26.

More details about the online notification process, information about how to submit requests, and the rules
regarding how events are considered and counted, is available through the online Liquor and Cannabis Licensing
portal.

Security Plans
For Temporary Use Area events with 500 or more people, the liquor inspector will require you to submit a security
plan. The security plan must describe the event in detail, including staffing levels and security, liquor service areas,
and the capacity at each activated Temporary Use Area location. It must describe how key safety and security risks
will be addressed, such as service to minors, overcrowding, intoxication and control and safety of guests, including
entering and exiting licensed areas.

Go to www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/employment-business-and-economic-development/business-
management/liquor-regulation-licensing/forms/lcrb052_security_plan_for_temporary_use_area_activations.pdf for
a template of the Security Plan.

Food Primary 40
Terms & Conditions

Compliance and Enforcement

As a licensee, you are required to:
1. Comply with the Liquor Control and Licensing Act, its Regulations and the terms and conditions in this
publication.
2.

Always allow Liquor and Cannabis Regulation Branch inspectors and/or police officers to enter your
establishment. Never impede their entry in any way.
3. Comply with the Liquor Control and Licensing Act, its Regulations and the terms and conditions in this
publication.
4. Never draw attention to liquor inspectors inside your establishment. This can affect the inspectors’
safety.
Drawing the attention of patrons to the fact that inspectors, minor agents contracted to the branch, and/or police are
present in your establishment may put the safety of the inspectors, minor agents contracted to the branch, and police
at risk. Accordingly, your actions must not cause the attention or focus of patrons to shift towards inspectors, minor
agents contracted to the branch, or police at any time; including at the time of entry, during an inspection, or when
exiting your establishment. Actions such as announcing the arrival of inspectors, raising or flashing lights, turning
down music, playing particular soundtracks (e.g. “Bad Boys” or “Hawaii Five O”), using spotlights, or any other similar
actions are not permitted. You may not take, save or distribute photographs or video of inspectors or minor agents
contracted to the branch in any manner (e.g.

on a staff bulletin board, print media, social media or the internet).

If your licence is suspended, you are not permitted to sell, serve or permit consumption of liquor in your
establishment.

For more information on Compliance and Enforcement, please visit our website.

Other ministries also have terms and conditions that licensees and employees must follow. Please refer to this
page on the LCRB website for more information.

Posting Signs Relating to Suspensions or Monetary Penalties
If a suspension or monetary penalty is imposed on your licence, the Branch may post a sign in a prominent
location in the interior or on the exterior of your establishment.

You must ensure the signs are posted for the entire period of the suspension or for monetary penalties, the period
specified on the sign. During the period that the signs must be posted, you must ensure the signs are not
defaced, obstructed or moved.

Food Primary 41
Terms & Conditions

Glossary

“The Act” means The Liquor Control and Licensing Act, the provincial legislation that guides the licensing of
establishments that manufacture or sell liquor in B.C.

“The Branch” means the Liquor and Cannabis Regulation Branch, the government agency that administers the
Act.

“Licensee” refers to any individual, individuals or corporate body that holds a British Columbia liquor licence.

The
term covers both the licensee and any person acting in the place of the licensee, such as a manager or person in
charge of an establishment in the licensee’s absence.

“Licensee retail store” or “liquor store” means an establishment that is permitted to sell all types of packaged
liquor.

“Manufacturer” refers to a person who manufactures liquor (beer, wine, spirits, cider, coolers).

“Agent” refers to a holder of an agent licence who represents products manufactured outside British Columbia.
An agent may advertise and promote liquor to licensees, liquor stores and the public, but can only sell liquor from
any manufacturer they represent to the Liquor Distribution Branch in a manner authorized by the Liquor
Distribution Branch.

“Catered event” means any event that is not held in a residence and where liquor is sold by a licensed caterer.

“Caterer” refers to a licensee with a catering licence or a catering endorsement.

“Catering Authorization” means the approval granted by the Branch for a catered event.

“Catering Endorsement” means an endorsement that may be added to a food primary or liquor primary licence
to allow the licensee to sell liquor at residential and catered events.

“Event” includes Temporary Use Area events, catered and residential events, as the case may be.

“Event site” means the place referred to in the Temporary Use Area or catering authorization.

“Host” refers to the client that hired you (if you have a catering endorsement) to cater food and liquor at an
event.

“Food primary” means an establishment where the service of food is the primary focu

s in the service area during
hours of liquor service.

“Liquor primary” means an establishment where the service of liquor is for on-premises consumption.

“Marketing representative” refers to a person hired by a licensed agent to promote their products.

“Occupant load” means the number of people permitted in an establishment or event site at one time. The
number is calculated by designated professionals.

Food Primary 42
Terms & Conditions

“Patron capacity” means the maximum number of customers permitted in an establishment at one time.

“Patron-participation entertainment” means entertainment that patrons may participate in, such as "dine and
dance" or karaoke.

“Patron non-participation entertainment” means entertainment that patrons may watch, such as musicians or
comedians.

“Person capacity” means the maximum number of people (customers and staff) permitted in a service area or
event site at one time.

“Residence” means a private dwelling (where someone lives) and the land surrounding it.

“Residential event” means an invitation-only event held at a residence where liquor is sold by a licensed caterer,
such as a dinner party or wedding.

“Service area” means the area within an establishment or event site where liquor may be sold, served and
consumed.

“Temporary Use Area Authorization” means the approval granted by the Branch to hold an event at a
Temporary Use Area.

“Temporary Use Area Endorsement” means a licence endorsement available to licensees who operate a ski hill
or golf course, which allows them to hold events at outdoor locations on their property using
a Temporary Use
Area authorization.

Food Primary 43
Terms & Conditions

PROGRAM
This manual provides guidance and direction to the Liquor and Cannabis Regulation Branch’s, (the branch), or
(LCRB) Compliance and Enforcement (C&E) staff on the conduct of their duties. The information and procedures
contained within this manual are not a complete statement of all policies or procedures guiding the branch’s C&E
Program.

heading: 1.2 Overview
text:
This manual is comprised of six parts as follows:
Part 1 - provides background information for the C&E Program,

Part 2 - specifies the policies and procedures specific to the inspection program, such as compliance strategies
and the enforcement process,

Part 3 - specifies the procedures for identifying the specific contraventions of the Liquor Control and Licensing
Act and Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation,

Part 4 - specifies the procedures for identifying the specific contraventions of the Cannabis Control and
Licensing Act and the Cannabis Licensing Regulation,

heading: Part 5 - specifies the Enforcement Hearing Process, and
text:
Part 6 - specifies the procedures for Fit and Proper Investigations and Financial Integrity Assessments.

Each of the six parts is divided into sections and sub-sections that follow a similar layout. Each section begins by
outlining the reasons why the information, activities or procedures referred to in that section are in effect. This is
followed by a description or explanation relevant to the activity or contravention with the legislative reference as
applicable. Lastly each sub-section identifies the procedural direction to inspectors, regional managers and other
compliance and enforcement staff on how to perform the activity or identify the specific contravention.

Unless otherwise provided within (but specific only to) the Liquor Control and Licensing Act, wherever this
manual uses the term licence or licensee that term also refers to permit or permittee.

Unless otherwise provided, the authority for all sections described within this manual is by Liquor and
Cannabis Regulation Branch policy.

heading: 2.0 Introduction
text:
The policies and procedures outlined in this manual must be considered in light of the context or environment
within which the branch and the Compliance and Enforcement Program operate.

The branch’s operating environment is largely defined by:
• the Liquor Control and Licensing Act (the LCLA),
• the Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation (the LCLR),
• the Cannabis Control & Licensing Act (the CCLA),
• the Cannabis Licensing Regulation (the CLR).

Other aspects of the operating environment are discussed in this section under the following headings:
• Role of the Branch, and
• Operating Assumptions and Principles,

heading: 2.1 Role of the branch
text:
The general manager administers both Acts and supervises all establishments licensed under the LCLA and the
CCLA, including manufacturers of liquor, places where a special event permit has been issued and all non-
medical cannabis retail stores, producer retail store and cannabis marketers. In doing so, the general manager
must:
• issue, renew, amend, transfer, suspend or cancel licences as provided by the LCLA and the CCLA and
associated regulations,
• specify which regulations apply to a licence,
• supervise the conduct and operation of establishments licensed under both the liquor and cannabis
legislation,
• appoint or designate any person they consider advisable as an analyst for the purposes of the LCLA and the
CCLA,
• authorize persons to issue licences and permits under the LCLA and the CCLA, and
• perform all other acts required to administer their responsibilities properly and efficiently as defined by the
minister and under the LCLA and the CCLA and associated regulations.

Under its responsibility and authority to administer and enforce both the LCLA/LCLR and CCLA/CLR, the
following distinct functions are the major focus of branch efforts:
• issuing, amending, and transferring licences for resale and manufacture of liquor,
• issuing, amending, and transferring licences for non-medical cannabis retail stores, producer retail store and
cannabis marketers,
• regulating and monitoring product advertising,
• regulating and monitoring promotional activity between retailers and wholesalers of these products in BC,
• administering regulatory exemptions for medicinal, toi

heading: 2.1 Role of the branch
text:
let, confectionary, cleaning or disinfecting products
containing alcohol,
• inspecting and educating licensees to ensure they follow the laws,
• maintaining public relations with law enforcement, local government, and other regulatory agencies,
• taking appropriate compliance action for contravention of either one of the LCLA and the CCLA or
associated regulations, and
• liaising with stakeholders to develop more effective policies and legislation.

heading: 2.2 Operating assumptions and principles
text:
Operating Assumptions:
The functions listed above are based on operating assumptions that contribute to the policies and procedures of
the branch.

Under the Liquor Control & Licensing Act and the Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, the following
assumptions are the most influential ones for the branch:
1. While moderate alcohol consumption may have some modest health benefits, long term excessive drinking has
adverse health effects.
2. Alcohol is a drug that, if taken in sufficient quantities, will affect short-term mental judgment and physical
dexterity.
3. Although seen as a pleasant complement or accompaniment to social occasions, alcohol has addictive
properties and can lead to socially unacceptable behaviour when abused.
4. Minors should be protected from the negative effects of alcohol consumption.
5. Neighbourhoods and communities are impacted by the sale, service and manufacture of liquor and their
opinions are essential to licensing decisions.
6. Control of the number and location of liquor primary licensed establishments prevents a proliferation of
licensed establishments that may lead to the sale of liquor to minors and intoxicated persons, overcrowding
or other actions that may be harmful to the community.
7. It is in the best interests of the liquor and hospitality industries to encourage responsible drinking behaviours
that contribute to the well-being of their customers and the public.
8.

heading: 2.2 Operating assumptions and principles
text:
Licence holders are responsible for designing their operations and conducting their businesses in such a way
as to realize the outcomes and principles articulated in liquor licensing statutes and regulations.

Under the Cannabis Control & Licensing Act and the Cannabis Licensing Regulation, the following
assumptions are the most influential ones for the branch:
1. Protect minors from the negative effects of cannabis and restrict youth access to cannabis.
2. Protect young people from promotions or enticements to use cannabis.
3. Protect public health through strict product safety and quality requirements.
4. Help reduce the burden on the criminal justice system through its regulatory scheme.
5. Allow adults to possess and access regulated, quality-controlled legal cannabis.
6. Encourage responsible cannabis consumption behaviours that contribute to public well-being and adherence
to community.
7. Enhance public awareness of the health risks associated with cannabis.
8. Consider the impact of sale and use in communities.

Operating Principles:
The most important elements of the branch operating environment are the operating principles that guide the
regulation of liquor and non-medical cannabis in British Columbia.

heading: 2.2 Operating assumptions and principles
text:
These Acts and regulations require that the
general manager’s decisions be made in the “public interest.” The branch has articulated the requirement to act in
the public interest in the form of the two operating principles: public safety and public interest.

In these operating principles, the branch asserts that public interest is best served by targeting the negative
impacts of the manufacture and sale of liquor and the negative impacts of the cultivation and sale of cannabis,
while, at the same time, appreciating and balancing the unique interests of individuals and communities in the
application of any regulations.

Public Safety under the Liquor Control and Licensing Act and the Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation
It is in the public interest to safeguard individuals and communities from the harm caused by:
1. the inappropriate or reckless sale and/or manufacture of alcohol which might arise in instances of destructive
competition, and the abuse of alcohol and other irresponsible drinking behaviour.
2. this principle is aimed at correcting what economists refer to as “market failure.” Two types of market failure
are primarily associated with the liquor industry:
• destructive competition.

heading: 2.2 Operating assumptions and principles
text:
A form of severe competition in which industry participants act improperly or even
illegally to gain a competitive advantage, and
• spill-over effects and negative impacts on individuals and communities beyond the industry and its clients
which occur due to industry activity.

Examples of these types of market failure might include:
• over-consumption due to low liquor prices
• unsafe conditions or riotous behaviour caused by overcrowding
• neighbourhoods and communities negatively affected by noise and traffic from poorly operated
establishments or events, and
• violent or abusive behaviour by drunken patrons in the streets or at home.

While a degree of market protection may result from regulation of the industry, this is neither the intention nor the
focus of regulation. The purpose of liquor regulation is not to ensure the economic viability of existing licensed
establishments but, rather to safeguard the public interest against harm that may result from industry activity.

Public Safety under the Cannabis Control and Licensing Act and the Cannabis Licensing Regulation
It is in the public interest to safeguard individuals and communities from the harm caused by:
1. Illegal trafficking of non-medical cannabis and cannabis products, and money laundering of proceeds of
illegal trafficking,
2. Criminal associations to the sale and cultivation of non-medical cannabis,
3. Sale of illicit products from licensed stores,
4. Minors having access to cannabis or cannabis products,
5. Abuse of non-medical cannabis and other irresponsible substance use,
6.

heading: 2.2 Operating assumptions and principles
text:
Effects of increased intoxication where cannabis and alcohol are combined in consumption,
7. Mental health effects: cannabis use increases risk of mental illnesses such as psychosis or schizophrenia,
especially those who start at an early age, use cannabis often, and/or have a personal or family history of
psychosis and/or schizophrenia,
8. The increased risk of suicide, depression, and anxiety disorders with frequent use of cannabis,
9. The increased risk of harms when cannabis use is frequent, continues over time, and begins early in
adolescence,
10. Obtaining non-medical cannabis from illegal sources may involve health risks such as ingesting
contaminants, inconsistent dosage of psychoactive components, and exposure to unsafe or improper
product handling, and
11.

heading: 2.2 Operating assumptions and principles
text:
Obtaining non-medical cannabis from illegal sources may involve serious safety risks such as interacting
with criminals or criminal organizations, violence or threats of violence, criminal charges, and/or
prosecution.

Regard for Community Standards
It is in the public interest to have regard for:
• the impacts of alcohol sales, service, and manufacture,
• the impacts of non-medical cannabis sale, and
• the extent to which these impacts are understood and supported by individuals and their communities.

These principles address the need to find a balance between competing interests and recognize that different
communities have different requirements and standards.

Inspector Safety
To promote a safe work environment the C&E Division has established inspector safety protocols as specified
with the C&E Safety Procedures Manual which is updated from time to time. Inspectors are to become familiar
with and follow those procedures as specified within the safety procedures manual when carrying out their duties.

heading: 3.0 Introduction
text:
There are a number of concepts that provide background necessary for a full understanding of the policies and
procedures outlined in this manual. These include broad concepts, such as the principles of administrative law,
and narrower concepts that relate to the use of a particular word or term. These key concepts are discussed in this
section under the following headings:
• Legislation, Regulation and Policy,
• Administrative Law Principles,
• Definitions

heading: 3.1 Legislation, regulation and policy
text:
Policy plays a significant role in the work of a regulatory body. To understand this role, inspectors need to be
familiar with the relationship between the Act, regulation, and branch policy.

Legislation:
The primary statement of law is written in legislation. Legislation provides “hard rules” that must be followed
without exception or the exercise of discretion. Because legislation sets out strict rules, it is broadly written. The
finer points of law are set out in regulation and policy. This allows for greater flexibility and, in the case of policy,
the exercise of some discretion.

The LCLA is a broad statement or expression of laws regulating the sale and consumption of liquor. For example,
sections 48 through 53 of the LCLA, allow the general manager to take enforcement action, including cancelling a
licence or imposing a monetary or suspension penalty, but provide few guidelines for imposing those penalties.
The LCLR and related branch policy provides those guidelines.

The CCLA regulates the retail sale, public cultivation, and consumption of non-medical cannabis. Sections 38 and
39 of the CCLA allow the general manager to take enforcement action, including cancelling a licence or imposing
a monetary or suspension penalty, but provide few guidelines for imposing those penalties. The CLR and related
branch policies provide guidelines on imposing penalties.

Regulation:
Regulations primarily fill in the details of legislation. Like legislation, regulations are law.

heading: 3.1 Legislation, regulation and policy
text:
Most regulations are
also “hard rules” that must be followed without exception or the exercise of discretion. However, they are
subordinate legislation made under the authority of the statute. This means there must be authority in the
legislation for a regulation. In most pieces of legislation, a section commonly known as an “enabling section”
appears near the end of an Act. The enabling section describes the regulations the regulatory body may develop to
support the legislation.

Under the LCLA, sections 81 through 85 are the enabling sections. They describe what information and rules the
government may set out in regulation. For example, section 85 of the LCLA allows for regulations prescribing
administrative actions and penalties the general manager may take against a licensee or permittee. Schedule 2 of
the LCLR then outlines the suspension and monetary penalty ranges.

Under the CCLA, sections 127 to 138 are the enabling sections. They describe what provisions the government
may set out in the CLR. The regulations set penalty provisions for offenses and contraventions of the CCLA and
CLR. “Schedule 2” of the CLR then outlines the suspension and monetary penalty ranges. An advantage of
regulations over legislation is that regulations are easier to change or repeal than legislation. By amending
regulations, government can adapt quickly to changing program needs and operational issues.

Policy:

Policy is the next step in filling in the details of legislation.

heading: 3.1 Legislation, regulation and policy
text:
It is an important aspect of the work of all regulatory
bodies.

The branch controls policy:
Policy, unlike legislation and regulations, is not passed by the government but developed and approved by the
branch. Policy is controlled by the branch and reflects its philosophy. As the needs of industry and the standards
of the community shift, the branch can respond quickly by reviewing policy with major stakeholders and
amending it when necessary.

Consistent application of the law:
Policy provides guidelines that direct the actions of staff and administrators in applying legislation and
regulations. Without policy, a regulatory body could not make consistent and equitable decisions about
regulations.

Regulatory bodies and administrators need standards and principles to provide a framework for the exercise of
their discretionary powers. If there are no criteria to guide decisions, the decisions will be arbitrary and
inconsistent over time. The development of criteria through policy structures decisions and the exercise of
discretion.

Discretion in policy to ensure fair decisions:
Policy does not set out “hard rules.” When making a decision affecting a licensee, the branch will consider the
legislation, the regulation, policy, and the circumstances of the situation. Some situations require that the general
manager exercise discretion and act in a manner different than that expressed in policy.

heading: 3.1 Legislation, regulation and policy
text:
Each case is decided on its
own merits and not to blindly follow policy without considering whether it should not apply.

This is one of the advantages of policy: it can be flexible in a situation when warranted. Unlike legislation that
may require one course of action, the general manager can exercise discretion and move outside of policy to
ensure that the law is upheld, the public interest is protected, and all parties are treated fairly.

Policy supports legislative objectives:
Policy must be consistent with the intent and content of written legislation and regulations. A clear understanding
of the goals of legislation is necessary to develop standards and policy. The branch mandate outlined above in
“Role of the Branch” is drawn from the legislation. Branch policy supports this mandate.

Policy is enforceable:
Policy informs program operations and will be upheld by a judicial or quasi-judicial body. For example, section
15 of the LCLA and sections 30 to 32 of the CCLA gives the general manager authority to set terms and
conditions on a licence. Section 51 of the LCLA and section 38 of the CCLA allows the general manager to act
against a licensee for not following a term or condition of the licence. The licence terms and conditions are
expressions of branch policy.

heading: 3.2 Administrative law principles
text:
The branch has several administrative processes in place to facilitate decisions on issuing licences and taking
enforcement action. The decisions made by the branch through these administrative processes can have serious
consequences for licensees.

To enhance the meaningfulness, credibility, and influence of the Liquor and Cannabis Regulation Branch with
licensees, it is important to provide licensees with the right to fairness in administrative law.

Administrative law is the law that governs how public programs are implemented, particularly at the point of
service delivery. Administrative law can have the most immediate impact on people’s lives and rights, including
businesses.

The General Manager supervises the conduct and operation of all licensed establishments through their delegates,
a liquor and cannabis inspector. That means, to the extent of their delegated powers, inspectors and investigators
may or may not choose to recommend taking enforcement action and propose a recommended penalty. When the
branch does act, those actions must be seen as procedurally fair from an outsider’s viewpoint.

Procedural fairness – a fair and just process, suggests “Justice must be done, and it must be seen to be done.”

Before taking action that may adversely affect someone’s interests, the General Manager, and their delegates are
under a legal duty to act in a manner that is procedurally fair, and the decision is based on relevant facts and that it
is made without bias.

heading: 3.2 Administrative law principles
text:
The basis for these rules is to support public confidence in the daily operation of the branch.

In their dealings with the branch, licensees have the right to “administrative fairness.” Fairness in administrative
law may be summed up as the right of a person to effective participation in the decision-making process if the
decision may affect that person. The term “administrative fairness” encompasses the following principles that are
described in detail in the paragraphs that follow:
• statutory authority or jurisdiction,
• fairness,
• no abuse of discretion,
• neutral decision maker,
• right to know the case against you, and
• right to be heard.

Statutory Authority or Jurisdiction:
Jurisdiction refers to the statutory authority of an administrative body to undertake a contemplated action or
decision. An administrative body can only exercise the powers and duties that are expressed or implied in its
enabling statute. An action taken, or a decision made by an administrative decision maker without statutory
authority is void.

The statutory authority of the branch is derived from:
• the Liquor Control and Licensing Act and the Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, and
• the Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, and the Cannabis Licensing Regulation.

When investigating or when inspecting an establishment, inspectors should remain aware of the jurisdiction of the
branch and the specific authorities delegated to them by the general manager.

heading: 3.2 Administrative law principles
text:
Like the general manager and other
branch staff, inspectors must operate within the scope of the jurisdiction set out in legislation and regulation.

Fairness:
Licensees should not be subject to the arbitrary application of rules but should be treated in an equitable manner.
This does not mean identical treatment, but rather an objective approach to each situation.

Gathering and reviewing evidence is an important part of this principle. It is the role of the inspector to gather
enough evidence to establish that a contravention occurred. That evidence is reviewed, and a course of action
taken based on the circumstances of the contravention and the compliance history of the licensee.

No Abuse of Discretion:
This concept requires that an administrative body make decisions based on law, facts, and policy and not on
feelings. It also requires that a decision maker must not allow their discretion to be fettered by policy. While
policy is important, it is not binding in every case. The decision maker must consider all relevant factors when
applying policy.

Neutral Decision Maker:

A decision maker must approach each situation with an open mind and consider only relevant information.
Fairness requires that the decision maker must not have any apparent bias with respect to the outcome of a
particular situation. The principle of a neutral decision maker does not require a decision maker who is
independent of the regulatory agency taking enforcement action.

heading: 3.2 Administrative law principles
text:
The decision maker approaches each situation
with an open mind and makes reasoned and balanced decisions.

Both the LCLA and the CCLA give the general manager broad authority to supervise the conduct and operation
of licensed establishments and to take enforcement action against licensees. This results in a situation where the
general manager, through their delegates, may act as both an investigator and adjudicator. Such overlap of
functions, where authorized by statute, does not in itself give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias.

Right to Know the Case Against You:
This principle requires that the branch disclose to a licensee the enforcement action the branch will recommend to
the general manager in an enforcement hearing, the facts that support the proposed action and a summary of the
evidence gathered by the branch. This information allows a licensee to answer the allegation. The branch will
disclose all information that it will rely on at the enforcement hearing. The licensee is expected to do the same.

Right to be Heard:
The right to be heard means that the licensee has the right to present their case, whether in person or in written
form before the general manager makes a decision. The general manager has the power under section 48 of the
LCLA and section 36 of the CCLA to take immediate temporary enforcement action against a licensee without a
hearing.
However, to ensure a licensee’s right to be heard, the general manager will hold an enforcement hearing
to allow the licensee an opportunity to present evidence, bring witnesses and make argument about whether a
contravention occurred and/or the appropriate penalty.

heading: 3.3 Definitions
text:
General Manager:
The term “general manager” refers to both the general manager in person and delegates of the general manager.
The general manager must administer the LCLA and CCLA and supervise all licensees. Of course, in practice the
general manager does not do all the operational work of the branch. To perform all the functions associated with
this mandate, the general manager delegates authority to others. For example, inspectors, regional managers, and
hearing delegates (also known as “adjudicators”) all carry out the duties of the general manager.

For the purposes of this manual, the term “general manager” has been used both for consistency and because the
general manager has the legal authority to perform the functions required by the LCLA and CCLA. However, the
reader must be aware that delegates of the general manager may take the action or have the authority of the
general manager in certain situations.

Inspector:
Wherever this manual uses the term “inspector,” the policies and procedures apply to any other branch staff
member performing the duties of an inspector. For example, branch investigators, branch auditors, regional
supervisors, liquor and cannabis inspectors and regional managers may take part in inspections of licensed
establishments and are governed by the same policies and procedures applicable to inspectors.

Licensee:
“Licensee” includes both the licensee of record and any person acting in the place of the licensee, e.g.: a licensee
representative.

heading: 3.3 Definitions
text:
The procedures for identifying specific contraventions often refer to the inspector interviewing the
licensee. This does not mean that the inspector must contact the licensee of record. It means that, if a
contravention is found during an inspection, the inspector may speak to the licensee or whoever oversees the
establishment at that time. All enforcement actions are addressed to the licensee of record.

Permittee:

“Permittee” is the liquor permittee of record and is responsible for the special event.

Throughout this manual where the term “licence” or “licensee” is used shall also mean “permit” or “permittee”
unless otherwise specified in the LCLA.

Standard of Proof:
The Supreme Court of British Columbia has confirmed that the standard of proof for contraventions of the
legislation and regulations is the civil standard of “on a balance of probabilities” rather than the criminal standard
of “beyond a reasonable doubt.”

On a balance of probabilities means that:
• there is more evidence in favour of the conclusion that a contravention occurred than against the conclusion.

Permit/Allow:
Several of the contraventions in the LCLA and the CCLA and respective regulations use the terminology “must
not;” “must not allow;” “must not sell.” For example:
• s. 77(1)(a) LCLA: “must not sell, give or otherwise supply liquor to a minor,”
• s. 61(2)(b)(i) LCLA: “must not allow a person to become intoxicated,”
• s. 48 CCLA: “must not sell cannabis or a cannabis accessory (a) by means of a display that allows for self-
service or (b) by means of a dispensing device”.
• s.

heading: 3.3 Definitions
text:
49(2)(a) CCLA: “must not sell cannabis to a person who is intoxicated or shows signs of intoxication”.

The above terminology in the context of the legislation has a passive connotation. There is no requirement on the
branch to prove that the licensee was negligent or active in allowing the contravention. Nor does the branch need
to show that the licensee or its directing mind had knowledge of the circumstances of the contravention. The
branch does not have to prove any element of the licensee’s state of mind.

In the case of an allegation that the licensee allowed a minor to enter [s.79(1) of the LCLA and s.70(2) of the
CCLA] for example, the branch must prove that the individual in question was a minor and that the individual
entered the establishment. The branch has no obligation to prove what door the minor used, who they were with,
why they were there, how they got there, if staff or the directing mind knowingly let them in, how long they were
there, what identification they used or any other factor.

Due Diligence:
The defence of due diligence is available to licensees as a complete defence to all contraventions of the
LCLA/LCLR or the CCLA/CLR and the terms and conditions of a licence (not just for those contraventions
where the words permit, allow, authorize are used).

heading: 3.3 Definitions
text:
Where the licensee can show that it exercised all reasonable
care by establishing a proper system to prevent commission of the contravention and by taking reasonable steps to
ensure the effective operation of the system, the licensee will not be held responsible for the occurrence of the
contravention.

The underlying principle for the defence of due diligence is that punishment should not be inflicted on those
without fault. The doctrine of due diligence assumes that the licensee could have avoided the contravention
through the exercise of reasonable care and the licensee is given the opportunity of showing that it did in fact
exercise such care.

The onus is on the licensee - not the branch - to prove that it exercised due care and diligence by taking all
reasonable measures to prevent or avoid the contravention. In other words, that it did not allow the events.

The degree of diligence necessary to guard against contraventions will depend upon the circumstances faced by
the licensee.

heading: 3.3 Definitions
text:
What constitutes “all reasonable measures” depends on the nature of the alleged contravention and
the circumstances particular to the licensee.

Deciding whether a licensee has proven this defence rests with the general manager or the hearing delegate who
adjudicates at the enforcement hearing.

Compliance History:
Liquor:
“Compliance history” is defined in section 149 of the LCLR which states:
“For the purposes of the Act, "compliance history" means, a record of
(a) actions taken by the general manager under the Act or former Act as a result of the regulated person
(i) contravening the Act or former Act,
(ii) contravening this regulation or the former regulation, or
(iii) failing to comply with a term or condition imposed by the general manager,
(b) actions taken by the general manager under section 48, 49 or 50 of the Act in respect of the regulated
person,
(c) actions taken by the general manager or peace officer under section 7(4.1) of the former Act or by the
general manager under section 20, 22, 23 or 92 of the former Act in respect of the regulated person, and
(d) convictions for committing an offence under section 57 or 58 of the Act, an offence referred to in section 148
of this regulation or an offence under the former Act.

Cannabis:
“Compliance History” is defined in section 30 of the CLR which states:
“For the purposes of the Act, "compliance history" means, in respect of a licensee or former licensee, a record of
(a) actions taken by the general manager under the Act or former Act as a result of the licensee or former
licensee
(i) contravening the Act,
(ii) co

heading: 3.3 Definitions
text:
ntravening this regulation, or
(iii) failing to comply with a term or condition of the licence,
(b) actions taken by the general manager under section 36 or 37 of the Act in respect of the licensee or former
licensee,
(c) convictions of the licensee or former licensee for committing an offence under section 109(1) of the Act, and
(d) convictions, for committing an offence under section 111 of the Act of an officer, director or agent of a
corporation that is the licensee or former licensee.

Importance of Compliance History:
Compliance history will be considered when a penalty is being decided for a contravention. If a licensee has no
compliance history, depending on the nature and circumstances of the contravention, the penalty imposed may be
at the low end of the applicable penalty range prescribed for that contravention.

heading: 3.3 Definitions
text:
If a licensee has a significant
compliance history, the general manager may consider imposing a penalty greater than the range prescribed.

Terms and Conditions:
Sections 51 & 52 of the LCLA states: “the general manager may take enforcement action against a licensee for
the licensee’s failure to comply with a term or condition of their licence”.

Section 53 of the LCLA states: “the general manager may take enforcement action against a permittee for the
permittee’s failure to comply with a term or condition of their permit”.

Schedule 2 of the LCLR indicates that it is a contravention to fail to comply with certain terms and conditions of
the licence [penalty schedule items 11 (disturbance), 31 & 32 (entertainment), 39 (s.5 LDA) and 43 (tied house)]
or to breach any terms and conditions of the licence that are not specifically referred to elsewhere in Schedule 2,
[Item 54, Table of the LCLR (penalty schedule)].

Section 38(1)(c) of the CCLA states: “the general manager may take enforcement action against a licensee for
the licensee’s failure to comply with a term or condition of their licence”.
Schedule 2 of the CLR indicates that it is a contravention to fail to comply with the terms and conditions of the
licence [penalty schedule items 12 (display of accessories), 18 (disturbance), 21 & 22 (advertising & branding)
and 24 (tied house)] or to breach any terms and conditions of the licence that are not specifically referred to
elsewhere in Schedule 2, [Item 33, Table of the CLR (penalty schedule)].

Terms and conditions particular to an individual licence may be found by refe

heading: 3.3 Definitions
text:
rring to the face of the licence. In
addition, under the authority of both the LCLA and CCLA, the general manager has imposed general terms and
conditions on all licensees with respect to general operations, entertainment and relations with liquor and/or non-
medical cannabis manufacturers/producers. These terms and conditions are outlined in the Terms and Conditions
Handbook for each type of licence.

Inspectors should refer to the face of the licence and/or to any letter issued to the licensee by the branch, such as
the Approval in Principle (AIP) letter, to determine whether the licensee has been authorized to operate under
terms and conditions that differ from those outlined in the applicable Terms and Conditions Handbook.

A breach of either the terms or conditions outlined on the licence, or those contained in the related Terms and
Conditions Handbook, is a contravention.

heading: 4.0 Introduction
text:
The Compliance and Enforcement (C&E) Program encompasses activities focused on ensuring compliance with
the LCLA and CCLA. Activities under the LCLA are to ensure the sale and consumption of liquor follows the
requirements of the LCLA, regulation and terms and conditions of individual licences and special event permits.
Activities under the CCLA are to ensure compliance by non-medical retail sellers and marketers of cannabis with
the CCLA, associated regulations and terms and conditions of individual licences. The C&E program is
administered by the branch’s Compliance and Enforcement Division.

The terms “compliance” and “enforcement” each describe a distinct and separate component of the program.

Compliance is the desired outcome of the program. For the branch, it means that licensees voluntarily comply
with the applicable Act, regulation and terms and conditions of their licences.

Program activities that encourage compliance include:
• inspections,
• compliance meetings, and
• stakeholder liaison sessions.

Enforcement is the set of actions taken to correct or halt non-compliance, including identifying and substantiating
an alleged contravention. Enforcement activities include:
• issuing Electronic Notification of Noncompliance (NC),
• recommending enforcement action (Notice of Enforcement Action - NOEA),
• conducting enforcement hearings, and
• imposing penalties.

Note: The NC is not a legislated process or document and as such has no legal force and effect.

heading: 4.0 Introduction
text:
The NC is a
method used as an LCRB initiative to provide an added step in the enforcement process for administrative fairness
by providing a notice of an alleged contravention to the licensee. Branch policy establishes that the NC is issued
prior to the issuance of the written notice of enforcement (NOEA) as required by the legislation.

This section provides an overview of the C&E Program organized under the following headings:
• Program Goals,
• Role of the Liquor and Cannabis Inspector,
• Communication and Partnering Activities,
• Multi Agency Inspections,
• Stakeholder Liaison Sessions,
• Briefing and Training Sessions, and
• Role of the Licensee.

heading: 4.1 Program goals
text:
The C&E Program has the following five goals:
1. Voluntary compliance:
To minimize the number of contraventions and achieve voluntary compliance through knowledgeable licensees
and early intervention when problems are found. Licensees are educated through:
• branch publications, including the Terms and Conditions Handbooks,
• compliance meetings, and
• inspections.

2. Focused enforcement on public safety issues:
To increase compliance by licensees through enforcement focussed on key public safety issues, such as:

• intoxication,
• service to minors,
• overcrowding,
• unlawful liquor or unlawful non-medical cannabis
• unlawful activities in licensed establishments, and
• community disturbances associated with the operation of licensed establishments.

3. Implementation of consequences for non-compliance:
The branch has established a set of policies and procedures to ensure a file is reviewed and an enforcement
strategy is made in an expedient manner consistent with the principles of administrative fairness.

4. Effective penalties consistently applied:
The regulations for both the LCLA and the CCLA have set out prescribed penalties. Those penalties are found in
Schedule 2 of the LCLR and Schedule 2 of the CLR and are commonly known by the branch as “Penalty
Schedules.” These penalty schedules ensure that all licensees within the province are subject to similar penalties
for similar contraventions.

5.
Fair and equitable decision making:
The Compliance and Enforcement Procedures Manual, the LCLA and the CCLA and their respective regulations,
set out comprehensive legislative and administrative procedures to ensure fair and equitable decision making
throughout the enforcement process.

heading: 4.2 Role of the liquor and cannabis inspector
text:
Authority:
Following section 4 of the Liquor Control and Licensing Act, Liquor and Cannabis Inspectors (“Inspector”) are
appointed under the Public Service Act to exercise authorities under the LCLA.

Following section 5 of the Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, Liquor and Cannabis Inspectors are delegated the
General Manager’s powers and duties under the CCLA.

Per section 9 of the Police Act, LCRB Investigators [applicable only to those appointed as Special Provincial
Constables (SPC)], are peace officers by virtue of their SPC appointment. Inspectors do not require SPC status to
perform their duties other than for information sharing purposes with law enforcement. Branch inspectors and
investigators do not have authority to make arrests or exercise other powers normally those of police officers or
certain peace officers. The authorities of a branch inspector or investigator are restricted to those authorities as
defined in the LCLA and CCLA, and/or as in the case of branch investigators, as specified within an SPC
appointment.

Inspectors may collect any information necessary for the purposes of exercising the powers or performing the
general manager's duties under the LCLA and the CCLA or their respective regulations.

heading: 4.2 Role of the liquor and cannabis inspector
text:
Inspectors have the
authority to inspect any licensed establishment and its associated storage facilities.

Inspectors can seize unlawful liquor or unlawful cannabis as well as records and other relevant items, as required.
Inspectors also have the delegated authority to issue 24-hour licence suspensions under both the LCLA and
CCLA.

Under the Offence Act, inspectors have the authority to issue violation tickets for certain contraventions of both
the LCLA and the CCLA as prescribed within the related schedules of the Violation Ticket Administration and
Fines Regulation (VTAFR).

Functions:

Each inspector works independently under the direction of a manager and is the key contact and advisor for
compliance and enforcement activities within an assigned geographical area.

heading: 4.2 Role of the liquor and cannabis inspector
text:
These activities include:

Developing and implementing compliance strategies:
• conducting reviews and risk assessments of individual licensed establishments and developing strategies and
tactics to address compliance risks,
• planning, developing, implementing, managing, and coordinating an inspection program to ensure
compliance with legislation, regulations, and other applicable requirements, and
• making recommendations on a course of action regarding inspections or complaints.

Identifying contraventions:
• developing inspection and investigation plans regarding the operation of licensed establishments including
determining scope and justification, finding issues, sources of evidence, resources required, logistics, and
operational details in accordance with standards and practices consistent with case law, policy, and
legislation,
• collecting evidence by interviewing witnesses, obtaining, and securing physical evidence, and taking notes
and photographs of observations,
• investigating compliance, serious incidents, and complaints regarding public safety
• identifying contraventions of the LCLA and CCLA, their respective regulations or the terms and conditions
of the licences, and
• issuing Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance to licensees.

Recommending enforcement action:
• reviewing evidence and file information and deciding whether to recommend enforcement action for an
alleged contravention,
• documenting reasons for taking or not recommending enforcement action,
• preparing notification to the licensee of proposed enforcement action,
• preparing waiver notic

heading: 4.2 Role of the liquor and cannabis inspector
text:
es,
• preparing reports and briefings,
• attending and presenting evidence at enforcement hearings, and
• enforcing penalties resulting from an enforcement decision or waiver notice.

Issuing violation tickets:
• identifying if a contravention has occurred for which a violation ticket may be issued,
• issuing violation tickets if appropriate,
• attending provincial court and presenting evidence for disputed tickets, and
• withdrawing or cancelling tickets if appropriate.

Interacting with legal counsel:
There are a variety of circumstances where an inspector may interact with legal counsel. The most common are:

1. Legal counsel for the branch: The branch has assigned legal counsel from Ministry of Justice legal services
branch. Counsel advises the branch on a broad range of issues. Other ministry legal counsel represents the branch
in court, primarily on judicial review applications. Where an inspector is engaged on a file that requires legal
counsel, legal counsel will be provided through headquarters via their direct manager.

2.

heading: 4.2 Role of the liquor and cannabis inspector
text:
Legal counsel for a licensee: Inspectors may be contacted by legal counsel for a licensee with respect to a
variety of issues, the most common being matters related to a compliance or enforcement action.

Legal counsel for a licensee may be referred to:
• the Branch Registrar,
• Branch Advocates,
• Regional Managers,
• the Manager Integrated Provincial Compliance Assistance Team,
• the Provincial Director C&E Operations,
• the Deputy General Manager Compliance and Enforcement, or
• to headquarters’ Policy and Legislation for any further response.

When first contacted by counsel for a licensee, the branch inspector (or investigator) will require a written
authorization from the licensee allowing any communication to be conducted with the legal counsel. The
inspector/investigator will advise the legal counsel that prior to responding to any questions or concerns, they
need to consult with their manager, as needed. The manager will consult with headquarters.

The result will depend on the nature of the enquiries. In most cases, legal counsel will be asked to put their
questions in writing. With respect to the process around any ongoing enforcement action, it is the branch advocate
and or the branch registrar who will respond. With respect to queries about licensing concerns, branch licensing
division will respond.

3.

heading: 4.2 Role of the liquor and cannabis inspector
text:
Legal counsel for a member of the public who is not a licensee or an applicant to become a licensee: At
times, members of the public who have had interactions with police and or licensed establishments become
engaged in legal action, which may be either criminal or civil in nature.

Where legal counsel for a member of the public contacts an inspector or an investigator with queries on any
subject, they will advise the counsel that prior to any response the inspector must consult with their manager. The
manager will consult with headquarters and branch legal counsel will be consulted and direction will be provided.
In most cases, legal counsel for the member of the public will be asked to put their questions in writing.

heading: 4.3 Communication and partnering activities
text:
The Compliance and Enforcement Division (C&E) handles delivery of the compliance and enforcement program
in the regulation of both the liquor and cannabis industries. In fulfilling its statutory duties, the C&E Division
looks to support positive relationships with licensees and other stakeholders, including police, local government,
Indigenous Nations, and other regulatory agencies.

Close liaison with police forces is integral to the Compliance and Enforcement Program. Police forces throughout
the province take part in a walk-through program called Licence Premises Checks (LPC) consisting of regular,
unannounced visits to licensed establishments. The police LPC program plays a significant role in preventing
contraventions and promoting a greater awareness of the laws that licensees, staff, and patrons must follow.

Local government and Indigenous Nations have a direct role in the licensing processes for liquor and non-medical
cannabis and have an interest in ensuring that the regulations are followed, and the licensed establishments and
retail stores enjoy the support of the communities in which they are located. Local government is responsible for
protecting the peace and good order of communities and is often the first to receive complaints if problems arise
with the operation of a licensed establishment, special event, or retail store.

Ongoing communication with licensees ensures they are equipped with the knowledge needed for voluntary
compliance with the legislation, regulation and terms and conditions of their licences.

heading: 4.3 Communication and partnering activities
text:
Good communications and
working relationships with police, local governments and other regulatory agencies ensures these stakeholders are
knowledgeable about the laws and policies and promotes cooperation in addressing issues of non-compliance.

Inspectors are responsible for:
• establishing and supporting positive relationships with licensees, management, and employees of licensed
establishments,

• providing advice and guidance on how the licensee may best follow the legislation and regulatory framework
and minimize enforcement action,
• fostering awareness and educating the public industry and industry associations, local governments, police
and other enforcement agencies and stakeholders on the administration of the respective Acts and
regulations,
• delivering education and training seminars and briefings, and
• acting as an expert resource to local government committee meetings, task forces and advisory councils on
the administration of the LCLA and CCLA and respective regulations.
Leading or taking part in multi-agency inspections as prescribed at “Conduct of a Multi-Agency Inspection,” is an
effective tool in program delivery through the conduct of overt public safety inspections in cooperation with local
police and other regulatory agencies.
Stakeholder liaison sessions, such as licensee meetings or industry association meetings, provide the branch with
an opportunity to educate both the liquor and non-medical cannabis retail industries, licensees and their staff on
laws and policies and to build stakeholder relationships.

heading: 4.6 Definition of stakeholder liaison session
text:
A stakeholder liaison session is attended by an inspector following these criteria:
• attendees include licensees and/or their employees, or stakeholder groups, such as Barwatch, Committee to
Approve Public Event (CAPE) or Outdoor Event Committee (OEC), that may include licensees and/or their
employees as members, and
• the inspector’s attendance is predicated on the discussion of issues regarding compliance with liquor and/or
cannabis laws and licence terms and conditions.
The content of all presentations must be provided to the inspector’s regional manager in advance of the
presentation for the regional manager to obtain branch approval of the presentation.

heading: 4.8 Briefing and training sessions
text:
Briefing and training sessions with agencies such as police (i.e.: Police Roll Call), local governments or First
Nations allow inspectors to develop working relationships with staff from other regulatory and law enforcement
agencies within their areas of jurisdiction. They also provide inspectors with an opportunity to share information
on liquor and/or cannabis laws and policies, branch priorities, operational issues, or areas of concern.
Inspectors will pursue opportunities to organize, host, and take part in briefing and training sessions with other
agencies within their areas of responsibility.
The content of all presentations must be provided to the inspector’s regional manager in advance of the
presentation for the regional manager to obtain branch approval of the presentation.

heading: 4.11 Role of the licensee
text:
Licensee responsibilities are specified within both Acts and their respective regulations and as outlined in the
Terms and Conditions Handbook for the type of licence held. Each licensee is responsible for understanding and
complying with the LCLA or CCLA, as well as regulations and terms and conditions of their licence as
applicable.

Licensees are liable for contraventions committed by their employees. Licensees must ensure that their
employees follow the LCLA or CCLA, respective regulations and licence terms and conditions as applicable,
even when the licensee is not on site. Licensees must cooperate with inspectors and police officers when they
inspect their establishments.

heading: 5.0 Introduction
text:
Policies and procedures for final licence inspection activities are described in this section under the following
headings:
• Conduct of Final Licence Inspections

General:
The general manager will issue an “Approval in Principle” (AIP) letter and floor plans to an applicant for all
licences issued under the LCLA or the CCLA.

At the time of the final licence inspection, the new licence applicant has met all the requirements for licensing.
The inspector conducts the final licence inspection to ensure that the applicant has realized, in practice, the
commitments made on paper. The final licence inspection offers an opportunity to discuss the practicalities of
meeting the terms and conditions of the licence. It is at this stage that the inspector establishes a relationship with
the new licensee.

Where the situation or practicality exists, the inspector may review the terms and conditions of the licence with
the applicant during the final licence inspection.

heading: 5.0 Introduction
text:
At minimum, the inspector will ensure the applicant is aware of
the Branch web page link, and that the applicant understands their responsibility to understand and follow the
terms and conditions of their licence.

Final licence inspection - transfers, third party operators, re-location:
The final licence inspection takes place once per establishment at or about the time of new licence issuance.
Inspectors at their discretion may conduct a routine inspection of an establishment where the licence has recently
been transferred, where there has been a change in the third-party agreement, or the licence has been re-located.

Final licence inspection not satisfactory:
If the results of the final licence inspection for a new licence are not satisfactory, the inspector informs the
applicant of the deficiencies and advises the applicant to re-contact the inspector for another final licence
inspection once the deficiencies have been remedied.

heading: 5.1 Conduct of final licence inspections
text:
Procedure:
In all cases of the conduct of a final licence inspection, the inspector will:
1. inspect the establishment to ensure that it has been constructed in accordance with the AIP letter and all other
statutory and policy requirements,
• confirm with the applicant requirements that must be met by the licensee for both routine and public safety
inspections,
• take photographs of the establishment to show the interior design of the establishment and exterior signs,
2. confirm the floor plans/site plans for the establishment/facility are consistent with the AIP floor plan/site
plan, and
3. upload photos to branch database in accordance with branch policy on records management.

heading: 5.2 Scheduling and planning for final licence inspections
text:
Procedure:
Upon issuance of the “Approval in Principle” (AIP) letter and floor plans/site plans to an applicant for a licence
under the LCLA or the CCLA:
• The inspector may contact or be contacted by the applicant to schedule a final licence inspection of the
establishment (except where the inspector decides that an on-site inspection is not necessary, such as for a
final inspection that would only include an education component),

• Once the inspector has confirmed the applicant is ready for the final inspection, a specific date can be set and
that the applicant is present for the final inspection,
• The inspector will obtain and review the following information prior to attending the final licence inspection:
- Approval in Principle letter,
- Approval in Principle floor plans/site plans,
- Proposed signage,
- Licence specific terms and conditions,
- Terms and Conditions Handbook, and
- ID Stickers and Social Responsibility Materials
Procedure:
Will be conducted in accordance with “Conduct of final licence inspections” and “Scheduling and planning for
final licence inspections.”
Procedure:
Will be conducted in accordance with “Conduct of final licence inspections” and “Scheduling and planning for
final licence inspections.”

heading: 5.5 Final licence inspection for a liquor manufacturer licence
text:
Note: Each manufacturing licence (winery, brewery, and distillery) has its own distinctions. Once the application
has reached the Approval in Principle (AIP) the inspector should:
• contact the applicant to ensure they are ready for a final licence inspection. At this time, the inspector can
determine which jobs will require a final inspection and an approximate timeline for any endorsement finals.
It is common for a manufacturer to ask for an inspection of the manufacturing area only so they can begin
producing product,
• advise the applicant what is expected of them to be ready for the final inspection,
• should the applicant indicate they are ready for the final inspection, the inspector may ask the applicant to
send photos of the manufacturing area and equipment for confirmation.

Procedure:
Will be conducted in accordance with Section 5.1 - “Conduct of final licence inspections” and Section 5.2 -
“Scheduling and planning for final licence inspections,” as well as the final licence inspection checklist:

heading: MANUFACTURER FINAL LICENCE INSPECTION
text:
PROCEDURES CHECKLIST

The purpose of this document is to provide inspectors with a guide to the minimum final
licence inspection requirements for a manufacturer.

Upon receipt of notification of the Approval in Principle (AIP) letter, the inspector will

heading: 5.10 Final licence inspection for a catering licence or endorsement
text:
Procedure:
Upon licensing of a catering licence applicant or an endorsement on an existing FP or LP licence, the inspector
will, as soon as practical, conduct a final licence inspection of the establishment to ensure compliance with all
regulatory requirements. At the time of the inspection is the optimal opportunity for the inspector to review the
terms and conditions of the catering licence or endorsement with the applicant (where practical) and ensure that
the business location meets the requirements of a catering licence by verifying the following eligibility
requirements:
• primarily in the business of preparing and serving food, and
• personnel and infrastructure are adequate to prepare and serve food at events hosted by others, and
• any other requirements as specified in the AIP letter.

heading: 5.11 Reviewing person capacity and occupant load during final licence inspection
text:
Procedure:
After considering occupant load, local government/First Nations input and other considerations, the general
manager may establish the approved person capacity as equal to or less than the occupant load, but not higher
than the occupant load. Where a final inspection is required, the inspector will confirm the approved person
capacity as shown in the issued AIP letter and ensure the licensee understands their person capacity as shown in
the AIP letter, and the consequences if they exceed person capacity or occupant load.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.72 and s.73]

heading: 5.12 Licence inspection for a structural alteration
text:
General:
Where the completed alterations are consistent with the AIP plan, the inspector shall take photographs of the
structural alterations and will upload the photos following branch policy on records management.

If the inspection is for a structural alteration to an existing establishment, the inspector will inspect the
establishment to ensure that the structural alterations have been constructed following any approved plans and
with all statutory and policy requirements.

If the results of the inspection are not satisfactory, the inspector will inform the licensee of the deficiencies and
inform the licensee to contact the inspector for another inspection once the deficiencies have been remedied.

heading: 5.13 Recording the final licence inspection for a LCLA licence
