heading: 6.66 Minor Agent appearance, conduct and protocols
text:
• Minor agents must possess valid identification. During MAP inspections, the agent’s identification will
be secured in the government vehicle.
• Minor agents must wear safe and environmentally appropriate footwear.
• MAP inspections may include more than 1 minor agent.
• MAP inspections may include police officers who accompany the minor agent(s) to the point of sale.
• Inspectors or police officers are to enter and sit or locate themselves in the establishment separately from
the minor agent but within adequate observation distance from the minor agent during the attempted
liquor or cannabis purchase to observe the attempted purchase.
• MAP inspections may mirror the conduct and manner of youth culture, e.g.: smart phones, headwear,
tattoos, youthful attire, sunglasses, etc. are permitted where this is the normal attire as presented by the
minor agent. Overt, planned or designed attempts to obscure or distract a server or clerk, such as dressing
up, costuming, or decorating minor agents, is not permitted.
• Inspectors are not permitted to direct minor agents how to dress, how to speak, or what to purchase.
Multi-agency inspections are an opportunity for enforcement personnel from a number of regulatory agencies to
work cooperatively to address issues of non-compliance in licensed establishments.
Inspectors will pursue opportunities to organize and/or participate in multi-agency inspection teams within their
areas of responsibility.

heading: 6.69 Role of the lead inspector in a Multi-Agency inspection team
text:
Each multi-agency inspection team that the branch is participating in will include a lead inspector and may
include any number of additional inspectors. The lead inspector will be responsible for liaising with the other
members of the team, assigning inspector roles and conducting any follow-up activities resulting from the multi-
agency inspection, for example, issuing Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance and recommending
enforcement action.
If the branch is organizing a multi-agency inspection team, the lead inspector will consider whether the team
should include representatives from:
• police,
• municipal by-law enforcement,
• public health,
• fire department, and
• other regulatory agencies such as Security Programs Division and Community Safety Unit.

heading: 6.71 Conduct of an outside licensed hours inspection
text:
There may be occasions where inspectors identify an establishment that continues to serve liquor after hours of
liquor service has ended and/or after which the establishment’s authorized hours of operation have ended, and
which may include staff and/or patrons consuming liquor in the establishment. In addition, and although less
frequent, there may be occasions where a licensee may sell or serve liquor prior to the start of their licensed
hours of liquor service.

The sale or service of liquor outside the licensed hours of liquor service negatively impacts efforts to ensure
responsible liquor consumption; support for community standards and risks the safety of the public especially
where it occurs after hours and where patrons have already been consuming liquor before end of liquor service
hours.

Where an inspector has reason to believe the consumption of liquor is continuing outside of the hours of liquor
service, the inspector should conduct an “Outside Licensed Hours” inspection in accordance with the procedures
detailed below.

Procedure:
1. Before entering the establishment, the inspector will conduct a site risk assessment to determine if it is safe
to conduct the inspection. The procedure for conducting a site risk assessment is specified within the C&E
Inspector Safety Manual. Where possible, the inspector should enlist the assistance of other inspectors or
police when conducting the inspection.

heading: 6.71 Conduct of an outside licensed hours inspection
text:
Where the inspector is working alone and has determined it may be
a risk to enter the establishment, the inspector may try and gather evidence of the continued operation of the
establishment through surveillance,
2. Prior to entering the establishment, the inspector will note the time and enter the establishment,
3. The inspector will make an initial observation of the establishment, including:
• the number of staff/patrons and their behaviour, and
• if liquor is being sold, served, or consumed,
4. If appropriate, the inspector will advise the licensee of the inspection,
33. If appropriate, the inspector will question the licensee on any previous concerns and what follow-up action
has been taken,
34. The inspector will make a critical observation of the patrons, entertainers, staff, and physical condition of
the establishment as the inspector moves through the establishment. Items that the inspector should be alert
to during the inspection include:
• confirming the time with staff or licensee and/or another inspector,
• patrons consuming liquor,
• liquor being sold,

• patrons within service area,
• presence of minors,
• unlawful activities,
• disorderly or riotous conduct,
• intoxicated persons,
• presence of weapons,
• overcrowding,
• in the case of a food primary whether the establishment is operating in a manner outside of licence
purpose,
• unauthorized games or entertainment,
• licensee, management, or staff consumption of liquor,
• liquor in unauthorized areas, and
• liquor promotions, contests or advertising that promotes or is likely to promote intoxication,
5.

heading: 6.71 Conduct of an outside licensed hours inspection
text:
The inspector may conduct a formal count of the number of patrons using a mechanical counter to ensure
the establishment is within the approved capacity,
6. The inspector may check identification of patrons to ensure patrons being served liquor are 19 years of age
or older. He/she may request that a staff member request the identification from patrons as necessary, and
7. If a staff member is found consuming, he/she should be addressed if safe to do so. The inspector should
speak to them to determine if it is liquor in their possession and if they are exhibiting signs of intoxication.
Additionally, if the inspector is in a position to seize the liquor container, he/she should do so.

heading: 7.0 Introduction
text:
Inspectors have a variety of compliance strategies other than inspections at their disposal in order to achieve
voluntary compliance. Strategies with an educational focus during final licence inspections where the inspector
may provide an education session, as well as stakeholder liaison sessions as discussed in section 4 “Program
Overview”.

Procedures for these compliance strategies are presented in this section under the following headings:
• Licence Suspensions and Catering Authorization Cancellations,
• Temporary Suspensions or Terms and Conditions up to 14 days,
• Compliance Meetings, and
• Other Compliance Strategies.

heading: 7.1 Licence and catering authorization suspensions/cancellations
text:
In the interests of public safety, the general manager has the power under section 48 of the LCLA and Section
36 of the CCLA to take immediate action and temporarily close an establishment or suspend or cancel a catering
authorization where patron or employee conduct is riotous, violent, drunken or disorderly, and/or the safety of
any persons is threatened. The general manager has delegated this power to police, inspectors, regional
supervisors, regional managers, Director C&E Operations and the DGM Compliance and Enforcement. The
decision to temporarily close a licensed establishment or suspend or cancel a catering authorization pursuant to
this power is a serious one and will only be taken if the local police are in attendance to ensure the safety of
patrons, employees and adjacent residents and businesses.

heading: 7.2 Authority to impose a 24-hour suspension
text:
An inspector, peace officer, or other person delegated by the general manager may suspend a licence or suspend
or cancel a catering authorization and order the immediate removal of patrons and closure of establishment in
which:
• patrons or employees are engaging in riotous, violent, drunken, or disorderly conduct, or
• the safety of one or more persons at the licensed establishment is threatened.

The suspension and closure of the establishment or the suspension or cancellation of a catering authorization
may take effect without a hearing and may be for a period of not more than 24 hours.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.48]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.36]
If a licensed establishment or catered event is required to be vacated, the licensee must take all reasonable steps
to ensure that the licensed establishment is immediately vacated and closed.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.48]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.36(4)]

heading: 7.4 Factors to consider before suspending the licence or the catering authorization
text:
In determining whether to suspend the licence or suspend or cancel the catering authorization and order the
removal of patrons, the inspector will consider the following factors:
• the number of patrons or employees engaged in the riotous, violent, drunken, or disorderly conduct,
• the risk of immediate harm to members of the public due to the patron or employee conduct, including
members of the public within the licensed establishment and adjacent residents or businesses,
• the risk of immediate harm to employees due to the patron or employee conduct,
• the actions and ability of the licensee and employees to regain management of conduct in the establishment,

• the availability of police support, and
• whether the safety of patrons and employees can be assured without ordering a suspension of the licence
and evacuation of the establishment.

heading: 7.5 Police presence before imposing a licence suspension or catering authorization
text:
Note: An inspector will not take enforcement action pursuant to these sections of the legislations unless the
police are in attendance at the licensed establishment.

Procedure:
1. The inspector will consider the factors outlined in “Factors to consider before suspending the licence or
the catering authorization” and determine whether or not to suspend the licence or suspend or cancel the
catering authorization and order the immediate removal of patrons and closure of the licensed
establishment. An example of when the suspension of a catering authorization could be considered instead
of a cancellation would be for multi-day events where a suspension is considered for part of the event (i.e.:
one day), not the entire event’s duration,
2. If the inspector decides it is necessary to suspend the licence or suspend or cancel the catering authorization
and order the immediate removal of patrons, the inspector will contact the local police and ask for their
attendance at the licensed establishment. The inspector will not take any further action to suspend the
licence or suspend or cancel the catering authorization until the police are in attendance,
2. If the inspector believes the establishment may be overcrowded, the inspector will arrange for a police
officer or compliance and enforcement inspector to be in attendance at all exits and to count the number of
patrons as they exit,
3. If applicable, the inspector will determine the period for which the licence should be suspended, to a
maximum of 24 hours.

heading: 7.5 Police presence before imposing a licence suspension or catering authorization
text:
Catering authorizations can also be suspended by inspectors but without a maximum
suspension time period (i.e.: 24 hours),
4. The inspector will inform the licensee or manager on duty:
• that the licence is being suspended or the catering authorization is being suspended or cancelled under
the authority of section 48 of the LCLA or 36 of the CCLA,
• if applicable, the time period for the suspension, and
• that the establishment must be vacated.
3. The inspector will collect evidence in accordance with the policies and procedures outlined in this manual
for the specific contravention(s) identified. Generally, the inspector will interview the licensee and may
obtain any relevant evidence or information before leaving the establishment,
5. The inspector will fully document:
• the factors which led the inspector to determine that a suspension of the licence or suspension or
cancellation of the catering authorization was required,
• the terms and length of the suspension or cancellation,
• the comments and actions of the licensee when informed of the suspension or cancellation, and
• the identity of the police officers in attendance,
6. The inspector will ask that the police officers forward a copy of their notes and/or the relevant general
occurrence report to the inspector,
7. The inspector will transcribe into the branch database the information recorded in the inspector's notebook
for the inspection, and
10. As soon as possible after the event, the inspector will inform the regional manager of the suspension or
cancellation.

heading: 7.6 Suspensions or terms and conditions up to 14 days
text:
1. Under section 48 of the LCLA and 36 of the CCLA the general manager, on having reasonable and
probable grounds to believe that it is in the public interest because of extraordinary circumstances may,
suspend a licence or catering authorization or impose terms and conditions for a period not exceeding 14
days, without a hearing. This decision should be made in the interest of public safety.

2. This authority is available to address extraordinary circumstances where a 24-hour suspension is not
adequate to ensure safety or protect the public interest. Some examples are when there has been violence or
extensive criminal activity, there is the risk of retaliatory gang violence, or a possibility of public unrest
(i.e., during or after a community event). In such circumstances, a longer licence or catering authorization
suspension may be needed to provide sufficient time for the branch to assess the situation and determine
what is needed to eliminate the safety risks and rectify the situation.

Authority to make decision:
This authority has not been delegated, and the exercise of this power is the sole prerogative of the general
manager.

Written Notice:
The general manager must provide the licensee with written notice of the suspension or the imposition of terms
and conditions under these sections. The notice must include the reasons for taking the action as well as the
details of the action including, if a suspension is imposed, the period of the suspension and the dates of the
suspension.

Procedure:
1.

heading: 7.6 Suspensions or terms and conditions up to 14 days
text:
Compliance staff who believe that circumstances warrant a suspension or terms and conditions under section
49 of the LCLA or 36 of the CCLA, should promptly contact a supervisor (usually the regional manager
and/or deputy general manager) to discuss,
2. If the supervisor agrees that circumstances warrant a suspension or terms and conditions under this section,
the general manager will promptly be provided with details of the circumstances of concern,
3. Any decision to impose a suspension or terms and conditions under this section will be in writing and must
be signed by the general manager or deputy general manager as delegated,
4. The written notice must contain the reasons for taking the action, the details and the dates for the suspension
or terms and conditions, and
5. If either personal delivery of the written notice or attendance at the establishment is required, compliance
staff must, with their supervisor or deputy general manager, plan how to do so safely.

heading: 7.7 Compliance Meeting
text:
Compliance meetings are an important part of the Compliance and Enforcement Program and in particular a key
step in the efforts to achieve voluntary compliance through the branch’s progressive compliance and
enforcement strategy. The compliance meeting is conducted only after issuing an Electronic Notification of
Non-Compliance where the inspector has determined on a balance of probabilities that there is sufficient
evidence to prove the elements of a contravention and where the inspector is not recommending enforcement
action.

Compliance meetings are not, however, a required step prior to an inspector recommending an enforcement
action. However, compliance meetings are not to be used as a substitute to enforcement action where such
enforcement action is warranted. Through ongoing branch communication activities, the licensee is provided
with all relevant information prior to and during holding a licence and as such, is otherwise deemed to know and
understand their responsibilities as the licensee.

heading: 7.8 Purpose of the compliance meeting
text:
The purpose of the compliance meeting is to discuss an alleged contravention for which a Electronic
Notification of Non-Compliance has been issued and to assist the licensee and their employees in understanding
that the inspector has determined on the balance of probabilities that there is sufficient evidence to prove the
elements of a contravention and what steps can be taken to anticipate future or repetitive problems and to
identify and implement solutions. It is an opportunity for the inspector to:
• bring concerns to the licensee’s attention,
• discuss circumstances surrounding the alleged contravention,

• educate the licensee on the related provisions of the legislation and/or terms and conditions,
• notify the licensee of the related penalty provisions, and
• obtain commitments from the licensee on how they will ensure future voluntary compliance.

heading: 7.9 Compliance meeting not enforcement action or compliance history
text:
Sections 51(3)(a) of the LCLA and section 38(4)(a) of the CCLA establishes that the general manager must
consider the licensee’s compliance history when taking action against a licensee. The compliance meeting is an
internal strategy used by the branch as part of the branch’s C&E progressive compliance program delivery
methodology. Compliance meetings are not legislated and are not deemed enforcement action, nor do they form
part of the licensee’s compliance history. However, compliance meeting reports may be included under section
H “Other Relevant Factors” within the NOEA, for the purpose of consideration when recommending
enforcement action.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.51(3)(a)]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.38(4)(a)]
[LCRB policy]

heading: 7.10 Convening a compliance meeting
text:
The compliance meeting is held at the discretion of the branch. An inspector may convene a compliance meeting
with a licensee:
• on their own initiative, or
• at the request of a regional manager, provincial director C&E operations, deputy general manager or
general manager.

When determining whether to convene a compliance meeting the inspector may consider:
• the alleged contravention,
• previous compliance meetings,
• whether the licensee is a new licensee,
• whether the establishment is a new establishment,
• whether the licensee has been issued an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance in the previous 24
months, and
• whether the licensee has been subject to enforcement action in the previous 24 months.

Where an inspector convenes a compliance meeting, the licensee must be informed of the reasons for the
compliance meeting.

heading: 7.11 Compliance meeting not to be undertaken
text:
Compliance meetings are not to be undertaken for any purpose other than to bring to the attention of the licensee
where there is sufficient evidence to establish that on the balance of probabilities a contravention has occurred
and to inform the licensee how to achieve voluntary compliance and the possible consequences where
compliance is not achieved. If a compliance meeting is held on an alleged contravention where there is not
enough evidence available to satisfy the elements, the record of the compliance meeting would be
administratively unfair to the licensee.

Where a licensee otherwise wishes to discuss methods or measures to achieve voluntary compliance, or where
the inspector wishes to discuss an allegation where there is not sufficient evidence to prove a contravention has
occurred, the inspector may hold a “Licensee Meeting” with the licensee. Licensee meetings with licensees and
their staff that are only educational in nature are addressed under “Stakeholder liaison sessions.”

Compliance meetings are not to be undertaken:
• where enforcement action is being recommended on an alleged contravention, a compliance meeting may
be held for any contravention where enforcement action is not being recommended)
• after a penalty has been imposed by a delegate to the general manager,

• where a waiver has been signed by the licensee, or
• where an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance has not been issued.

heading: 7.12 Attendees at a compliance meeting
text:
In addition to the inspector and the licensee, attendees at the compliance meeting may include any or all of:
• the establishment manager,
• key staff from the establishment such as the Licensee Representative with the authority to make decisions
on behalf of the licensee regarding specific issues related to the compliance meeting,
• a police officer familiar with the establishment,
• the responsible regional manager,
• another inspector familiar with or involved with an inspection of the establishment,
• another inspector and regional supervisor for operations and training purposes of new inspectors,
• a local government representative, and/or
• a fire department representative.

heading: 7.13 Meeting not a requirement before taking enforcement action
text:
The compliance meeting is to be convened only as a result of the issuance of an Electronic Notification of Non-
Compliance. The compliance meeting is not to occur where the inspector is proceeding with a recommendation
for enforcement action as a result of determining a contravention has occurred where enforcement action is
warranted. Where an inspector convenes a compliance meeting the licensee must be informed in writing of the
reasons for the compliance meeting.

Should the licensee fail or refuse to attend a compliance meeting, the inspector may attempt to re-convene the
meeting including advising the licensee of the seriousness of the meeting and the expectation of the branch that
the licensee attend. Where a licensee does not attend a compliance meeting or re-scheduled meeting, the
inspector may proceed with a recommendation for enforcement action where warranted.

heading: 7.14 Scheduling, planning, conducting, and recording a compliance meeting
text:
Procedure:
1. Scheduling and planning for a compliance meeting:
1. In consultation with the licensee, the inspector will set the time and place for the meeting,
2. The inspector will determine whether any LCRB participants may attend the compliance meeting, and
3. The inspector will inform the licensee and any LCRB invited participants of the time, date, location, and
agenda for the compliance meeting. The inspector will provide the meeting agenda to the licensee as
established below in procedure # 2 “Conducting the compliance meeting”.
4. It is the responsibility of the licensee to inform any persons they wish to attend the meeting.

Note: Where possible it is preferred that compliance meetings be held at a location other than the licensee’s
establishment (i.e.: government boardroom, police interview room). Where necessary a compliance
meeting may be held remotely through use of remote meeting technology (Microsoft Teams, etc.).

2. Conducting the compliance meeting:
The inspector will conduct the compliance meeting based on the below pre-determined agenda.

heading: 7.14 Scheduling, planning, conducting, and recording a compliance meeting
text:
The agenda is to
include:
• Licensee acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of the alleged contravention,
• Inspector will provide the licensee information about the circumstances surrounding the alleged
contravention referenced in the reason for the meeting,
• The inspector will review the applicable section(s) of the Act, regulation(s), or Terms and Conditions
with the licensee,
• The inspector will discuss the consequences of non-compliance in the future including the related
penalty provisions,
• Licensee acknowledgment they understand their responsibility and the commitment to voluntary
compliance.

3. Documenting the compliance meeting:
• The inspector will document the details of the compliance meeting using the compliance meeting record
format as established within the branch database,
• During the compliance meeting, the inspector will record those items that have been reviewed and make
notes on the compliance meeting format or within the inspector’s notebook as necessary,
5. If the licensee makes any contributions during the meeting, the inspector will record these contributions
on the compliance meeting format or within the inspector’s notebook.

Note: there is no requirement for a licensee to sign any document acknowledging the meeting or the
discussion.

4.

heading: 7.14 Scheduling, planning, conducting, and recording a compliance meeting
text:
Recording and distributing the compliance meeting form:
• No more than 5 days after the compliance meeting, the inspector will provide the licensee with a
database generated electronic copy of the completed compliance meeting record, and
• The inspector will save the completed compliance meeting record into the branch database as per

7.15 - 7.17 Licensee Meeting/Education Sessions – No longer part of the inspection process
Inspectors will work cooperatively with other regulatory agencies to address compliance problems. Inspectors
may report instances of non-compliance with other regulatory requirements to the appropriate agency.

Procedure:
Inspectors will prepare a written report of any instances of alleged non-compliance with other regulatory
requirements and forward to the responsible agency.

heading: 7.19 Using additional terms and conditions to increase compliance
text:
Under section 15 of the LCLA, the general manager has the authority to “impose, in the public interest, terms
and conditions (a) that vary the terms and conditions to which the licence is subject under the regulations, or (b)
that are in addition to those referred to in paragraph (a)”. Section 16 of the LCLA also gives the general
manager the authority to impose, rescind or amend terms and conditions on a licence “with or without a
hearing”.

Section 26 of the LCLA also states: “the general manager may, in respect of a catering authorization, impose
terms and conditions that vary or are in addition to the terms and conditions to which the catering authorization
is subject under the regulations”.

Section 31 of the LCLA gives the general manager the authority to impose terms and conditions on special event
permits and section 34 of the LCLA authorizes the general manager to impose, rescind or amend terms and
conditions on a permit.

Under Section 30 of the CCLA, the general manager may impose terms and conditions and may suspend,
rescind, or amend terms and conditions for a class of licensees or establishments without prior notice.

Under Section 31 of the CCLA, the general manager may impose terms and conditions and may suspend,
rescind, or amend terms and conditions for a specific licensee or licensees with prior written notice.

Under Section 32 of the CCLA the general manager may impose terms and conditions respecting all matters
related to the sale, supply, production, packaging, purchase, and consumption of cannabis under a licence and to
the operation of an establishm

heading: 7.19 Using additional terms and conditions to increase compliance
text:
ent.

All licences, including liquor and non-medical cannabis are subject to a general set of terms and conditions as
specified in the relevant Licensee Term and Conditions Handbooks but some establishments may be identified
as having particular characteristics or operating environment that warrant additional terms and conditions being
applied to their licence.

There are a number of circumstances including as a result of enforcement action where it may be appropriate for
an inspector to recommend the use of additional terms and conditions to achieve voluntary compliance.

When planning to make use of additional terms and conditions to achieve compliance, the inspector will involve
their regional manager in the process as early as possible. The regional manager must approve any additional
terms or conditions recommended as part of enforcement action and where the addition of a term or condition to
a licence has been encouraged or required. The following outlines the various situations where inspectors are
encouraged to consider how additional terms or conditions might be used to ensure compliance:

Procedure:
1. Impose additional term and condition on a new licence:
Should the general manager determine that it is appropriate to place additional terms or conditions on a
licence, the applicant or licensee must be informed as early in the process as possible and given time to
respond. Inspectors may consider any potential additional terms or conditions that may be appropriate to be
placed on a licence during the initial site visit or as a result of a routine inspection.

heading: 7.19 Using additional terms and conditions to increase compliance
text:
The additional term or
condition and licensee response must form part of the licence decision.
2. Impose additional terms or conditions on licence transfer:
Terms or conditions imposed as a result of a licence transfer are similar to those that might be imposed on a
new licence. Again, specific characteristics or risks associated with an establishment, or concerns with the
new licensee may make additional terms or conditions necessary. The history of an establishment will also
impact what additional terms or conditions might be added.

As with a new licence, should the licensing manager decide to add terms or conditions to the licence that
are over and above those terms and conditions as specified in the Licensee Terms and Conditions
Handbook licensing staff must inform the applicant as early in the process as possible and given time to
respond. Again, the inspector should engage with the licensing manager as soon as possible in the process.
The term and/or condition and licensee response must form part of the licence record.
3. Discuss possibility of adding term or condition during compliance meeting:
In some cases, an inspector will hold a compliance meeting with a licensee to discuss problems associated
with their establishment, but the inspector is not intending to pursue enforcement action.

heading: 7.19 Using additional terms and conditions to increase compliance
text:
In such a case, the
inspector could discuss with a licensee what they might do to avoid non-compliance or problems in the
future.

Any discussion with the licensee that results in the adding of a voluntary term or condition to the licence must
be documented on the compliance meeting form and entered into the branch database on the establishment
licence file. The Inspector will discuss the terms and/or conditions being added with the regional manager and
contact the branch’s licensing division to have the term or condition added to the licence document. A new
licence document would then be issued to the licensee stating the term or condition. The compliance meeting
record could be introduced in an enforcement hearing if future related contraventions do result in enforcement
action against the licensee.
Inspectors could take into consideration what additional terms or conditions may prevent problems with a
licensee in the future whenever they take enforcement action. Additional terms or conditions could be
recommended in addition to monetary or suspension penalties, where appropriate.

heading: 7.21 Recommended additional terms and conditions must correlate with the contravention
text:
• Additional terms or conditions applied to a licence also have the option of being applied temporarily,
contingent on the licensee remaining compliant.
• Inspectors must not discuss the removal of existing terms or conditions with a licensee without seeking
direction first from the deputy general manager of compliance and enforcement through the regional
manager.

The table at “Suggested additional terms and conditions” outlines some suggested additional terms and
conditions that may be effective for addressing some compliance issues. The suggested additional terms and
conditions are not an exhaustive list, and inspectors are encouraged to think about the specific situation they are
dealing with and how to best address it through the use of additional terms and conditions.

heading: 7.22 Impose additional term and condition on a special event permit
text:
Additional terms or conditions may be imposed on a special event permit for events that require inspector
review. Concerns with a permittee, risks associated with an event venue, or specific characteristics of an event
may make additional terms and/or conditions necessary. The history of a permittee or event will also impact
what additional terms and/or conditions might be added.

Inspectors may impose additional terms and/or conditions on a special event permit to address a specific
risk. Where an inspector wishes to impose a term and condition on a special event, the inspector will follow the
procedures established at “Procedure for adding a term and condition on a special event permit.”

Once an additional term and/or condition is imposed, inspectors must inform the permittee of the additional term
and/or condition as early as possible in order for the permittee to have time to respond or implement measures to
address the risk.

heading: 7.23 Procedure for adding a term and condition on a special event permit
text:
Procedure:
1. Where an inspector considers it necessary to add a term and condition to a special event permit, the inspector
will make the request through their regional supervisor with sufficient lead-time to ensure that where a term
and condition is approved and added to a special event permit, and affords the permittee a minimum of 2
working days to both implement the term and condition as well as print the new permit,
2. The regional supervisor will ensure the proposed term and condition is:
• within the liquor and cannabis inspector’s role and authority at the special event (i.e.: liquor service
requirements),
• the proposed term or condition is not a duplicate of a term and condition that already is established within
the Terms and Conditions Handbook for a Special Event Permit, and
• the term and condition is not proposed at the request of a stakeholder (police or local government who are
able to request terms and conditions via their on-line portal access.),
4. Additional terms and conditions should not be recommended to be added to the special event permit unless
there were previous compliance issues and have been discussed with and approved by the regional
supervisor,
5. The inspector (with regional supervisor approval) will add the term and condition to the permit and will be
responsible to notify the permittee, and
6.

heading: 7.23 Procedure for adding a term and condition on a special event permit
text:
The regional supervisor will update a spreadsheet on the I Drive of the approved terms and conditions that
are added to permits for tracking of term and condition approvals.

Note: Where the Client Support Team (Licensing) adds a term and condition for a stakeholder (police etc.),
they will email the regional supervisor who will then determine if the inspector will need to be notified. The
regional supervisor will then update the approved term and condition spreadsheet.

heading: 7.24 Requiring all catering events be approval events
text:
The LCRB may require all events from certain caterers be approval events. There are a number of circumstances
where it may be appropriate for an inspector to have all of a licensee’s submitted events require approval. The
licensee, business location, or associated establishments may be identified as being potentially higher risk, or the
caterer may have a compliance history that warrants this action.

When planning to make use of this approval event requirement to achieve compliance, the inspector will involve
their regional manager in the process as early as possible.

PRODUCTION OF RECORDS

heading: 8.0 Introduction
text:
Evidence is testimony, writing, material objects or other things that are offered to prove the existence or non-
existence of a fact. Inspectors may gather several types of evidence relating to contraventions, including:
• the inspector’s own observations,
• information from third parties, such as police or other regulatory agencies,
• samples,
• purchase records and other documents,
• security videos and other things, and
• statements of witnesses.

This section outlines general policies and procedures for gathering and handling various types of evidence and is
organized under the following headings:
• Recording Observations,
• Inspector Recorded Media,
• Complaints from Other Agencies and the Public, and
• Interviewing Licensees, Staff and Witnesses.

heading: 8.1 Recording observations
text:
Inspectors may gather and receive considerable amounts of information during the course of an investigation. If
observations are not recorded, they may be forgotten. An inspector’s observations recorded in notes, photographs
or sketches may be referred to when preparing reports and during enforcement hearings. Unrecorded observations
do not become part of the establishment file. In the event that an inspector is unavailable or no longer working for
the branch, essential information may be lost.

heading: 8.2 Documenting and recording observations
text:
Subject to sub-section 8.1, an inspector’s observations regarding an alleged contravention will be documented or
recorded either in the branch issued inspector’s notebook or through an electronic means and transcribed into the
branch database as per established policy and timelines. Observations will be recorded at the time an alleged
contravention is identified or as soon afterwards as is practical.

heading: 8.3 Use of notebooks during inspections
text:
If an inspector is attempting to observe the operation of an establishment undetected, the inspector may choose
not to record observations in the inspector’s notebook. Other options may include recording observations
electronically on the inspectors’ branch issued iPhone. If notes are made in a notebook, as soon as practical, the
inspector will transcribe the notes into the branch database.
Inspectors will retain their notebooks.

Procedure:
4. Where a notebook is used, an inspector will use only one notebook at a time. Inspectors will file completed
notebooks as branch records, and
1. Where a notebook is used, inspectors will clearly record all observations relating to a contravention in their
notebooks, including:
• time, date, day of the week,
• licence name and number,
• the nature and details of the contravention,
• complete and correct - names, addresses and telephone numbers of staff and witnesses,
• details of any evidence found, including who found it, where it was found, how it was marked and how
it was disposed of,

• sketches or diagrams, if required,
• details of any conversations with the licensee, staff, or witnesses,
• details of any photographs taken, and
• the number of any Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance issued.

Note: The collection or recording of any information, records or evidence via an iPhone that would otherwise be
collected by an inspector writing into a notebook, will only be accomplished using BC Government issued
iPhone.
At no time will information be collected on personal devices or any device that is not an asset of the
Government of BC. The use of a privately-owned iPhone by an inspector to collect government information is
strictly prohibited.

Subsequent to every inspection the inspector will enter the inspection information into the branch database
as per established policy.

heading: 8.4 Recorded media - photographs and video evidence
text:
Photographs or video recordings taken by an inspector are a useful tool in the conduct of an inspection or
investigation. They are used for the purpose of corroborating the inspector’s notes and observations so long as it
can be established that they are authentic and reliable and must include information as to date and time of taking
and the identity of who took it.

Note: Inspector recorded media should be to the minimum extent necessary to obtain information or evidence
relevant to the identified contravention. Inspector recorded media shall only be taken using government issued
media recording devices. Personal devices will not be used for work purposes.

Inspectors may take photographs or videos during an overt or covert inspection for the purpose of complementing
their notes and observations. Inspector recorded media may only be gathered when conducting an authorized
inspection or investigation associated with a licenced establishment or special event. The photo or video recording
must accurately and truly represent the facts. Inspector recorded media once gathered, is an electronically stored
information which may be produced as evidence. The procedure specific to regarding maintaining continuity of
evidence for recorded media is prescribed at “Maintaining continuity of evidence and exhibits.”

heading: 8.5 Recorded media - collection, protection, retention and disposal
text:
The Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FOIPPA), section 26 “Collection, Protection and
Retention of Personal Information by Public Bodies” establishes the provisions by which a public body may
collect, protect, retain, and dispose of personal information:
• Collection: Inspectors are authorized to collect personal information, including recorded media, for the “law
enforcement” purpose of the delivery of the inspection program in the regulation of the liquor and cannabis
industries.

Note: The collection of any recorded media will only be accomplished using BC Government issued assets such
as issued camera, iPhone, or other audio/video recording device. At no time will information be collected on
personal devices or any device that is not an asset of the Government of BC.

heading: 8.5 Recorded media - collection, protection, retention and disposal
text:
The use of a privately-owned
camera, iPhone, or other audio/video recording device by an inspector to collect government information is
strictly prohibited.

• Protection: Inspectors will protect all personal information in their custody or under their control by making
reasonable security arrangements against such risks as unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, or
disposal.

All inspector recorded media will be uploaded on to the I Drive as follows:
• I Drive,
• Compliance,
• Applicable Regional Office Folder (i.e.: Surrey),

• Video Downloads,
• using the naming convention “Establishment Licence # and date: yyyy/mm/dd” (i.e.:
123456/2020/01/02).

• Retention: Government of BC Records Information Management provisions specify that information
collected will be maintained for the period remaining in the current year (CY) from the date the information
was collected, plus one additional year. (CY+1)

• Disposal: After the CY+1, information collected may only be destroyed in accordance with the provisions
specified by Government of BC Records Information Management and in accordance with Ministry/Branch
policy.

All C&E collected information (including information or records in paper or electronic format) that is not retained
in the branch database and is scheduled for disposal/destruction, will be facilitated only by branch Management
Services staff appointed and authorized to dispose of/or destroy records.

heading: 8.6 Complaints process
text:
Inspectors are unable to constantly monitor the operation of each licensed establishment or permitted event.
Complaints of alleged contraventions from industry and the public as well as information from police, local
government, and other regulatory bodies are a useful source of evidence and information for inspectors.

The branch documents and reviews all complaints in order to track the numbers and types of complaints received
against an establishment. While the branch reviews and assesses each complaint it receives, policies and
procedures differ depending upon the source.

heading: 8.7 Complaints from the public or industry
text:
Receiving a complaint:
Unless a complaint relates to an eminent or immediate public safety concern, all complaints must be submitted in
writing to the branch.

The complaint must include:
Complainant Information
• name and address,
• contact details (phone and email),
• date complaint is being submitted,
• licence # of complainant is a licensee,
• if a message can be left at complainant phone number
Complaint Information
• the name and address of the establishment,
• details of the incident/situation (witness information, action that may have been taken)
• date of incident,
• time of incident.

Where a member of the public or either industry makes a complaint directly to a branch inspector, the inspector
should refer the complainant to submit the complaint directly to the branch by mail, fax, or email.

heading: 8.8 Responding to a complainant
text:
Procedure:
All complaints against licensed establishments or permitted events received by the branch will be directed to the
branch complaint email account LCRBComplaints@gov.bc.ca. Where a complaint is received at the complaints
email address an auto-generated response email is sent to complainant’s email address clarifying the information
that must be provided by the complainant (if not already provided). The regional administrative assistant will

enter the complaint into the branch database whether or not all the required information is provided or not. Where
the information may be subsequently received, the regional administrative assistant will update the information
within the complaint job in the branch database.

heading: 8.8 Responding to a complainant
text:
Where a complaint is entered into the branch database, the
regional manager will receive a system auto generated notification of the complaint.

Within 30 days of receipt of the complaint from the public or either industry, the regional manager will respond to
the complainant acknowledging receipt of the complaint and indicating whether the complaint has been accepted
for investigation.

The regional manager may determine not to investigate a complaint for one or more reasons as prescribed in the
below chart:

If the complaint has not been accepted for investigation, the regional manager will outline the reason for this
decision in the letter and may indicate any other recourse that may be available to the complainant.

heading: 8.9 Recording and follow-up on complaints in the branch database
text:
Procedure:
The inspector shall follow the below procedures for recording and follow up actions on complaints received from
public or industry:
• all complaints will be recorded in the branch database by the regional administrative assistant,
• where a complaint is made directly to an inspector and the inspector accepts the complaint due to a potential
and immediate public safety concern, the inspector shall enter the complaint into the branch database and
inform the regional manager of the complaint prior to or as soon as practically possible during the
investigation of the complaint,
• the complaint, unless dismissed by the regional manager, will be assigned to a branch inspector for
investigation as directed by the regional manager,
• the branch inspector will enter all investigative activities into the investigation log during the conduct of the
investigation,

• the inspector will enter into the log either an investigative step or a note summarizing the status of the
investigation at a minimum once every 14 days until the investigation is concluded. This will ensure the
status of the investigation can be readily determined by management and where necessary further direction
may occur where necessary,
• upon conclusion of the investigation, the inspector will forward the investigation to the regional manager for
review and approval or decision.
(Note: where an investigation report may become necessary, a report may
be accessed and downloaded accordingly),
• all associated documents shall be scanned into the establishment file as facilitated between the regional
administrative assistant and management services.

heading: 8.10 Investigating a complaint from the public or industry
text:
If the regional manager decides to accept the complaint for investigation, it will be assigned to the appropriate
inspector for investigation.

During the investigative process, the inspector may contact the complainant to discuss the matter in more detail.
If the inspector requires more information from the complainant but is unable to reach them for 30 days after
receipt, the inspector can outcome the investigation job with comments in the comments box recommending to
the regional manager the closure of the investigation.

The regional manager may, depending on the allegation determine that assigning an inspection rather than an
investigation is the appropriate action necessary to address the complaint. Upon the conclusion of an
investigation or inspection conducted by the branch into a complaint made by the public or industry, the
inspector shall submit an investigation report or inspection report to the regional manager. The regional manager
will review the investigation or inspection report and where satisfied will close out the complaint.

heading: 8.11 Requesting a review of a decision not to investigate a complaint
text:
Within 30 days after the receipt of a letter from the regional manager informing the complainant that a
complaint has not been accepted for investigation, the complainant may request in writing that the deputy
general manager review the decision of the regional manager not to investigate. The complainant must show the
nature of the complaint was misunderstood, and that further information was not available at the time the
complaint was first considered. Within 30 days of the receipt requesting review of the decision not to
investigate, the regional manager will inform the complainant if the complaint will be investigated.

heading: 8.12 Information from police/local government/other regulatory agencies
text:
When police attend at an establishment or special event, they look for evidence of a contravention. Police
generally record evidence of contraventions on a “Licensed Premises Check” (LPC) booklet and give a copy of
the LPC to the licensee or permittee at the time they identify an alleged contravention. However, police may
also record evidence of contraventions in general occurrence reports or in their notes. The delivery of
information from police regarding possible non-compliant activities of a licensed establishment or special event
may vary in format or manner.

The branch may also receive information about licensed establishments or special events from local government
and other regulatory agencies. As a result of their own audit, inspection or complaint gathering functions, these
agencies may obtain evidence of possible compliance problems within an establishment or at a special event.
The branch relies on information from these agencies as key sources of information regarding the operation of
licensed establishments and special events.

The policies and procedures for response to information from police and other government agencies varies
somewhat from the branch response to complaints received from members of the public or other licensees or
permittees. In recognition of the fact that they may have a professional interest in the operation of the
establishment or special event in question, the branch where warranted, keeps police and other regulatory
agencies informed of follow-up activities or enforcement action resulting from their information.

heading: 8.13 Investigating information from police, local government or other regulatory agencies
text:
Inspectors can use their discretion to either treat LPCs or information received from police and other regulatory
agencies similar to complaints received from public/industry which requires entry into the branch database. The
information may result in an investigation or inspection or retained as intelligence for future reference or use
during covert or Minors as Agents Program (MAP) operations or other inspection. Where an inspection or
investigation is to be undertaken, the information is to be forwarded to the regional administrative assistant to be
entered into the branch database as a complaint and the inspection or investigation to be approved by the
regional manager.

Inspectors, where applicable, will inform police, local government or regulatory agencies of the follow-up
actions they take as a result of the information or LPC; however, it is the responsibility of the regional manager
to formally communicate with the complainant with respect to the initial response and to close out the complaint
at the conclusion of the investigation.

heading: 8.14 Recording and follow-up on information in the banch database
text:
Procedure:
The inspector shall follow the below procedures for recording and follow up actions on information received
from police, local government, or another regulatory agency:
• record the details of the LPC or information in the branch database,
• record the follow-up taken as a result of the LPC or information into the branch database. If the inspector
determines that follow-up action is not warranted, the inspector will indicate the reasons why no follow-up
action was taken as a result of the LPC or information,
• where appropriate, contact the police, local government, or regulatory agency to advise what action the
inspector took as a result of the LPC or information,
• forward a copy of the LPC or information to the regional administrative assistant along with a copy of any
follow-up notes to file or other associated documents. If the inspector issued an Electronic Notification of
Non-Compliance (NC) as a result of the LPC or information, the inspector will include a copy, and
• the regional administrative assistant will in conjunction with management services, facilitate the scanning of
the documents to the establishment file.

Note: Inspectors may choose not to enter “information” received by police or other regulatory agencies into the
branch database where the information received is determined to be for information or intelligence purposes
only.
To obtain information about an alleged contravention, inspectors may interview licensees, their staff, or other
persons with relevant information, either at the time an alleged contravention occurs or during an investigation.
Interviews may range from formal sessions with a prepared list of questions, to follow-up phone calls with a
licensee regarding a complaint.

heading: 8.16 Authority to conduct interviews
text:
Inspectors may question persons who may have relevant information regarding an alleged contravention; but
cannot compel a person to answer. Where a person is reluctant to answer questions, the inspector may tell the
person that the general manager can issue a summons and require a person to answer questions under oath at an
enforcement hearing.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.67]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.10 and s.44]
Inspectors will adopt appropriate interview techniques to ensure that necessary information is obtained while at
the same time ensuring a fair and respectful interview climate.
Inspectors will record the results of personal interviews in their notebooks. Inspectors will not record interviews
by audio or video without the consent of all parties to the interview. Inspectors may take as evidence, a signed
written statement from a licensee, employee, or witness.
Where an inspector takes a signed written statement, the statement should be taken using the below
format:

Ministry of
Attorney General

Liquor and Cannabis
Regulation Branch

heading: SIGNATURE: _______________________________ DATE: ______________________________
text:
YYYY/MM/DD
8.20 Interviewing persons under the age of 19
Before interviewing a person under the age of 19, the inspector will inform the person that:
• the information the person provides may be used as evidence in an enforcement hearing,
• the person is under no obligation to answer questions,
• the person may be summoned to present evidence at an enforcement hearing, and
• the person may have a parent or guardian present during the interview.

The inspector will document the interview with the young person in the inspector’s notebook.

Procedure:
5. Inspectors will interview witnesses individually. Inspectors may ask witnesses not to discuss the incident
with each other while waiting to be interviewed,
1. When appropriate, inspectors will prepare a list of questions in advance of the interview,
6. Inspectors will identify witnesses by obtaining the witness’ name, address, and telephone number,
7. Whenever possible, inspectors will use open ended and direct questions. Inspectors will avoid using leading
or suggestive questions when interviewing witnesses, and
2. Inspectors will record the questions and the witness’ responses in their notebooks.

heading: 8.21 Obtaining records, liquor, cannabis and other things
text:
To determine whether a licensee is in-compliance with the Act, regulations and terms and conditions of its
licence, the branch may access records, liquor, cannabis, and other things pertaining to the operation of an
establishment, such as sales records, agreements with manufacturers, equipment receipts or security videos.
Inspectors may also wish to examine records, liquor, cannabis, and other things in the possession of third parties
that may provide evidence of a contravention. These may include coroner’s reports, police reports, LDB records
or reports from local government.

The procedures outlined in this section ensure that records, liquor, cannabis, and other things are properly
acquired and handled so as to be admissible as evidence at an enforcement hearing or court proceeding. A
licensee’s failure to produce requested records, liquor, cannabis, and other things is a contravention. Procedures
for identifying this contravention are outlined in:
• Liquor: “Failure to produce a record, other thing” or
• Cannabis: “Failure to produce records or things for inspection.”

require a licensee through request or issuance of a Notice to Produce (see “Requesting records, liquor, cannabis
and other things – Notice to Produce”), to produce any of the following records relating to the operation of its
business:

heading: 8.23 UBrew and UVin records
text:
In addition to the records listed above at “Records the general manager may require be produced,” the general
manager may require the following records from a UBrew or UVin licensee be produced:
• purchase records for all the ingredients used in the manufacture of beer or wine in the establishment
indicating the source and volume of the ingredients,
• copies of receipts provided to customers under section 43(2) regulations,
• records of the type and quantity of beer, or wine manufactured by the licensee or employees of the licensee,
and
• records detailing disposal of any beer, wine that is spoiled, spilled, unclaimed or returned to the licensee.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.43(2) and s.51]

heading: 8.24 Winery records
text:
In addition to the records listed above at “Records the general manager may require be produced,” a winery
licensee must make the following records available for inspection:
• records of tonnage of grapes or fruit harvested,
• purchase records for grapes or fruit,
• purchase records for juice or concentrate,
• purchase records for bulk and bottled wine purchased,
• purchase records for additives to wine,
• production records,
• records of the movement and disposition of bulk and bottled wine, and
• records of spillage, sampling and tasting.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.31]
An inspector may inspect:

• all records, liquor, cannabis, establishments, and storage sites associated with the operation of a licensed
establishment.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.42(1)(c)]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.84]
The general manager may summon a person to produce records that may contain information relating to goods or
liquor or cannabis transported or received for transport in British Columbia.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.42(1)(b)]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.44(2)(b)]

heading: 8.27 Retaining records or other things to make copies or extracts
text:
An inspector may:
• retain documents produced by a licensee, or
• remove relevant records and other things for the purpose of making copies or extracts.
The inspector must:
• give a receipt for the documents, records, or other things, and
• return the documents, records, or other things within a reasonable time.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.42(4)]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.84]
A copy or extract certified by the inspector as a true copy or extract from the original licence, floor plan, or order
of the general manager is admissible in evidence the same as the original record.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.69]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.123]

heading: 8.29 Requesting records/liquor/cannabis/other things - Notice to Produce
text:
Procedure:
1. Requesting records, liquor, cannabis, and other things:
(a) If an inspector concludes that:
a record, liquor, cannabis, or other thing associated with the operation of the establishment should be
produced or inspected, the inspector will ask the licensee to produce the item,
(b) If the licensee does not produce the item in response to a verbal request, the inspector will make a written
request in the form of a “Notice to Produce” for the item. The Notice to Produce will include:
• a date of production that is within 7 to 10 days from the date of the notice or a reasonable time given
the nature of the item,
• a description of the item. The description may be general if the inspector does not have sufficient
information to specifically identify the item, and
(c) The inspector will deliver the notice, through the Secure file Transfer Service (SFTS) to the licensee’s
email address of record,
Requesting CCTV footage:
(a) To avoid possible virus contamination, CCTV footage may not be viewed on a BC Government issued
computer via licensee owned devices such as thumb drive. All CCTV footage is to only be received from
licensees through the Secure File Transfer Service (SFTS). The procedures for SFTS may be found at
I:\LCL_Compliance\SECURE FILE TRANSFER SERVICE PROCEDURES MANUAL.pdf,

was acquired.
Inspectors are authorized to seize liquor or cannabis product from a licensee that is kept contrary to the:
• Liquor Control and Licensing Act and Regulation,
• Cannabis Control and Licensing Act and Regulation, or
• Liquor Distribution Act (LDA) and Regulation, or
• Cannabis Distribution Act (CDA) or Regulation.

heading: 9.1 Seizing product and taking samples
text:
Liquor and non-medical cannabis sold by licensees under the LCLA and the CCLA must be purchased, kept, and
sold in compliance with those Acts, related regulations and the terms and conditions of the licence or permit. Any
liquor or cannabis products found to be kept contrary to this will be considered unlawful. Where the contravention
relates to unlawful liquor or cannabis, seized liquor/cannabis product and/or samples may be vital pieces of
evidence required to establish a contravention.

Seizing product and taking samples are separate and distinct activities. To ensure that samples or seized product
are properly obtained and admissible as evidence at an enforcement hearing or other proceeding, it is important
for inspectors to follow specific procedures in the process of seizing products and to ensure the principles of
continuity of evidence are adhered to from the time of seizure throughout the enforcement process.

heading: 9.2 Seizure kits
text:
The following items will form part of an inspector’s seizure kits:
Liquor:
• LCRB neck labels,
• LCRB exhibit labels,
• LCRB Request for Product Analysis forms,
• envelopes and boxes for shipping,
• fine point Sharpie marking pens,
• exhibit ledger books (located in exhibit secure lock up),
• exhibit receipt books,
• product bar code scanners (LISS guns; located in exhibit secure lock up),
• pipettes,
• glass containers,
• Teflon caps, and
• seizure kit travel/storage case.

Cannabis:
• self-seal exhibit bags,
• disposable gloves (latex/non-latex),
• micro filter masks,
• large heavy-duty polythene bags and/or stackable plastic boxes to batch bagged exhibits,
• fine point Sharpie marking pens,
• clip board,
• box cutters,
• LCRB Request for Product Analysis forms,
• LCRB exhibit labels,
• Health Canada exhibit cards,
• exhibit ledger (located in exhibit secure lock up),
• exhibit receipt books,
• product bar code scanners (located in exhibit secure lock up),
• Sani-wipes and hand cleaners,

• digital scales (Triton T3 or equivalent),
• exhibit label maker gun, and
• seizure kit travel/storage case.

heading: 9.3 Authority to seize liquor or cannabis product
text:
If an inspector finds liquor or cannabis in circumstances and is satisfied that it is being possessed or kept contrary
to the LCLA, CCLA, LDA or CDA, the inspector may immediately seize and remove the product and packages in
which the product is contained.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.45]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.84(1)(i)]

Inspectors may only seize liquor or ethyl alcohol or cannabis product, or take samples from licensed
establishments, event sites, and storage areas associated with the operation of the establishment or event site
where a special event permit has been issued.

To obtain information respecting the administration or enforcement of the LCLA or CCLA or applicable
regulation, an inspector may take reasonable samples of liquor or cannabis product for testing and analysis.
Samples may be needed to determine whether the liquor or cannabis is illegal, unauthorized, adulterated, or
contaminated. An inspector does not need evidence that the Act or regulations have been breached in order to take
a sample.

A reasonable liquor sample is:
• one three ounce or 100 ml sample of each brand being sampled, or
• an entire bottle of a beer or wine product sold by the bottle.

A reasonable cannabis sample is:
• 2 grams weight of either:
- marijuana plant material,
- lump of cannabis resin (solid), or
- marijuana cigarettes.

Inspectors may take more than one sample of a product if they consider it appropriate to do so.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.42]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.84]

heading: 9.4 Seizing liquor or cannabis product
text:
Procedure:
1. The inspector will:
• notify the licensee that he/she has determined that the products are being considered as unlawful and that
they are being seized,
• take photographs of the product being seized,
• label the seized product in a numeric sequential manner with the date (yyyy/mm/dd) and time of seizure and
the inspector’s initials, (i.e.: 2019/02/13 14:00 RWB)
5. record on an exhibit label the complete brand name of the product and the CSPC number (if one is recorded
on the container) as well as the volume and type (e.g.: glass, plastic) of the container. If there is no product
identification on the bottle or container, the inspector will ask the licensee what the product is and record the
response.

heading: 9.4 Seizing liquor or cannabis product
text:
If an exhibit label is not available, the inspector will record this information in the inspector’s
notebook cross referencing the numbers on the exhibit label and the inspector’s notebook,
• if labels are available, the inspector will place an exhibit label on the body of each container of product
seized and in the case of seized liquor, a neck label over the top of bottles of liquor,
• record in the inspector’s notebook:

- the observations or events that led to the seizure,
- a description of the product seized,
- the numbers recorded on any labels,
- in the case of liquor, the number of bottles, cans, or packages,
- in the case of cannabis, the number of packages and the amount of product in weight,
- names of any witnesses to the seizure,
- the locations from which the product was seized, and
- the date and time of the seizure,
• if available, the inspector will complete an exhibit receipt describing the seized product and all other items
seized,
6. provide a copy of the receipt to the licensee and ask the licensee to sign the receipt. If the inspector does not
have a receipt available, the inspector will ask the licensee to sign the inspector’s notebook, or the Electronic
Notification of Non-Compliance if one was issued, to acknowledge that the product was seized,
• if the licensee refuses to sign, the inspector will indicate “refused to sign” on the receipt signature line or in
their notebook.
2.

heading: 9.4 Seizing liquor or cannabis product
text:
The inspector will advise the licensee that a claim may be made to the general manager for return of the
product, or, if the product has already been destroyed, for monetary compensation equal to the LDB retail list
price of the product, under section 47 of the LCLA or section 105 of the CCLA within 30 days from the date
of the seizure. The licensee’s claim must establish lawful right to possess the product, and
7. The inspector will maintain continuity of evidence and safeguard the seized product in accordance with the
procedures outlined in “Maintaining Continuity of Evidence and Exhibits.”

heading: 9.5 Taking samples
text:
Procedure for liquor:
1. The inspector will:
• use only sterile branch-issued sample containers and ensure that samples do not become contaminated,
8. use one container for each sample. The inspector will use the appropriate type of container for the type of
liquor being sampled:
- spirits (glass containers),
- wine or beer in bottles (entire bottle is used as the sample),
- wine or beer from an opened container (glass containers with Teflon caps), and
- fermenting juice (plastic bottles and salicylic acid powder). Salicylic acid stops fermentation, allowing
the alcohol content of a sample to be determined,
9. use pipettes to transfer samples into containers. The inspector will use a new pipette for each sample
taken,
10. if the sample is being taken from a liquor dispensing machine, the inspector will take the sample from the
feed bottle or reservoir in the manifold of the dispenser. The dispenser or lines may be contaminated with
other liquor. Before taking a sample from a pressurized canister, the inspector will ask the licensee to
depressurize the canister,
11.

heading: 9.5 Taking samples
text:
fill sample bottles approximately ¾ full in order to prevent leaks from expansion of the liquid due to heat,
pressure, or humidity change,
• if the inspector believes that there may have been contamination of the liquor sample during the sampling
process, the inspector will:
- place the pipette in an envelope,
- seal the envelope,
- label the envelope to correspond to the liquor sample, and
- include the pipette in the package with the samples sent for analysis, and
• reserve one unused glass container from each batch of bottles used for samples and include it with the
samples sent for analysis.

Procedure for cannabis:
2. The inspector will:
• use only sterile branch-issued zip-lock plastic bags and ensure that samples do not become contaminated,

• use one zip-lock bag for each cannabis sample, and
• reserve one unused zip-lock plastic bag from each batch of plastic bags used for samples and include it
with the samples sent for analysis.

heading: 9.6 Marking product samples
text:
Procedure for liquor:
1. The inspector will:
• seal the sample container,
12. complete and affix a branch exhibit label for each container including the brand name of the product and
the Canadian Standard Product Code (CSPC number) if one is recorded on the bottle or container from
which the sample was taken. If there is no product identification on the bottle or container, the inspector
will ask the licensee what the product is and record the response, and
• record the branch exhibit label number for future reference.

Procedure for cannabis:
2. The inspector will:
• seal the zip-lock plastic bag and complete and affix the branch exhibit label to the zip-lock plastic bag,
• record the branch exhibit number on the label for future reference,
• place the zip-lock plastic bag into an “exhibit” plastic bag and affix the Drug Analysis Service (DAS)
exhibit label to the exhibit plastic bag,
• record the DAS exhibit label number for future reference,
• seal the exhibit plastic bag by using the adhesive flap, and
• place only one (1) type of exhibit in each exhibit plastic bag

heading: 9.7 Recording details of the sampling
text:
Procedure for liquor:
1. The inspector will:
• if liquor samples were taken from a liquor dispensing machine, record the level of fluid in the canister,
• record the condition of the roof in the area where the product is located, i.e., any evidence of water
damage or leaking, and any security measures in place in the area where the product is located, e.g.:
whether the area is locked, how many people have access to the area,
• record the branch exhibit number using the approved exhibit number sequential format of yyyy/mm/dd-1;
yyyy/mm/dd-2; etc., and
• make comprehensive notes in the inspector’s notebook recording all the circumstances pertaining to the
sampling, including:
- observations or events that led the inspector to take the sample,
- the names of any witnesses to the events and the sampling,
- the locations from which samples were taken,
- the date and time of the sampling,
- the number recorded on each label, and
- a physical description of the samples taken.

Procedure for cannabis:
2.

heading: 9.7 Recording details of the sampling
text:
The inspector will:
• record the amount of cannabis by weight in the container prior to taking the sample as well as the weight of
the sample taken,
• record both the branch and DAS exhibit numbers using the approved exhibit number sequential format of
yyyy/mm/dd-1; yyyy/mm/dd-2; etc., and
• make comprehensive notes in the inspector’s notebook recording all the circumstances pertaining to the
sampling, including:
- observations or events that led the inspector to take the sample,
- the names of any witnesses to the events and the sampling,
- the locations from which samples were taken,

- the date and time of the sampling,
- the number recorded on each label, and
- a physical description of the samples taken.

heading: 9.8 Submitting liquor or cannabis product samples for analysis
text:
Procedure:
1. The inspector will:
13. Complete the LCRB Product Analysis Request Form (see sub-section 9.9) requesting analysis. The form
will include the following information:
- the date the seizures were made, or samples taken,
- the name or brand of the suspect product, if it is known,
- the name, address, phone number, fax number and email address of the inspector,
- all available background information pertaining to the seizure or sampling that might assist the analyst,
including the specific products to which the samples could or should be compared,
- a list of all the exhibits being submitted with the shipment,
• the type of analysis required, for example:
- identification of substance,
- determination of origin,
- whether the product has been diluted or adulterated, or
- determination of the alcohol or THC content, and
- the date by which the inspector requires the Certificate of Analysis or Analyst Report,
• wrap each exhibit container individually in shock absorbent material to minimize the chance of breakage,
14. pack the containers into a box issued by the branch specifically for the purpose of shipping liquor or
cannabis product for testing and analysis. The inspector will ensure that each container is held securely in
an upright position by inner packing material. The weight of the packed box must not exceed ten kilograms.
The inspector will only include samples in containers from the same batch in one box.

heading: 9.8 Submitting liquor or cannabis product samples for analysis
text:
The inspector will
include one unused sample container from that batch in the box,
• place the completed and signed Product Analysis Request Form in an envelope inside the box,
• affix a label to the box indicating the top of the box and that the box contains glass where applicable, and
• seal the box with tape and initial the seal.
2. The inspector will:
In the case of liquor, clearly label the box “TO BE OPENED ONLY BY LSSD ANALYST” and address the

15. The inspector will ship the box to the applicable lab via courier. To maintain continuity of the evidence, the
