heading: 9.10 Disposal of seized liquor or cannabis product
text:
Seized product shall be disposed of in accordance with the procedures established below:

Procedure:
17. The inspector will secure all seized liquor or cannabis product and samples until the enforcement processes
and charges, if any, have been completed and any appeals exhausted,
18. The general manager or delegate (deputy general manager or regional manager) has authority to direct the
manner in which seized product shall be disposed of, including potentially returning the product to the
LDB,
19. Upon the direction of the regional manager, the inspector will dispose of the product by:
• returning the product to the licensee,
• pouring the liquor down the drain and returning the empty containers to a recycling facility for donation;
and/or,
• in the case of cannabis disposing of the cannabis through an approved disposal facility, ensuring the
cannabis is destroyed or denatured to such an extent that its consumption, propagation, and cultivation
are rendered improbable. An example of a method of destroying cannabis is shredding a cannabis
product into pieces, mixing it with water to turn it into sludge, and adding cat litter to control odor
before discarding it.
1. Prior to pouring any liquor down the drain, branch staff must confirm the permissible levels of dumping
from the relevant local government,
2. The inspector will document the disposition on the rear portion of the exhibit receipt. Two individuals will
confirm the disposition by initialling the receipt, and
3. Inspectors will facilitate the disposal of liquor containers through local recycling facilities.

heading: 9.11 Return of/or compensation for seized liquor or cannabis
text:
Procedure:
In the case of liquor: a person wanting to apply for the return of liquor seized by either an inspector or police
officer must submit a written request (either by letter, email, or using form LCRB125 to the general manager of
the LCRB within 30 days of the date of seizure. In order to be successful, the claim must clearly demonstrate to
the general manager’s satisfaction that the liquor was lawfully possessed or kept for lawful purposes.

In the case of cannabis: a licensee wanting to apply for the return of cannabis seized by either an inspector or
police officer must submit a written request (either by letter, email, or using form LCRB135 to the general
manager of the LCRB within 30 days of the date of seizure. In order to be successful, the claim must clearly
demonstrate to the general manager’s satisfaction that the cannabis was lawfully possessed or kept for lawful
purposes.

If the general manager is satisfied that the liquor/cannabis was lawfully possessed, the general manager may
either:
• order that the liquor/cannabis be returned if it has not already been destroyed, or

• where the liquor/cannabis has already been destroyed, provide for monetary compensation to the person
either by the branch (where the liquor/cannabis was seized by an inspector), or by requiring the relevant
police force (where the liquor/cannabis was seized by a police officer) to provide compensation.

Compensation for destroyed liquor/cannabis is limited to the lower of the retail price, and if known, the actual
price paid for the liquor/cannabis.

heading: 9.11 Return of/or compensation for seized liquor or cannabis
text:
If there is no price set for the destroyed liquor/cannabis under the Liquor
Distribution Act, to the lower of the replacement value of the liquor/cannabis as determined as if the
liquor/cannabis were available through the Liquor Distribution Branch, and if know, the actual price paid for the
liquor/cannabis.

Note: Where the cannabis was seized from a person other than a licensee, by police or an officer of the
Community Safety Unit (CSU), the person, must apply for the return of the seized cannabis to the Director,
CSU. If no application is received within 30 days, or if the general manager is not satisfied that a claim
demonstrates that the seized liquor/cannabis was lawfully possessed or kept, the liquor/cannabis and packages
containing it will be forfeited to the government.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.156]

heading: 9.12 Continuity of evidence and exhibits
text:
Continuity of evidence refers to the ability of the inspector to ensure that physical evidence has been continually
secured and maintained throughout the enforcement process, from seizure of the evidence until it is produced in
an enforcement hearing. The inspector must be able to demonstrate that the evidence presented at an
enforcement hearing is the same evidence which was seized and that it has not been tampered with or
compromised. Continuity of evidence is also important as evidence seized by the branch may be used
subsequently by another agency, such as the RCMP or the Canada Border Services Agency, for charges under
federal statutes.
All evidence that comes into the possession of the branch will be safeguarded against loss, theft, or damage.

heading: 9.14 Maintaining continuity of evidence and exhibits
text:
Inspectors will maintain continuity of evidence that comes into their possession by:
• keeping strict and controlled possession of the evidence until it is securely stored, and
• limiting the number of people who handle or have access to the evidence.

Procedure:
1. Immediately upon seizing a piece of evidence, the inspector will mark the evidence with:
• the date of seizure,
• the time of seizure, and
• the inspector’s initials,
8. The inspector will complete an (“Exhibit Receipt Form”) for all seized evidence, asks the licensee to sign the
receipt and give a copy of the receipt to the licensee. Where an exhibit receipt is unavailable, the inspector
may list the seized items in the inspector’s notebook or on the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance if
one is issued, and ask the licensee to initial the notebook or the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance,
2. The inspector will maintain control of the seized evidence while transporting it to the field office or other
designated and secure location,
3. The inspector will record the following information in the field office exhibit ledger (see sub-section 9.16):
• exhibit number,
• date/time seized,
• from licensee/establishment the evidence was seized,

• detailed description of the evidence,
• inspector name,
• disposition where the evidence was deposited,
5. The inspector will assign the corresponding exhibit number from the exhibit ledger to the evidence and
include the exhibit number on the seizure label and exhibit receipt,
6. The inspector will place the original exhibit receipt in the exhibit ledger,
7.

heading: 9.14 Maintaining continuity of evidence and exhibits
text:
The inspector will secure the evidence in a designated branch evidence storage facility along with one copy
of the exhibit receipt,
9. If liquor, cannabis, or other things are seized to support pursuit of enforcement action, that exhibit must be
secured in a locked locker, locked room, or in the event of a large seizure, a designated and secure
warehouse/storage facility,
8. There should be a single key or combination for the lock retained by the inspector.
9. The inspector will record the time and location of the exhibit,
10. Any subsequent re-entries to the locked locker, locked room or warehouse/storage facility shall be recorded
by the inspector including reason for re-entry,
10. Where an inspector seizes a large amount or volume of liquor or cannabis, the inspector shall contact the
regional manager to facilitate approval for expenses related to the seizure, transportation, and storage of the
product, and
11. If evidence leaves the inspector’s possession, the inspector will record on the back of the exhibit receipt the
following:
• to whom the evidence was given and why,
• the time and date the exhibit receipt was given to that person, and
• the time and date the exhibit receipt was returned and by whom, and
12.

heading: 10.0 Introduction
text:
After gathering evidence of an alleged contravention, an inspector must decide whether a contravention, in fact,
occurred. This decision is made after analysing the nature, quality, and sufficiency of the evidence to determine
whether each of the elements necessary to establish that contravention can be proven. The evidence gathering, and
analysis processes are often combined, as only by analysing the evidence obtained can an inspector determine
whether further evidence is required to prove a contravention.

If an inspector determines that a contravention has occurred, the inspector will issue an Electronic Notification of
Non-Compliance.
The inspector will address the alleged contravention(s) through one of the following actions:
• In the case of one or two minor contraventions the inspector may inform the licensee verbally or in writing
what corrective measures the licensee must take to bring the licence into voluntary compliance, and (where
appropriate) may conduct a follow up inspection to confirm voluntary compliance,
• In the case of repeat or multiple (3 or more) minor contraventions the inspector may arrange a compliance
meeting with the licensee to discuss one or more of the alleged contraventions and to review the steps
necessary the licensee must take to bring the licence into voluntary compliance, or
• In the case of repeat contraventions or public safety contraventions the inspector may recommend the general
manager take enforcement action against the licensee for one or more of the alleged contraventions.

This section outlines the policies and procedures for
identifying contraventions organized under the following
headings:
• Determining whether a contravention occurred,
• Issuing an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance, and
• Correcting an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance.

heading: 10.1 Determining whether a contravention occurred
text:
Once an inspector has gathered evidence of an alleged contravention, the inspector must analyse the evidence to
determine whether a contravention occurred. A thorough analysis of the evidence and the elements of the
contravention at this stage ensure that Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance are not issued without
sufficient evidence and assists with the preparation of reports and the branch case if the matter proceeds to an
enforcement hearing.
To form the opinion that a contravention occurred and issue an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance, an
inspector will consider whether enough evidence exists to prove each element of the contravention on a balance of
probabilities. “Balance of probabilities” is defined in “Definitions.”

heading: 10.3 Considering the use of additional compliance strategies
text:
When analysing the evidence of an alleged contravention, the inspector will consider whether any of the
compliance strategies outlined in “Compliance Strategies” may be appropriate to bring the licensee into
voluntary compliance.

Procedure:
1. The inspector will review the elements of the alleged contravention,
2. The inspector will determine whether enough evidence exists to prove each element of the contravention,
11. If the evidence proves each element of the contravention, the inspector will issue an Electronic Notification
of Non-Compliance in accordance with “Issuing an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance,” and
3. Whether or not the inspector determines that a contravention occurred, the inspector will consider whether
additional compliance strategies are appropriate for the licensee.

heading: 10.4 Electronic Notification of Non-Complaince
text:
An Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance will be issued for every contravention identified. When an
Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance is issued, it is considered an allegation of contravening the legislation,
regulation, or terms and conditions of the licence. The Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance should be
issued as soon as possible after identifying the issue. The inspector will determine subsequent enforcement action
pursuant to “Determining Whether or Not to Propose Enforcement Action.” The Electronic Notification of Non-
Compliance, as well as the supporting evidence will form the basis of any subsequent action.

heading: 10.6 Issuing an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance
text:
An Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance is not issued where the inspector does not have the evidence to
establish that the contravention occurred. Where an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance is issued the
inspector may depending on the egregiousness of the contravention:
• inform the licensee of the alleged contravention
• hold a compliance meeting with the licensee and provide a record of the compliance meeting to the licensee,
• recommend enforcement action through Notice of Enforcement Action (repetitive or public safety
contraventions) as per “Proposing Enforcement Action.”

Procedure:
If an inspector forms the opinion that a licensee has committed a contravention, the inspector must provide notice
in the form of an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance to the licensee that the inspector is of the opinion
that the licensee has committed a specified contravention.

Generally, an inspector will advise the licensee of the contravention at the time of the inspection and direct the
licensee to correct the contravention. The inspector must deliver the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance
via the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance process within the branch database to the licensee within a
reasonable time (but not longer than 5 business days). Where a situation may exist that prevents use of the
Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance, the inspector may provide the licensee the Electronic Notification of
Non-Compliance via mail, registered mail, or email.
The inspector will include within the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance all contraventions for which
there is enough evidence to form an opinion that the contravention occurred. For example, an inspector may
allege two LCLA contraventions of:
• permitting a minor in licensed establishment, and
• supplying liquor to a minor for one incident involving one minor.

heading: 10.8 Issuing an Electronic Notification of Non-Complaince during licence transfer process
text:
The branch may initiate enforcement action against a licensee or a “deemed licensee.” If a new operator is using
a licence that is in the process of being transferred, the previous owner continues as the licensee of record until the
new operator becomes the deemed licensee under the LCLA or until the license transfer is approved under the
CCLA. If a contravention occurs under the management of the licensee, the inspector must issue the Electronic
Notification of Non-Compliance to the licensee. If a contravention occurs after the branch has notified the new
applicant that they are now the “deemed licensee” under the LCLA or CCLA, the inspector must issue the
Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance to the deemed licensee.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, section 52]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, section 21]

Procedure:
1. Completing the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance:
(a) The inspector will indicate the date and time that the contravention was identified within the Electronic
Notification of Non-Compliance,
(b) The inspector will indicate the sections of the legislation and/or regulation or term or condition that were
contravened, and
2. Distributing the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance:
(a) The inspector will enter the information into the branch database and issue the Electronic Notification of
Non-Compliance within 5 days of the identification of the contravention to the licensee.

heading: 10.9 Correcting an Electronic Notification of Non-Complaince
text:
Administrative law principles require that the licensee be able to fully answer an allegation that a contravention
occurred. This means that the branch must provide accurate information to the licensee about the nature of the
contravention in a timely fashion.

Mistakes on an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance may be corrected. However, the process of correcting
the mistake must meet administrative law principles and not compromise the right of the licensee to fully answer
the allegation.

At an enforcement hearing, the process used to amend an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance may be an
issue. Therefore, it is important for inspectors to closely follow these procedures and to bear in mind, at all times,
administrative law principles.
If an inspector notices an error in an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance that has been sent to the licensee,
the inspector will issue a new Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance with the correct information as soon as
possible and note that this Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance replaces the prior notice.

heading: 10.11 Error identified by regional manager
text:
If the regional manager, upon review of the notice of enforcement action, concludes that the evidence supports a
different contravention from the one identified on the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance, the inspector
will issue a new Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance with the correct information and note that this
Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance replaces the prior notice.

heading: 10.12 Withdrawing reversing a Electronic Notificaiton of Non-Compliance
text:
An inspector will withdraw an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance and inform the licensee of the
withdrawal if the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance was issued in error.

10.13 Determining whether or not to propose enforcement action on an amended Electronic Notification of Non-
Coplaince
When an Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance is amended as outlined in “Error identified after Electronic
Notification of Non-Compliance has been issued,” the regional manager will consider the following factors and
determine whether amending the Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance will allow the licensee to fully
answer the allegation:
• how much time has passed since the licensee was notified of the contravention and whether this passage of
time affects the ability of the licensee to fully answer the allegation,
• the information set out in the Alleged Contravention Details section of the original Electronic Notification of
Non-Compliance and whether that information is sufficient to indicate the contravention identified by the
regional manager,
• whether the contravention identified by the inspector and the contravention identified by the regional
manager are similar or related contraventions, e.g.: serving minors and allowing minors in the establishment,
and
• other matters that may affect the licensee’s ability to answer the allegation or the ability of the branch to
amend in a timely fashion.

If the regional manager concludes that the original Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance can be amended in
a manner that allows the licensee to fully answer the al

proposal. If the regional manager concludes that the original Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance cannot

(e) If the regional manager concludes that the original Electronic Notification of Non-Compliance cannot be

heading: 11.0 Introduction
text:
Violation tickets (VT) are designed to act as a record, a penalty, and a deterrent against certain contraventions.
While the branch’s compliance and enforcement program remain focussed on the licensee, Schedule 1 of the
Violation Ticket Administration and Fines Regulation (VTAFR) allows the discretionary issuance of violation
tickets by liquor inspectors and police, to achieve compliance with the LCLA and the CCLA.

Authority:
As a delegate of the General Manager for the Liquor Control and Licensing Act, Inspectors and Investigators
have the authority granted through the Offence Act and Violation Ticket Administration and Fines Regulation
(VTAFR) to issue Violation Tickets to Licensees or the public for violations of Sections 60 (1) to (3), 61 (2) (b)
(i) and (ii), 75, 77 (1) and 78 (1) to (3) of the Liquor Control and Licensing Act.
As a delegate of the General Manager for the Inspectors and Investigators have the authority granted through the
Offence Act and Violation Ticket Administration and Fines Regulation (VTAFR) to issue Violation Tickets to
Licensees or the public for violations of Sections 48 (a) and (b), 49 (2) (a) to (c), 69 (1) and (2), 70 (2) (a)
and (7) (a), 75 and 79 of the Cannabis Control and Licensing Act.

Schedule 2 of the VTAFR lists the offences and fine amounts for which a violation ticket may be issued. The
regulation limits liquor inspectors’ authority to issue violation tickets to certain contraventions under the LCLA
and the CCLA.
VTs may be issued to minors, licensees, managers and staff in licensed establishments or a SEP
event.

Refer to current Operational Bulletins for guidance on appropriate use of Violation Tickets.

heading: 11.1 Contraventions
text:
Contraventions by licensees will continue to be dealt with through standard policy and procedures. Where there is
a public safety contravention, an electronic notification of noncompliance must be issued to the licensee.
Licensees are not relieved of their statutory responsibilities by shifting accountability to patrons or staff.
Licensees remain responsible for any contraventions despite culpability on the part of server or patron, with the
proviso that the defence of due diligence is available to the licensee. It is the licensee’s responsibility to
demonstrate due diligence.

heading: 11.2 Ticketing as an appropriate enforcement action
text:
Ticketing is the enforcement action available to deal with specific contraventions by persons such as liquor
servers or patrons and cannabis workers or patrons. It is not appropriate to issue tickets in every situation,
regardless of whether there is a provision to do so. Issuance of violation tickets is discretionary, and guidance will
be communicated to staff through operational bulletins.

In deciding whether or not to issue a violation ticket, the inspector will first determine:

1. That the contravention is “ticket-able” under the provisions of the VTAFR, and
2. That the issuance of a ticket is the most appropriate enforcement option for the circumstances.

heading: 11.2 Ticketing as an appropriate enforcement action
text:
In making this
decision, the inspector will consider the following:
• Within the context of the standard of proof being "beyond a reasonable doubt", does the evidence support a
reasonable likelihood of conviction?
• Is there sufficient evidence to defend issuance of a ticket? Are there witnesses?
• Can identification be obtained? Can the identification provided be relied upon? Can the licensee/police assist
in verifying identification?
• Is the matter better dealt with by way of an electronic notification of noncompliance and administrative
proceeding?
• Will the ticket serve the public interest by its ability to act as a specific and/or general deterrent?
• Is the matter better dealt with by the licensee or SEP holder?
• Did the contravention put public safety at risk?
• Was the contravention deliberate? Did the person responsible know they were acting contrary to law?
• Is further investigation required to obtain complete answers to the above questions?

Having considered the above, it may or may not be appropriate to issue a violation ticket to a server or patron.
When in doubt, inspectors will consult operational bulletins and with their area supervisor and/or regional
managers.

heading: 11.3 Licensees and special event permit holders
text:
It is important to remember that the VT provisions of the legislation have a limited scope of application. Although
a violation ticket may be issued to a corporation or legal entity such as a licensee, the LCLA provides an
administrative penalty regime for licensees and permittees and the CCLA provides an administrative penalty
regime for licensees. The regulatory schedule of monetary penalties and suspensions applies solely to licensees
and permittees and does not apply to persons. Violation tickets issued under the Offence Act are quasi-judicial
monetary penalties at a level intended to obtain compliance from individuals.

Branch policy requires that an electronic notification of noncompliance be issued to a licensee where the
inspector forms an opinion that a contravention has occurred that warrants a “Notice of Enforcement Action
(NOEA)” where enforcement action is being pursued or where in the public interest the inspector elects to not
proceed with enforcement action and opts to either go to a “No Enforcement Action Required (NEAR)” and/or
Compliance Meeting. A NEAR will generally be recorded for contraventions of a minor nature and where it

would not otherwise be in the public interest to pursue enforcement action such as a first-time contravention for
fail to post licence, fail to post alcohol sense poster, etc.).

The disparity between a violation ticket and a minimum penalty specified within the penalty schedule is
significant. The purpose of any penalty is to promote compliance.

heading: 11.3 Licensees and special event permit holders
text:
The choice of which penalty will promote
compliance is one of the primary decisions an inspector must make when considering enforcement options. SEP
holders are permittees and as such, are also subject to violation tickets.

Liquor and Cannabis Inspectors may issue violation tickets for any contravention of certain provisions of the
LCLA or CCLA that constitutes an offence as specified within the VTAFR (see “VT Table VTAFR LCLA” and
“VT Table VTAFR CCLA”)

heading: 11.4 Licensee and employees and permittee and staff
text:
An inspector may ticket staff in a licensed establishment, including bartenders, servers, hosts, doorpersons,
supervisors of the server(s), or security staff at a special event where a special event permit has been issued.
Issuing a violation ticket to an employee or staff person does not bar the branch from taking enforcement action
against the licensee or permittee on the same evidence for the same or a similar contravention.

To reinforce the seriousness and resolve of the branch to keep liquor and cannabis from minors, an inspector may
ticket staff in a licensed establishment who sell or supply liquor/cannabis to a minor agent.
An inspector may ticket a minor in any licensed establishment or at any special event where the branch has
issued a special event permit. Issuing a ticket to a minor does not bar the branch from taking enforcement action
against the licensee or permittee on the same evidence for the same or a similar contravention.

heading: 11.10 Statute of limitations
text:
As directed by section 3(2) of the Offence Act, ticketing may not be pursued after six months from the time the
discovery of the violation occurred. Violation tickets are intended as an immediate penalty and their deterrent
value largely depends on this. Most violation tickets should be issued on the spot. It is possible, however, that a
violation ticket may be served to the responsible party at a later date in certain circumstances. Every effort should
be taken to issue violation tickets as soon as possible after the discovery of a violation.
Violation tickets are a form of prosecution. By paying a ticket fine, or by ignoring it, a person is deemed to have
pled guilty to the charge on the ticket. Undisputed tickets are handled by the Insurance Corporation of BC
(ICBC), which is responsible for processing payment.

heading: 12.1 Proposing enforcement action
text:
An allegation that a licensee has committed a contravention does not always result in enforcement action against a
licensee. The policies outlined in this section ensure that inspectors systematically review the evidence and
circumstances of each alleged contravention before deciding whether or not to propose enforcement action.

Inspectors must fully document the reasons for their decisions. If enforcement action is proposed and approved by
the regional manager, the notice of enforcement action must contain sufficient information to allow the licensee to
decide whether to proceed to an enforcement hearing or sign a waiver notice.

If enforcement action is not proposed, it is important for the inspector to record all evidence of the contravention
and the reasons for the proposal in the no enforcement action recommended report (NEAR). This information will
be useful when determining whether or not to propose enforcement action if further contraventions occur.

heading: 12.2 Determining whether to propose enforcement action
text:
The Inspector will make a determination for each contravention identified, taking into consideration the
following:
• the licensee’s compliance history, including education provided on the specific contravention type,
• the seriousness of the contravention,
• the evidence of the contravention, and
• any other relevant factors.
The inspector will discuss with the Regional Manager and the Regional Supervisor in making a determination as
to whether to bring forward a draft Notice of Enforcement Action (NOEA) letter to the regional management
team for peer review approval process.

Non-medical cannabis: There is an expectation that licensees understand the responsibilities of their licence
before they operate their establishment. The Branch will support this by providing resources and education to
ensure they understand how to come into voluntary compliance

A required step prior to taking enforcement action with a non-medical cannabis licensee for a non-public safety
contravention will include an educational component.

heading: 12.2 Determining whether to propose enforcement action
text:
The aim of the inspector is to assist the licensee and staff
with the potential compliance problem, to avoid future non-compliance.

As a new and developing industry it is important to ensure that licensees have time to understand the expectations
of their licence and of the LCRB.

Licensees have direct contact with Liquor and Cannabis Inspectors during their Final Licence Inspection, 30- day,
6 month, and 12 month scheduled inspections after opening their Cannabis Retail Store and Producer Retail Store.
The Branch’s focus is on progressive enforcement action and procedural fairness.

To maintain consistency throughout the C & E Division the following guidelines have been made:
• Generally, administrative contraventions should not be recommended for enforcement action until after a
licensee has been given the education and opportunity to come into voluntary compliance.
• Licensees should be provided two opportunities to come into compliance via education on the same alleged
contravention type before enforcement action recommendations are made. None the less, depending on
circumstances relative to repeat contraventions of the same alleged contravention type, the inspector may
discuss consideration for enforcement recommendation with the RM/RI.

While education is also necessary for Public Safety contraventions, the Branch must consider the elevated risk of
inaction to the public.
Public Safety contraventions should be considered for enforcement action at any-time, but
inspectors may still consider whether there are other means to generate immediate voluntary compliance.

The goal of enforcement is not to punish a licensee but to obtain voluntary compliance.

heading: 12.3 No enforcement action recommended (NEAR) or NEAR and Compliance Meeting
text:
Administrative contravention:
Where the inspector alleges an administrative contravention and has determined that enforcement action is not the
recommended strategy to achieve voluntary compliance, and that compliance can be achieved through education
and/or a Compliance Meeting, the inspector may outcome the administrative contravention as no enforcement
action required (NEAR) or NEAR and Compliance Meeting. The inspector will select the applicable reason in the
branch database and conclude the contravention.

Public safety contravention:
Where and inspector alleges a public safety contravention and has determined that enforcement action is not the
recommended strategy to achieve voluntary compliance, and that compliance can be achieved through education
and/or a Compliance Meeting, the inspector may outcome the administrative contravention as no enforcement
action required (NEAR) or NEAR and Compliance Meeting. For a NEAR or NEAR and Compliance Meeting, the
inspector must provide to the regional manager substantive reasoning for the recommendation. The regional
manager will review the reasons with the inspector and may approve or withhold decision on the
recommendation. Where the proposed action is not supported, the regional manager may discuss enforcement
options with the inspector.

heading: 12.4 Proposing enforcement action non-licensee
text:
The branch cannot take enforcement action against a person who is not a licensee or deemed licensee. The branch
may however take action against former licensees. Until an applicant for a licence transfer becomes the deemed
licensee, the legal entity that holds the licence is liable for contraventions associated with the licensed
establishment. At the time the applicant for a licence transfer becomes the deemed licensee, the deemed licensee
becomes responsible for contraventions associated with the establishment.

Where a new owner has been using the licence and has not initiated the process for transferring the licence, the
inspector will advise the new owner that they are selling liquor unlawfully and may take enforcement action
against the licensee of record. Where the new owner does not make application for licence transfer, the inspector
will inform the local police, and the Branch may cancel the licence.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.52]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.38]
The determination of whether or not to propose enforcement action and the factors that led to that determination
will be documented in either the notice of enforcement action (NOEA) or the no enforcement action
recommended (NEAR). A NOEA report may include proposals for one or more contraventions identified on the
same electronic notification of noncompliance.

heading: 12.6 Gathering the evidence/investigation
text:
The inspector will gather the evidence necessary to support the alleged contravention(s). Where possible and
practical, inspectors should aim to gather all of the evidence prior to issuing a NOEA.

An inspector may request, through the regional manager, assignment of a branch investigator on any file. Where
this occurs, the regional manager and the manager of integrated provincial compliance assistance team will
determine and set out specific responsibilities. The investigator may subsequently be assigned full responsibility
for the entire file, or the investigator may be assigned limited, specific duties related to the file and responsibility

for the entire file will remain with the inspector. The regional manager and the manager integrated provincial
compliance assistance team will make the determination as to what is most appropriate in each circumstance.

Where the regional manager, or the inspector, has concerns about the complexity of a file or the suitability of the
evidence, the regional manager may request a review and comment on the available information by an advocate.
The branch registrar will assign an advocate upon the regional manager’s request.

Special attention will be paid to Licensed Premises Checks [LPC] issued by police to a licensed establishment or
other police information reports provided to the branch. LPCs/police reports do not automatically result in a
NOEA. The inspector must assess evidence provided in the LPC/police reports and follow-up with the police
agency if further information is required.

heading: 12.6 Gathering the evidence/investigation
text:
Where the LPC or police information may meet the criteria for
investigation by the C&E integrated provincial compliance assistance team, the inspector may request their
regional manager transfer the file to the C&E integrated provincial compliance assistance team. The regional
manager will discuss with the manager of integrated provincial compliance assistance team the appropriate action
warranted.

In addition to the LPC/police report the best practice is to obtain any/all the following from the police prior to
issuing a NOEA:
• A “will say” statement from the officer/s involved,
• The police occurrence report,
• The officers’ hand-written notes, and
• Any police photos.

The above documents will be scanned by the inspector or investigator and held in the Documents Tab in the
branch database. In the event an alleged contravention is disputed, the advocate may seek to obtain these
documents from the police involved.

To assist in the collection of evidence, all those assigned to a particular file will now use the Disclosure and
Investigation Check List, which appears at the end of this section. The table is intended to clarify the
responsibilities of each person assigned to the file and to act as a summary of the file status.

heading: 12.6 Gathering the evidence/investigation
text:
The inspector or
investigator will review and complete the check list for each NOEA and attach it to the file.

The regional manager will review the evidence, the circumstances, and the Disclosure and Investigation Checklist
in order to assess the suitability of the evidence during the NOEA approval process.

Where a NOEA has been approved by the regional manager, the inspector/investigator will gather and provide the
check list and file to the assigned advocate. In order to ensure the accurate and orderly transmission of
information to the advocate, inspectors/investigators should send the entire scanned file in one lot, rather than in
stages. In some circumstances, the advocate may require certain documents before the investigation is complete.

heading: 12.8 Notifying the licensee of proposed enforcement action
text:
If an inspector proposes that enforcement action should be taken against a licensee, the inspector must notify the
licensee in writing. The alleged contravention(s) must be specifically cited in an electronic notification of
noncompliance (NC) before it can be included in a NOEA. Where the alleged contravention has not been
specifically cited in an electronic notification of noncompliance, the licensee has not received adequate notice.
The notice of enforcement action must include:
• the details of the proposed enforcement action,
• the reasons for taking the action,
• the information the inspector is relying on to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the contravention(s)
occurred, and
• notification to the licensee that, unless the licensee signs a waiver notice, the general manager may schedule an
enforcement hearing. At the enforcement hearing, the general manager will determine whether the alleged
contravention(s) occurred and what enforcement action, if any, will be taken.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.51(7)]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.38(7)]

heading: F. THE PROCEDURES
text:
The general
manager is not bound by the maximums and may impose a higher suspension or monetary penalty when it is in
the public interest to do so. Section 51(9)(a) of the LCLA [38(10) CCLA] states that the general manager is not
bound to order the proposed penalty specified earlier in this NOEA.

Schedule 2 of the Regulation sets out the range of penalties when a contravention occurs in an establishment
within a 24-month [12 months for CCLA] period of a contravention of the same type. It is the date that the
contravention occurred that is used for the purpose of determining if a contravention is a first, second or
subsequent contravention for penalty purposes.

If you (the licensee) agree that the contravention(s) took place and accept the enforcement action proposed, there
is no need for a hearing. In that case, you must sign a document called a “Waiver.” By signing a waiver, you are
irrevocably:
• admit the contravention or non-compliance referred to in this NOEA,
• accept the action that is specified in the waiver to be taken against you,

• waive the opportunity for an enforcement hearing; and
• agree that the contravention(s) and the penalty imposed will form part of your compliance history.

If you decide to sign a waiver, or if you have any questions regarding this matter, please contact me at XXX-
XXX-XXXX as soon as possible.

heading: 12.13 Determining the proposed penalty
text:
After an inspector decides to propose enforcement action for a contravention, the inspector must recommend a
proposed penalty. The proposed penalty includes the type(s) of enforcement action and the level and/or terms of
the penalty.

While Schedule 2 of the regulation guides the inspector in determining the proposed penalty, the inspector has a
large degree of discretion both in determining the appropriate type(s) of enforcement action and the appropriate
penalty within the range set out in the penalty schedule. The policies outlined in this section provide further
guidance to inspectors to ensure that all licensees within the province are subject to similar penalties for similar
contraventions.

heading: 12.14 Types of enforcement action
text:
The general manager may do one or more of the following if the licensee contravenes an Act or regulations or
fails to comply with a term of condition of the licence:
• impose terms and conditions on the licensee’s licence or rescind or amend existing terms and conditions on
the licence,
• impose a monetary penalty on the licensee in accordance with the prescribed schedule of penalties,
• suspend all or any part of the licensee’s licence in accordance with the prescribed schedule of penalties,
• cancel all or any part of the licensee’s licence, and/or
• order the licensee to transfer the licence, within the prescribed period, to a person who is at arm’s length
from the licensee.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.51(2), s.52 and s.53]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.36 to s.39]
When an inspector proposes to take enforcement action for a contravention, the inspector will also propose a
penalty. The inspector may consider the following when proposing a penalty:
• the licensee’s compliance history (see definitions at “Definitions”),

• the seriousness of the contravention,
• the circumstances of the contravention, and
• any other relevant factors.

heading: CCLA:
text:
(1) A contravention is a first contravention in respect of a licensee if (a) the contravention was committed at or
in respect of an establishment or event site under an authorization held by the licensee, and
(b) the licensee has not committed a contravention of the same type at or in respect of that establishment or
any event site within the 24-month period preceding the commission of the contravention.
(2) A contravention is a second contravention in respect of a licensee if (a) the contravention was committed at
or in respect of an establishment or an event site under an authorization held by the licensee, and (b) the
licensee has committed one contravention of the same type at or in respect of that establishment or any event
site within the 24-month period preceding the commission of the contravention.
(3) A contravention is a subsequent contravention in respect of a licensee if (a) the contravention was
committed at or in respect of an establishment or an event site under an authorization held by the licensee, and
(b) the licensee has committed a second contravention of the same type at or in respect of that establishment or
any event site within the 24-month period preceding the commission of the contravention.
(4) If the general manager is satisfied that imposing the period of suspension for a second contravention or
subsequent contravention set out in the table to this Schedule would create undue hardship on a licensee, the
general manager may impose a period of suspension that falls within the range of suspension for a first
contravention.

heading: 12.17 Proposing a minimum penalty
text:
The penalty schedule does not define whether a minimum suspension or a minimum monetary is “the” minimum
penalty. Inspectors may elect to propose a minimum monetary penalty or a minimum suspension consistent with
the penalty schedule. A licensee may view a monetary penalty as less onerous than a suspension, or vice versa.
The inspector may view a minimum monetary penalty or a minimum suspension as best suited to promote future
compliance.

When proposing a minimum penalty, the inspector will recommend and the NOEA will reflect that the inspector
is proposing either the minimum monetary penalty or the minimum suspension as the penalty best suited to
promote future compliance. Reasons will be included in the NOEA. A penalty should not be referred to simply as
the minimum penalty. Where a minimum penalty is referenced, it should always be referenced as the minimum
monetary penalty or the minimum suspension.
When a first contravention has occurred and either of the minimum penalties for that contravention is appropriate,
the licensee may be given the option to select one of those two penalties when they choose to sign a waiver. The
choice of penalties is noted within the NOEA under the section titled “Proposed Enforcement Action.”
The inspector may propose to the regional manager that the licensee be not afforded the opportunity to select the
penalty option should there be sufficient reason.

heading: 12.20 Proposing a penalty greater than the Schedule
text:
When it appears to be in the public interest to do so, an inspector may propose a suspension and/or monetary
penalty that is greater than the penalty set out in the Schedule to the applicable regulation. In making this
proposal, the inspector will consider:
• the particular circumstances of the contravention, and
• the licensee’s compliance history.

If an inspector proposes a penalty greater than the Schedule, the inspector must fully document the reasons for the
proposal in the notice of enforcement action.

heading: 12.21 Proposing a penalty for lesser included contraventions
text:
If an inspector alleges an alternative lesser included contravention in the notice of enforcement action (e.g.:
allowing a minor in the establishment may be alleged as an alternative to supplying liquor to a minor), the
inspector will determine a proposed penalty for the lesser included contravention and include the proposed
penalty and the reasons for the penalty in the notice of enforcement action.

heading: 12.22 Proposing the days on which a suspension will take effect
text:
A suspension will begin on the same day of the week as the day on which the contravention occurred, unless the
general manager considers a different day of the week is more appropriate. In determining the day of the week on
which the contravention occurred, the inspector will consider the contravention to have occurred on the business
day when the work shift began. For example, if a contravention occurs at 01:00 hours on a Sunday, the inspector
will propose that the suspension start on a Saturday, as the work shift began on a Saturday. The inspector will
propose that a suspension continue in effect on each succeeding business day until the number of days on which
the suspension has been in effect equals the number of days of the suspension.
If an inspector proposes more than one suspension penalty against a licensee in a notice of enforcement action, the
total proposed period of suspension must be the sum of the suspensions determined for each of the contraventions.

heading: 12.24 Proposing the terms of a UBrew or UVin lcence suspension
text:
If an inspector proposes a suspension penalty for a UBrew or UVin licensee, the inspector will also propose the
terms of the suspension. In general, the terms of a UBrew or UVin suspension will allow persons who have
already begun batches of liquor to continue with fermentation, filtration, racking, aging, and bottling, if required
to maintain product quality. Clients will not be allowed to begin new batches of liquor. Once a suspension has
been served, licensees must deliver sales records and receipts from the suspension period to the inspector.

However, where it appears to be in the public interest to do so, the inspector may propose a total suspension of a
UBrew or UVin licence. A total suspension of a UBrew or UVin licence prohibits the licensee from providing
goods, facilities or services to persons producing liquor in the establishment during the term of the suspension.

heading: 12.25 Proposing the terms of a liquor manufacturer licence suspension
text:
If an inspector proposes a suspension penalty for a manufacturer, the inspector will also propose the terms of the
suspension. A liquor manufacturer licence may be suspended in whole or in part, in accordance with the
prescribed schedule of penalties. In general, an inspector will propose a suspension of the liquor manufacturer
licence or endorsement only for that area of the manufacturing site where the contravention was identified, i.e.,
the sampling area, picnicking area, tour area, special event area or lounge.

heading: 12.26 Proposing a penalty for a caterer
text:
In general, an inspector will proposal a monetary penalty for contraventions at catered events. If an inspector
proposes a suspension penalty for a caterer, the inspector will also propose the terms of the suspension. A licence
may be suspended in whole or in part, in accordance with the prescribed schedule of penalties. For example, the
food primary or liquor primary establishment could be suspended, without suspending the catering endorsement.
In general, an inspector will propose that a licensee with a catering endorsement be prohibited from catering
events on the same property as the establishment being suspended, during the suspension period.

Where a food primary or liquor primary has a catering endorsement, and the contravention occurs at the catered
event, any suspension will generally apply to the endorsement and will not apply to the food primary or liquor
primary establishment that has the endorsement. Similar to a food primary licence, a caterer’s primary focus is
the service of food. Therefore, when a catering licence or catering endorsement is suspended, the caterer may
continue to provide food services.
If a contravention committed by a distillery or brewery involves the operation of a sampling area, an inspector
may propose a suspension of that part of the licence that allows the sale or service of liquor in the sampling area.
For all other contraventions committed by distilleries or breweries, the inspector will not generally propose a
suspension penalty.

heading: 12.28 Proposing enforcement action against a government liquor or cannabis retail store
text:
The LCRB has no jurisdiction to regulate LDB retail liquor or cannabis retail stores beyond a memorandum of
agreement for the purpose of delivery of the Minors as Agents Program and service to intoxicated persons. Each
LDB liquor or cannabis store will be treated as a separate store for the purposes of determining its compliance
history regarding those two contraventions.

The two contraventions that may be pursued in a government liquor store or government cannabis retail store by
the LCRB are:
• selling to minors, and
• selling to an intoxicated person.

Inspectors will follow the same procedures for liquor licensees when proposing a monetary penalty for a
government liquor or cannabis store for either of the two contraventions.

An electronic notification of noncompliance (NC) will be issued to the government store manager and to the LDB
Executive Director of Retail Services. The Executive Director of Retail Services contact information can be
obtained in the BC Government Directory.

Upon receiving a NC, the LDB may arrange a fact-finding meeting or telephone conversation with the inspector
who issued the NC. At the request of the LDB, the inspector will provide as detailed a description as possible of
the LDB employee who made the sale, the till number at which the sale was made, and the receipt, where
available. This information should also be routinely included in any NOEA and disclosure.

All information relating to the issuance of the NC should be documented in the branch database.

heading: 12.28 Proposing enforcement action against a government liquor or cannabis retail store
text:
All LDB stores
have an identifying number attached to them in the branch database by way of the address. Data entry will occur
as per standard procedures.

NOEAs will be issued to the store manager and copied to the Executive Director of Retail Services. The
Executive Director of Retail Services has the authority to sign a waiver. Store managers do not have the authority
to sign a waiver. The store manager and/or any other person authorized by the LDB may participate in a pre-
hearing conference. Hearing procedures for government stores are the same as for private licensees.

Inspectors will not issue violation tickets to government store employees.

Similarly, government employees are not required to undergo Serving It Right Training because of the internal

Inspectors may issue violation tickets to minors in government stores, following standard procedures, for the
following contraventions:
• purchase by a minor,
• minor in liquor or cannabis establishment,
• minor in possession, and
• presentation of false identification.

The administrative penalty scheme (monetary penalty only), as set out in Schedule 2 of the LCLR or Schedule 2
of the CLR, will apply to LDB liquor and cannabis stores for the two contraventions which will be pursued by the
LCRB.

Where a monetary penalty is assessed against the LDB:
• the monetary penalty will be paid into the Consolidated Revenue, and
• the affected store will post signs on the doors or windows and in a customer service area advising the public
that the store has received a monetary penalty due to a contravention of the LCLA or CCLA.

heading: 12.29 Proceeding with enforcement action
text:
If an inspector decides to propose enforcement action against a licensee, the regional manager reviews the
inspector’s proposal in the context of the larger program goals and policies of the branch, as well as considering
the sufficiency of the evidence of the contravention and the likelihood of success at an enforcement hearing. The
review process also ensures consistency in enforcement action and penalty proposal for similar contraventions
throughout the province.

heading: 12.30 Determining whether to proceed with enforcement action
text:
Every time an inspector prepares a notice of enforcement action, the inspector’s regional manager will review the
notice and decide whether to continue with enforcement action against the licensee. The decision of whether to
continue with enforcement action will be based on:
• a review of the information provided in the notice of enforcement action, including the analysis and proposal
of the inspector,
• the policies outlined in “Proposing Enforcement Action,”
• the goals of the Compliance and Enforcement Program outlined in “Program Goals,”
• whether the proposed enforcement action is consistent with branch policy and regulation,
• whether there is enough evidence to find a contravention, and
• whether taking no action may invite similar breaches by other licensees.
For each contravention, the regional manager may decide to:
• ask the inspector for further information before deciding whether to proceed with enforcement action,
• proceed with the proposed enforcement action and proposed penalty,
• proceed after changing the proposed enforcement action and/or proposed penalty, or
• decline to proceed with enforcement action for the contravention.
The inspector will not provide copies of all relevant documents with the notice of enforcement action sent to the
licensee. In all cases, the inspector will attach to the notice of enforcement action copies of the licensed premises
check(s) relating to the contravention(s).

heading: 12.33 Changing the proposed enforcement action After a NOEA issued
text:
After issuing a notice of enforcement action, the branch will only alter the proposed enforcement action when
further information shows that a change will more effectively:
• achieve voluntary compliance,
• serve the public interest, and/or
• achieve speedy application of consequences for non-compliance.
The branch will not alter the proposed enforcement action solely because the licensee asks for a change in
exchange for signing a waiver notice.

heading: 12.34 Discontinuing the enforcement process
text:
Because the decision to proceed with enforcement action is a serious one, the branch will only end the
enforcement process after issuing the notice of enforcement action in limited circumstances. If the branch
regularly decided to stop the enforcement process, this could result in licensees not taking notices seriously or
inspectors not conducting a thorough examination of the facts and evidence prior to proposing enforcement
action.

This section also addresses the situation where an establishment is destroyed, or a licence is surrendered after the
branch issues an electronic notification of noncompliance. In both cases, the licence is still valid. The branch must
continue with the enforcement process in these situations to ensure that the branch file accurately reflects the
licensee’s compliance history.

heading: 12.35 Circumstances when enforcement process may be discontinued
text:
The DGM Compliance and Enforcement will only end the enforcement process for an alleged contravention in
special circumstances, including:
• further information shows that the wrong licensee was sent the notice of enforcement action,
• further information shows that evidence, fundamental to the decision to continue, was incorrect, insufficient,
or unobtainable. Evidence is fundamental to a proceeding if an alleged contravention cannot be established
without that evidence,
• further information shows that it is not in the public interest to continue the enforcement process, or
• an enforcement decision delivered after the initiation of the process suggests that the legal basis for
proceeding with the enforcement action is incorrect.
The DGM Compliance and Enforcement may end the enforcement process for one or more of the contraventions
set out in the notice of enforcement action. The enforcement process will continue for the remaining
contraventions.

heading: 12.37 Licensee requests to discontinue the enforcement process
text:
A licensee or a representative of a licensee may not request a review of the decision to proceed with the
enforcement process. A licensee or a representative of a licensee must make all arguments on an alleged
contravention to the enforcement hearing adjudicator.

12.38 Continuing with the enforcement process - establishment is destroyed/licence surrendered
The enforcement process will not be ended solely because the establishment that is the subject of the notice has
been destroyed or the licensee has surrendered the licence for the establishment.

heading: 12.39 Cancellation of licence after voluntary surrender
text:
If a licensee voluntarily surrenders their licence to the branch after an electronic notification of noncompliance
has been issued, the branch will not cancel the licence until one of the following occurs:
• the inspector decides not to propose enforcement action,
• the regional manager decides not to proceed with enforcement action,
• the licensee signs a waiver notice, and the penalty is imposed, or
• the conclusion of the enforcement process and the imposition of any penalty.

heading: 12.40 Waiver Notice
text:
In most circumstances, when the general manager intends to take enforcement action, the licensee has the
opportunity to attend an enforcement hearing to make representations on the alleged contravention and/or the
proposed penalty.

An enforcement hearing can be a time consuming and costly event for all participants. At times, licensees
acknowledge that the alleged contravention occurred and accept the proposed penalty. To record this
acknowledgement, the licensee will sign a waiver notice. Waiver Notices must be signed by the licensee or
shareholder and a witness. Waiver Notices can be electronically sent and received with signatures.

heading: 12.45 Waiver Notice of licensee
text:
The general manager may hold an enforcement hearing to determine whether the licensee committed an alleged
contravention unless the licensee signs a waiver notice. In the waiver notice, the licensee expressly and
irrevocably:
• admits to the allegation referred to in s.51(7)(a) of the LCLA and section 38(7) of the CCLA (identified
contravention),
• accepts the action specified in the waiver, to be taken by the general manager,
• waives the opportunity to have an enforcement hearing on the matter, and
• agrees that the action of the general manager and the reasons for taking the action will form part of the
licensee’s compliance history.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.51.8]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.38(8)]
The licensee may sign a waiver notice for one or more of the contraventions included in the notice of enforcement
action. The enforcement process proceeds for any contraventions that are not the subject of a waiver notice.
Where a licensee wishes to sign a waiver notice for contraventions relating to multiple licences, each licence must
be the subject of a separate waiver notice.
In signing the waiver notice, the licensee accepts the enforcement action(s) specified in the waiver, which may not
be the enforcement action proposed in the NOEA.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.51.8]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.38(11)]
The inspector will not negotiate the dates when the penalty will be imposed with the licensee. The inspector will
include in the waiver notice the dates for imposition of the penalty.
A monetary penalty must be paid in a single payment within 30-days after the date of signing the waiver notice
unless a longer period is specified by the general manager. To ensure equal application of penalties to all affected
licensees, a monetary penalty cannot be paid in instalments.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.51.10]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.94(8)]

heading: 12.50 Date for posting monetary penalty sign
text:
A monetary penalty sign will be posted starting on the same day of the week as the day on which the
contravention occurred, unless the general manager considers a different day of the week to be more appropriate.
Furthermore, the first day the monetary penalty sign will be posted will generally be no fewer than 14 days and no
more than 21 days from the date of the signing of the waiver. In all cases the first day the monetary penalty sign
will be posted will fall within the 30-day period provided.

In determining the day of the week on which the contravention occurred, the inspector will consider the
contravention to have occurred on the business day when the work shift began. For example, if a contravention
occurs at 01:00 hours on a Sunday, the posting of the monetary penalty sign will start on a Saturday, as the work
shift began on a Saturday. The monetary penalty sign will continue to be posted on each succeeding business day
until the number of days on which the sign has been posted equals the number of days the sign must be posted.

heading: 12.51 Number of days a monetary penalty sign must be posted
text:
Monetary penalty signs are required to be posted for the same amount of time as the equivalent suspension. For
example, a first contravention within a 24-month period for selling liquor to a minor is either a 7 to11 day licence
suspension or a $7,000 to $11,000 monetary penalty. When a licensee receives the $7,000 penalty, they must post
the monetary penalty sign for the equivalent 7-day period.

If more than one monetary penalty is imposed against a licensee, the total monetary penalty must be the sum of
the monetary penalties determined for each of the contraventions. In the same way, the number of days that a
monetary penalty sign must be posted is the sum of the sign posting requirements for each of the contraventions.

heading: 12.52 Determining the dates for the posting of a monetary penalty sign

The general manager will determine the dates for posting the monetary penalty. The general manager will review
the branch database establishment file to determine the normal business days of the establishment on which the
monetary penalty sign should be posted.

The number of days that a monetary penalty sign must be posted for a contravention are equivalent to the licence

heading: 12.53 Date for imposition of a suspension penalty
text:
A suspension will begin on the same business day of the week as the day on which the contravention occurred,
unless the general manager considers that a different day is more appropriate. Furthermore, the first day of the
suspension will be no fewer than 7 days and no more than 14 days from the date of the signing of the waiver. A
suspension will continue in effect on each succeeding business day until the number of days on which the
suspension has been in effect equals the number of days of the suspension.
A suspension penalty sign will be posted starting on the same day of the week as the day on which the suspension
penalty is imposed, unless the general manager considers a different day of the week is more appropriate.
A change in terms and conditions of the licence will begin 7 days from the date of signing the waiver notice or the
date of notice by the general manager unless, in the opinion of the general manager, the licensee requires a longer
period of time to implement the change in the terms and conditions.
A licence cancellation will take effect 7 days from the date of signing the waiver notice, unless the general
manager considers that a different business day is more appropriate.
If a licensee does not sign a waiver notice, the general manager will generally hold an enforcement hearing to
decide whether a contravention occurred and whether to take enforcement action. The policies and procedures that
guide the enforcement hearing process and the conduct of enforcement hearings are outlined in the “Enforcement
Hearing Rules.”

The inspector must provide the advocate with copies of relevant documents that the advocate requests. The

The inspector will familiarize themselves with the file history for the licensee and establishment in question and

In some situations, the advocate and the inspector’s regional manager may request that the inspector gather further

heading: 12.59 Imposing penalties
text:
The signed waiver notice, or enforcement decision sets out the details of the penalty to be imposed. The branch
distributes a penalty letter following the signing of a waiver notice or an enforcement decision to provide
licensees with detailed information on how the penalty will be imposed, how to comply with the penalty, and the
consequences of failing to comply with the terms of the penalty. This letter is also sent to local police, the LDB,
local government and other interested parties to inform them of the imposition of the penalty.

heading: 12.60 Penalty letter
text:
After a penalty has been imposed by a waiver notice or enforcement decision, compliance and enforcement
headquarters will send the licensee a letter:
• confirming the penalty,
• confirming the date on which the penalty will take effect,
• describing the responsibilities of the licensee once the penalty is imposed, and
• describing the consequences of failing to comply with the terms of the penalty, e.g.: serving liquor during a
period of suspension or failing to pay a monetary penalty.
Signs stating that a monetary penalty has been imposed on the establishment will be placed by an inspector or
police officer in prominent locations such as public entrances or windows and clearly visible to the public. The
licensee must keep the signs posted in the same location for the period stated on the sign.
An inspector will generally conduct at least one inspection of the establishment during the period that the
monetary sign must be posted.

heading: 12.63 Imposing suspension penalties
text:
The licence will be removed from the establishment for the term of the suspension penalty by an inspector or
police officer. The licensee will allow signs1 stating that the licence of the establishment is suspended to be placed
by an inspector or police officer in prominent locations such as public entrances or windows and clearly visible to
the public. The licensee must keep the signs posted in the same location for the period of the suspension.

12.64 Refusal to renew/transfer licence if monetary penalty not paid/suspension not fully served
The general manager may refuse to renew or transfer a licence if a monetary penalty or suspension has been
imposed upon the licence and either:
• the monetary penalty has become payable,
• the time period for payment of the monetary penalty has expired,
• the monetary penalty has not been fully paid, or

1 Special event permits are not subject to sign posting due to the transient and temporary nature of these events.

• the suspension has not been fully served.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.20]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.27(2)]

heading: 12.65 Imposing a suspension penalty for failing to pay a monetary penalty
text:
If a monetary penalty is not paid by the date specified in the waiver notice or enforcement decision, the general
manager may pursue enforcement action for the failure to pay. The contravention of failing to pay a monetary
penalty and the associated suspension penalty are in addition to, not a replacement for, the original contravention
and monetary penalty. Outstanding monetary penalties will be collected in accordance with branch revenue policy
and procedures. Failure to pay a monetary penalty may also result in the branch refusing to renew the licence until
the penalty is paid.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.51(10) and s.53.1(12)]
[Cannabis Licensing Regulation, s. 38(11) and s.40(12)]

heading: 12.66 Transfer applicant must be arm’s length from the licensee

In addition to the applicant eligibility criteria normally considered by the general manager on a licence transfer
application, a transfer ordered as a result of an enforcement decision must be completed to a person who is at
arm’s length from the licensee, as defined in the Income Tax Act (Canada). A transfer applicant will not be
considered an arm’s length applicant if that person is related to the licensee or does not deal in an independent
manner from the licensee.

(f) The regional manager will send a copy of the notice by registered mail to the licensee’s office of record,
(g) At the end of the time-period specified for submissions from the licensee, the DGM Compliance and
Enforcement will review the notice and any reply from the licensee and decide whether the contravention
occurred and whether to impose a suspension penalty,
13. The DGM Compliance and Enforcement will prepare a letter outlining the decision. If the DGM
Compliance and Enforcement decides a suspension penalty will be imposed, the decision letter will set
out the suspension penalty to be imposed and the dates the penalty will be served,
(h) Compliance and Enforcement headquarters will send a copy of the decision letter by registered mail to the
licensee’s office of record,
(i) Compliance and Enforcement headquarters will record the information from the decision letter on the
branch database, and
(j) If a penalty is found, compliance and enforcement headquarters will prepare a new penalty letter and
distribute as outlined in procedure 1 above.
9.

heading: 12.66 Transfer applicant must be arm’s length from the licensee
text:
Cancelling the licence:
(a) On the date specified for cancellation, the licensing clerk will cancel the licence in the branch database
and prepare a licence cancellation letter, and
(b) The licensing clerk will:
• send a copy of the letter to the licensee,
• send a copy of the letter to any agency that needs to be informed of the licence cancellation, and
• file a copy of the letter on the headquarters establishment file and indicate on the file that the licence
has been cancelled.
10. Transferring the licence:
(a) Where the penalty includes an order to transfer the licence, the inspector will review the terms of the
transfer and note that the transfer must be completed to a person who is at arm’s length from the licensee,
(b) If the inspector receives any inquiries from potential purchasers of the establishment, the inspector will
inform them of the terms of the transfer as outlined in the penalty letter and provide them with a copy of
the arm’s length transfer questionnaire as part of the transfer application package,
14. A licensing clerk will receive the transfer application package and note the terms of the transfer order
outlined in the penalty letter. Once all the supporting documents are in order, including the arm’s length
transfer questionnaire, the licensing clerk will refer the application to the general manager for review,
15. The general manager will review the transfer application and determine whether the transfer applicant is
at arm’s length from the licensee.

text:
The general manager may contact the transfer applicant or licensee for
further information to make this determination,
(c) If the general manager is not satisfied that the transfer applicant is at arm’s length from the licensee, the

(d) If the general manager is satisfied that the transfer applicant is at arm’s length from the licensee, the

(e) The licensing clerk will process the transfer application, print the new licence and send a copy of the new

1 above.
PROVINCIAL COMPLIANCE ASSISTANCE TEAM (IPCAT)

heading: 13.0 Introduction
text:
The LCRB IPCAT is responsible for conducting investigations of an in-depth and ongoing nature. Inspectors may
refer cases to the IPCAT for investigation. The types of investigations include:
1. The licensee not being fit and proper to hold a licence by having criminal associations.

The integrity of both the liquor and cannabis control and licensing schemes must be protected from
involvement by criminal interests. At the time of licensing and at any time during the term of the licence, the
general manager may assess whether a licensee has any criminal convictions, criminal associations or previous
contraventions of the Act and regulation. These and other factors may indicate whether the licensee is a fit and
proper person who is likely to comply with the terms and conditions of a liquor or cannabis licence.

2. Accidents causing personal injury, death or property damage which may have been attributed to non-
compliance by a licensee.

At times there are incidents occurring in or outside of the establishment which have been resulted in a personal
injury, death or property damage that may have been connected with non-compliance by a licensed
establishment. The LCRB must investigate these incidents to ensure that the cause of those injuries, death or
damage is not the result of non-compliance by a licensee.

heading: 13.1 General Manager may take action against a licensee
text:
The general manager may take action against a liquor or cannabis licensee if, in the general manager’s opinion,
the person is not fit and proper to hold a liquor or cannabis licence. This may include cancelling the licence or
ordering the licence transferred to a person at arm’s length from the licensee.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.51 to s.53(13)]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.23]

heading: 13.2 Determining whether a person is fit and proper
text:
A fit and proper person must:
• be of good reputation and character, who does not have a history of behaviour that would render the person
unsuitable to hold a licence,
• not be involved in criminal activities or associated with anyone involved in criminal activities
• not be a member, or meaningfully associated with a member, of an organized crime group, and
• have financial integrity. The funding involved or in support of the licence must not be from a criminal source
or associated with any criminal source.

Procedure:
14. C & E Division IPCAT Investigators are responsible for conducting investigations into the fit and proper status
of licence applicants, licensees, transferees, or third-party operators,
1. Investigators will complete a staff report based on the information gathered during the investigation and
submit it to the manager of investigations and the two deputy general managers,
2. If the report indicates that the subject of the fit and proper investigation may not be fit and proper, the contents
of the report will be disclosed to the subject of the investigation and a licensing committee hearing may be
arranged,
3. The subject of the investigation will have an opportunity to respond to the investigation
report, and
5. Detailed procedures for the conduct of Fit and Proper Investigations are found in Part 6 of this manual.

heading: 13.3 Inspector referral for investigation
text:
Liquor and Cannabis Inspectors may submit a request through their regional manager that the C & E Division
IPCAT conduct an investigation on a licensee, transferee, or third-party operator to determine licensee or operator
eligibility.

In support of a request for an investigation, inspectors must provide sufficient evidence, information, and/or
documentation to the applicable regional manager to support the request and advance the request to the Manager
IPCAT for consideration. For ease of administration, consistency, and tracking, inspectors are to utilize the
Inspector Request for Investigation Report format at “Inspector Request for Investigation Format” when making
a request.
