CONTRA VENTIONS

heading: 14.0 Introduction
text:
The first item listed in the penalty schedule is the contravention of operating a licensed liquor establishment in a
manner that is outside the primary purpose of the licence. The primary purpose of the food primary licence can be
determined by referring to the LCLA, regulation and the terms and conditions of the licence.

Generally, this contravention involves food-primary establishments operating as liquor-primary establishments
and that is the focus of this section of the manual. However, inspectors may also allege this contravention where
another licensee is operating outside their primary licence purpose in relation to an event catered by the licensee,
such as:
• the holder of a catering licence,
• the holder of a food primary licence with a catering endorsement, or
• the holder of a liquor primary licence with a catering endorsement.

Procedures for identifying a food-primary establishment operating as a liquor-primary establishment are included
in this section under the headings:
• Food-primary licensee - operate outside of licence purpose,
• Caterer licensee - operate outside of licence purpose

heading: 14.1 Food-Primary licensee operate outside of licence purpose
text:
Food-primary establishments must be primarily engaged in the service of food in the service area during all hours
of liquor sales or service. Restaurants offer liquor service as an accompaniment to food, rather than as the primary
activity. This contravention occurs if the primary focus of a food-primary establishment shifts from the service of
food to the service of liquor.

It is contrary to the public interest for the branch to allow restaurants to operate as bars under a food-primary
licence. The current liquor licensing process requires public and local government or First Nations input for
liquor-primary licences but not for food-primary licences. Obtaining a liquor licence for a restaurant and then
operating as a bar circumvents this process. Restaurants operating as bars also tend to be associated with
community complaints from neighbours about noise, drunkenness, and unruly patrons.
A food-primary licence must not be issued, renewed, or transferred or amended unless the primary purpose of the
business is the service of food in the service area during all hours of liquor sales or service.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.17]

heading: 14.3 Terms and conditions specific to food-primary licences
text:
In addition to the general terms and conditions applicable to all licensees, the following terms and conditions
apply specifically to food-primary licences:
• the establishment must operate as a food-primary in all service areas of the establishment whenever liquor is
being sold or served,
• the kitchen must be fully equipped to produce the food on the menu and must be open and staffed whenever
liquor is sold or served,

• the menu must include a reasonable variety of appetizers and main courses which must be available whenever
liquor is being sold or served. Serving salsa, chips, peanuts, and other types of “finger food” is not enough to
meet this requirement,
• the décor must be suitable for dining and table service. There must be enough tables, chairs, and food service
equipment (glasses, plates, etc.) to serve full meals to patrons,
• any entertainment and games offered must not distract from the service of food,
• the name of the restaurant must not mislead the public regarding the establishment’s primary purpose,
• the food primary licensed establishment must be operated as a restaurant at all times when liquor is sold or
served.

heading: 14.3 Terms and conditions specific to food-primary licences
text:
A licensee cannot shift its operation to become a bar during certain hours of the day, unless the
establishment has also been licensed to operate as a liquor primary which enables the licensee to operate as a
bar when it is not operating as a restaurant,
• all financial records and receipts must be available for review upon request and must demonstrate that the
restaurant is involved primarily in food service, and
• advertising may not primarily focus on liquor sales or service or entertainment. This includes, but is not
limited to, on-line advertising, social media, signage, menu, and any associated material.

[Food-Primary Licence Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 14.4 Factors that may indicate operating outside of licence purpose
text:
Unlike other contraventions outlined in the penalty schedule, the inspector does not need to prove specific
elements to allege the contravention of operating outside of licence purpose. Rather, the inspector must consider
the following factors that may indicate whether the primary purpose of the business carried on in the
establishment is the service of food:
• kitchen equipment,
• menu,
• furnishings and lighting,
• type and hours of games and entertainment that are available or to be offered,
• establishment name,
• operating hours,
• financial records,
• advertising, and
• any other relevant consideration, such as:
- the ratio of receipts from food sales to receipts from liquor sales
- establishment operations,
- community impact, and
- staff, other than kitchen staff, on duty and the duties they are performing.

A combination of these factors or only one factor that indicates a shift in focus may be sufficient to support the
conclusion that an establishment is operating outside its licence purpose.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.18]

heading: 14.5 Contravention may consist of single instance of operate outside of licence purpose
text:
An inspector may gather evidence of a pattern over time of operating outside the primary purpose of the licence in
order to allege this contravention. Additionally, the contravention of operating outside of licence purpose may be
alleged if an inspector gathers enough evidence at an inspection to establish that the licensee was operating an
establishment outside its licence purpose at one particular time.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.18(1)(a)]

heading: 14.6 Elements of contravention: food-primary licensee “operate outside of licence purpose”
text:
To allege the contravention of food-primary operate outside licence purpose, the inspector must gather evidence
that:

• the licensee holds a food primary licence,
• the service of food in the licensee’s service area was not the primary purpose of the business

Procedure:
1. If an inspector suspects that a food-primary establishment is operating outside its licence purpose, the
inspector will observe the operation of the establishment and document their observations before notifying the
licensee of their concerns,
2. The inspector will review any specific licence terms and conditions for the establishment,
15. The inspector will gather further evidence of the contravention. The inspector may:
• interview staff,
• interview the licensee,
• if it is safe to do so, interview patrons,
• interview neighbouring residents or businesses,
• request tapes from any video surveillance cameras in the establishment, and/or
• obtain documents from the licensee, including:
- sales records,
- food purchase records,
- liquor register,
- sales receipts,
- drink lists,
- menus,
- advertising, and
- payroll records, and
4. The inspector will record the details of the contravention in the inspector's notebook and transcribe the
information onto the branch data base within their mobile device or once they have returned to the field office.

evidence based upon an analysis of the factors outlined in “Factors that may indicate operate outside licence
purpose” to conclude that an area1 of the establishment has shifted away from a primary focus on the service
of food, the inspector will issue an electronic notification of noncompliance alleging a contravention of:
• Operate outside of licence purpose. ("Service of food in the service area under a food primary licence not
the primary purpose of the business"), s.18(1)(a) LCLR (Food-Primary Licensee)
Catering licensees and endorsement holders must be primarily engaged in the service of food. Caterers offer
liquor service as an accompaniment to food, rather than as the primary activity. This contravention occurs if the
primary focus of a catering event shifts from the service of food to the service of liquor.

heading: 14.8 Primary purpose of a catering licence or endorsement
text:
A catering licence may be issued, renewed, or transferred if the general manager is satisfied that the primary
purpose of the business is the preparation and serving of food. A catering endorsement can be added to a food
primary licence or a liquor primary licence if the general manager is satisfied that the primary business of the
licensee, in relation to a catered event or a residential event, is the preparation and serving of food.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.21]

heading: 14.9 Terms and conditions specific to catering licences and endorsements
text:
In addition to the general terms and conditions applicable to all licensees, the following terms and conditions
apply specifically to catering licences and endorsements:
• the caterer must be the owner of the catering business to which the licence or endorsement applies,
• the caterer must store at the caterer’s business location the liquor to be sold at events catered by the caterer,
• the caterer may maintain in or on the outside of the caterer’s business location a sign displaying the name of
the caterer and the fact that the caterer is licensed under the LCLA, if the sign complies with local government
bylaws and is approved by the general manager. Other signs must not be displayed inside or outside the
caterer’s business location unless they are approved by the general manager,
• the caterer must not change the location of the caterer’s business location without the written consent of the
general manager,
• the caterer must provide to the general manager, on request, any document relating to the caterer’s catering
business,
1.

heading: 14.9 Terms and conditions specific to catering licences and endorsements
text:
the caterer must hold, in good standing, all municipally, regionally, provincially, or federally granted licences,
permits, or certificates that the caterer is required to hold in order to operate the catering business and the
caterer’s business location,
• the caterer must not be convicted of an offence under the laws of Canada or British Columbia or under the
bylaws of a municipality or regional district that relates to the caterer’s business location or the conduct of it,
or the catering business or the conduct of it,
• the caterer must not promote, or invite people to, an event catered by the caterer unless the event is to express
appreciation for the caterer’s employees or customers, the liquor is provided at no charge, and the only persons
who attend the event are the persons personally invited by the caterer or named in an invitation issued by the

heading: 14.10 Factors that may indicate operating outside of licence purpose
text:
Unlike other contraventions outlined in the penalty schedule, the inspector does not need to prove specific
elements to allege the contravention of operating outside of licence purpose. Rather, the inspector must consider
the following factors that may indicate whether the primary purpose of the business is the preparation and service
of food at events:
• kitchen equipment,
• food selection,
• advertising,
• financial records,
• staffing,
• catering contracts,
• the ratio of receipts from food sales to receipts from liquor sales, and
• any other relevant consideration.

A combination of these factors or only one factor that indicates a shift in focus may be sufficient to support the
conclusion that an establishment is operating outside of its licence purpose.

heading: 14.12 Contravention may consist of single instance of operate outside of licence purpose
text:
An inspector need not gather evidence of a pattern of operating outside of the primary purpose of the licence in
order to allege this contravention. The contravention of operating outside of licence purpose may be alleged if an
inspector gathers enough evidence to establish that the licensee was operating an establishment outside of its
primary purpose at one particular time.

at catered events,

heading: 15.0 Introduction
text:
Contraventions involving minors are a serious public safety concern for the branch. Items 7 (s. 77 [1]) and 8 (s. 79
[1] or [2]) in Schedule 2 of the LCLR reference the most common contraventions involving minors. However,
inspectors may allege other contraventions involving minors, such as:
• a contravention of the terms and conditions of a licence/permit by allowing a minor server in a food-primary
establishment to mix drinks or pour liquor, or
• a contravention of section 77(1)(c) of the LCLA by allowing as minor to consumer or possess liquor in or at
a place under the person’s control.

Police and liquor inspectors have the authority, under the Offence Act, to issue violation tickets directly to minors,
and payment of the associated fines is tied to issuance and renewal of driver or vehicle licences.

[Offence Act, Violation Ticket Administration and Fines Regulation, Schedules 1 and 2]

The following violation tickets may be issued to minors:

Liquor Control and Licensing

Contravention Amount
Section 78(1)(a) Purchase of liquor by minor $230
Section 78(1)(b) Consumption of liquor by minor $230
Section 78(1)(c) Possession of liquor by minor $230
Section 78(3) Presentation of false identification by minor $230

This section outlines policies and procedures for identifying contraventions involving minors organized under the
following headings:
• Sell, give, or otherwise supply liquor to a minor,
• Allow a minor to consume or possess liquor at a place under the person’s control,
• Employ minor contrary to regulation,
• Minor in establishment, liquor store, or event sit
e, and
• Minor in service area at special event site

heading: 15.1 Sell, give or otherwise supply liquor to a minor
text:
Selling, giving, or otherwise supplying liquor to minors or permitting minors to consume liquor are significant
public safety issues because of:
• the effects of alcohol abuse on growing bodies and developing minds,
• the effects on individuals and society of irresponsible drinking behaviour learned at an early age,
• a minor’s lack of capacity to metabolize alcohol in the same manner as an adult; therefore, liquor has a
more intoxicating effect on minors, and
• liquor is a significant factor in many crimes committed by youth, including serious driving offences,
assault, sexual assault, and theft.

heading: 15.2 Prohibition against supplying liquor to minors
text:
A person must not sell, give, or otherwise supply liquor to a minor, except as allowed under “Minors employed as
servers in licensed establishments.”

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.77(1)(a)]
[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.159]

15.3 Prohibition against allowing a minor to possess or consume liquor at a place under the person’s control
A person must not permit a minor to possess or consume liquor in a place under their control.

15.4 Elements of contravention: “allowing a minor to consume or possess liquor at a place under the person’s
control”
To allege the contravention of allowing a minor to consume or possess liquor at a place under the person’s
control, an inspector must gather evidence that:
• the person in question is a minor,
• the minor was in or at a place under the licensee’s control,
• the minor was consuming or in possession of liquor, and
• the licensee/permittee allowed the minor to consume or possess liquor.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.77(1)(c)]

heading: 15.5 Minors employed as servers in licensed establishments
text:
Minors must not be employed as servers in licensed establishments, except for food-primary establishments and
stadiums. Minors employed in food-primary establishments and stadiums that are at least 16 years of age are
permitted to serve liquor, but they are not permitted to open bottles, pour or mix liquor, or hawk liquor. They
must be supervised by adult staff.

Minors may be employed as servers at all other licensed establishments or special event permit sites for any
employment purpose other than selling or serving liquor.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.79(2)]
[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.161 to s.167]
To allege the contravention of sell, give or otherwise supply liquor to a minor, an inspector must gather enough
evidence to prove each of the following elements on a balance of probabilities:
• the person in question is a minor,
• the minor was in possession of liquor, and
• the licensee/permittee directly or by way of its staff sold, gave, or otherwise supplied liquor to the minor.

heading: 15.7 Acceptable types of identification
text:
The terms and conditions handbooks requirement for age verification is two pieces of identification. The first
piece of identification must be:
• a passport,
• a driver's licence that displays a photograph and date of birth, or
• an identification card issued by a government agency that displays a photograph and date of birth.

The second piece of identification must display the person's name and either the person's signature or picture.

Other than the terms and conditions on the licence/permit, there is no legal requirement to verify age; rather the
legal obligation is to prevent minors from entering licensed establishments/events sites with age restrictions and to
prevent service to minors in the same circumstances.

Section 158 of the Regulation sets out the identification requirements that would meet the criteria of section 77 of
the Act, which establishes a defence to a “charge” of supplying liquor to a minor where the person can
demonstrate to the court that the person took these prescribed steps in verifying age. It is reasonable that where a
licensee/permittee could demonstrate the same in the administrative context that this may constitute a defence of
due diligence. The terms and conditions requirements for age verification are consistent with section 158 of the
Regulation.

When a piece of ID is presented, the licensee/permittee must be able to read the words and identify the person in
the picture as its customer.

heading: 15.7 Acceptable types of identification
text:
If, for example, a person presents a foreign passport and the licensee/permittee (or

staff member) can read the words indicating it is a passport and the age of the person, that can be accepted for the
first piece of ID. If, however, someone presents a foreign passport and the licensee/permittee (or staff member)
cannot read it, that would not be acceptable since the licensee/permittee would not know what the ID was or the
person’s age. Many foreign passports are written in the national language and English. Similarly, a driver’s
licence from another jurisdiction is acceptable ID if it can be read, the person and their age can be identified and
there is no reason to suspect the ID is fraudulent.

An expired driver’s licence (or other expired government ID) may be accepted by the licensee/permittee as ID as
long as it can be read, and it is possible to recognize the customer from the picture. This is because the licence is
for age verification not for entitlement to drive and the fact it is expired does not affect the age verification. Of
course, if the licence is so old that it is not possible to identify the holder as the person pictured or it is in such
poor condition as to raise doubts about its authenticity it cannot be accepted as valid ID.

ID cards issued by band councils (or the Nisga’a Lisims Government or a Treaty First Nation) may be accepted
by the licensee as a second piece of ID as long as it has the person’s name and picture or signature. As with any
type of ID, if there is a reasonable doubt about its authenticity it should not be accepted as proof of age.

heading: 15.7 Acceptable types of identification
text:
This may
happen because the laminate is not completely stuck together on all sides, the picture appears to have been
tampered with, the printing is smudged or unreadable or, because of age or discolouration, a reasonable person
could not say for sure that the person carrying the card is the person in the picture. Licensees/permittees may take
into account reports from police that particular types of counterfeit ID are circulating in the area in assessing the
authenticity of ID. If in doubt do not serve the person.

For the second piece of ID, an interim licence (the yellow paper) issued by ICBC may be accepted by the licensee
since it will have the person’s name and signature. If the interim licence expired a significant time before it was
presented, a reasonable person may be suspicious of its authenticity since it is to be destroyed as soon as the
renewed licence is received. An interim licence is not acceptable as a first piece of ID since it does not include a
picture.

In all cases, it is the responsibility of the licensee to verify age, and it is up to the licensee/permittee to determine
on a “case by case” basis where the identification presented verifies to the licensee/permittee’s satisfaction that
the person checked is not a minor

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.158]

the inspector will observe and document the actions of the patron and staff before notifying the
licensee/permittee of their concerns,

any information the person provides to verify the identification. If the person refuses to provide identification

Based on the evidence gathered, if the inspector forms the opinion that a contravention occurred, the
inspector will issue an electronic notification of noncompliance alleging a contravention of:
• Sell, give, or otherwise supply liquor to a minor, s.77(1)(a) LCLA (Licensee/Permittee), or
• Allow a minor to consume or possess liquor in or at a place under the person’s control, s.77(1)(c)
LCLA (Licensee/Permittee)

Where the facts of the case warrant, and a penalty for each would be appropriate, the inspector may allege that the
licensee/permittee contravened both section 77(1)(a) of the Act and section 77(1)(c) of the Act. This would only
be used for those cases where the branch believes that two discrete contraventions occurred, each warranting its
own penalty. For example, the inspector may observe a licensee/permittee selling liquor to a minor and also
observe that elsewhere in the establishment/event site there are other minors consuming liquor. (See
“Recommending a penalty for lesser included contraventions”).

In cases where there may be some question whether the licensee/permittee supplied liquor to a minor observed to
be consuming liquor, and the branch feels that only one penalty is warranted for the events, the inspector may

allege a contravention of section 77(1)(a) of the Act, AND in the alternative, a contravention of section 77(1)(c)
of the Act.

contravention, in the event that the section 77(1)(a) contravention cannot be proven, and, at the same time,
provides the licensee with notice. (See “Recommending a penalty for lesser included contraventions”).

The inspector will ask the licensee/permittee to tell the minor to leave the establishment/event site and to escort
them out of the establishment/event site.

heading: 15.8 Minor in establishment or liquor store or event service area
text:
To avoid selling or serving liquor to minors and exposing them to adult-oriented entertainment or activities, the
Act restricts their entry into licensed establishments service areas, liquor retail stores and service areas at special
event sites.

Minors are permitted in food-primary establishments, stadiums, concert halls, trains, airplanes, and other
establishments where the primary focus is not the service of liquor. In addition, minors are permitted in liquor
primary establishment service areas for employment purposes other than selling or serving liquor.

Minors are also permitted in liquor primary establishment service areas where a family food service endorsement
has been issued but only in respect of the hours as specified on the endorsement and where supervised by an adult.
A licensee must not allow a minor to enter or remain in the service area of a licensed establishment except as
otherwise “Where minors are permitted.”

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.79(1)]
[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.157 to s.160]

heading: 15.10 Minor in liquor retail store
text:
A minor may accompany a parent or guardian who is shopping into establishments where patrons purchase liquor
exclusively for consumption off the premises. The following establishments fall within this category:
• licensee retail stores,
• rural licensee retail stores,
• winery operated wine stores, independent wine stores, and VQA wine stores; special wine stores in grocery
stores, and
• government liquor stores.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.79(1)]
[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.160]

Minors are permitted without a parent or guardian in sacramental wine stores and tourist wine stores.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.160]
Minors are permitted in a liquor primary establishment/event site when they are employed as per section 163
Regulation or as outlined in the terms and conditions of the licence or permit.

heading: 15.12 Minors must be supervised
text:
As per section 162 of the Regulation the employment of minors in an establishment or at an event site is subject to
the condition that the minor while working in the establishment or at an event site must be under the direct and
continual supervision of the licensee or permittee or an adult employee of the licensee or permittee. This
requirement does not apply to the establishment under a catering licence.

heading: 15.13 Minor working in a liquor primary licence
text:
As per section 163 of the Regulation, A minor may be employed in an establishment under a liquor primary
licence that is not a stadium for any employment purpose other than the selling or serving of liquor if:
• if the minor was hired on or after January 23, 2017, during the period that minors are allowed to enter and be
in the service area, and
• if the minor was hired before January 23, 2017, during any period.

heading: 15.14 Minor employed in a stadium
text:
A minor may be employed in an establishment under a liquor primary licence that is a stadium during the period
that minors are allowed to enter and be in the service area if:
• if the minor is at least 16 years of age, for the purpose of selling and serving liquor other than:
- mixing or preparing drinks containing liquor,
- opening bottles, cans, or other containers of liquor, or
- performing the function commonly described as hawker, which involves carrying drinks containing liquor
in the stands for the purpose of selling the drinks, and
• for any other employment purpose not related to the sale or service of liquor.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.163(2)]

heading: 15.15 Minor as entertainer
text:
A licensee or permittee must not employ a minor for the purpose of entertaining patrons except in accordance
with section 166 of the regulation. A minor may perform in an establishment under a liquor primary or food
primary licence; service area of a lounge, special event area, or picnic area endorsed on a manufacturer licence;
event site under a catering or temporary use area authorization under a special event permit but must not be in the
establishment, service area or event site before and after their performance and during intermission unless the
licence permits minors in the licensed area; and must not take part in entertainment involving patron participation

Minors may be employed for the purpose of entertaining patrons only in the following areas:
• the establishment under a liquor primary or food primary licence,
• the service area under a lounge, a special event area or picnic area endorsement endorsed on a manufacturer
licence, and
• the event site under a catering or temporary use area authorization or under a special event permit.

The following conditions apply to the employment of minors for the purpose of providing entertainment to
patrons:
• the terms and conditions of the licence or permit allow entertainment in the establishment, service area or
event site, and
• minor must not be employed in providing adult entertainment.
If adult entertainment is provided in an establishment, service area or event site, minors must leave the
establishment, service area or event site when the adult entertainment takes place.

If minors are not allowed in an establishmen

who is an entertainer:
• must not be in the establishment, service area or event site before and after their performance and during
intermissions, and
• must not take part in entertainment involving patron participation.

heading: 15.18 Procedures to ensure minors do not enter an establishment or event site service area
text:
A responsible licensee/permittee will implement procedures to ensure that minors do not enter an
establishment/event site where they are not allowed, such as:
• asking for additional identification if the primary pieces of identification are inconclusive,
• providing a well-lit area in which to show identification,
• having an experienced doorperson on the front door or access point,
• securing uncontrolled exits in accordance with any fire safety rule, regulation, or code,
• ensuring each doorperson is properly instructed on the age verification procedures, and/or
• using identification scanning devices provided the collection and retaining of the information is in
compliance with the Personal Information Protection Act.

As required, a licensee/permittee operating an establishment or event site that is likely to be particularly attractive
to young people may have additional age verification procedure terms and conditions on their licence/permit
individually tailored to the needs of their establishment/special event.

Identification Scanning Devices
Collection of any information on patrons by licensees/permittees must be conducted in compliance with the
Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA). If a licensee/permittee requests any further details regarding the
collection of personal information and the use of identification scanning devices, they should be directed to
contact the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner (OIPC).

heading: 15.19 Verifying authenticity of identification
text:
A licensee/permittee may do one or more of the following to verify that identification is authentic:
• have the person provide a sample signature and compare the signature to the signature on the identification,
• ask for additional pieces of identification. If the additional identification still leaves some uncertainty, the
licensee/permittee should ask the patron to leave,
• ask the person what their zodiac sign is,
• ask the person for their middle name and how to spell that name, and/or
• ask the person for information that is on the identification such as address, postal code, etc.

Licensees/Permittees have no legal authority to retain identification that is false. Inspectors will not accept or
collect false identification from licensees/permittees.

15.20 Procedures to ensure minors do not enter an establishment or service area as a term and condition of a
licence
The general manager may impose procedures for ensuring minors do not enter an establishment or service area or
special event as terms and conditions on a licence or permit.

heading: 15.19 Verifying authenticity of identification
text:
The terms and conditions may include any or all of
the procedures described in “Procedures to ensure minors do not enter an establishment or event site service
area.”

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.15(1)(a)]

15.21 Elements of contravention: “minor in establishment, liquor store or special event service area”
To allege the contravention of permitting a minor in an establishment, liquor store or special event service area, an
inspector must gather evidence to demonstrate that:
• the Act prohibits minors to enter or be in the service area or at the establishment or liquor store or the special
event service area except as provided by regulation or under the authority of the general manager,
• the person in question is a minor, and
• the minor was allowed entry or to be in the service area at the establishment, liquor store or special event
service area.

Procedure:

1. If an inspector observes a patron who appears to be a minor in an establishment, liquor store or special event
service area where minors are restricted or not permitted, the inspector will observe and document the
activities of the patron and staff before notifying the licensee/permittee of their concerns,
2. The inspector may ask the person for identification. The inspector will review the identification and consider
any information the person provides to verify the identification. If the person refuses to provide identification
to the inspector, the inspector will ask the licensee/permittee to ask the person for identification,
3.

heading: 15.19 Verifying authenticity of identification
text:
If the person does not have proper identification, the inspector will gather further evidence of each element of
the contravention. The inspector may:
• review the terms and conditions of the licence/special event permit,
• interview each staff member who had contact with the minor, e.g.: servers, door staff,
• interview the licensee/permittee,
• if it is safe to do so, interview the minor and obtain name and contact information,
• seize any forged, altered or impostor identification,
• obtain sales receipts for the minor’s table,
• if it is safe to do so, interview other patrons and obtain names and contact information, and/or
• obtain any surveillance videos from the licensee/permittee

SECTION 16: ALLOW DISORDERLY OR UNLAWFUL
CONDUCT
The penalty schedule includes two contraventions under the above heading “Allow Disorderly or Unlawful
Conduct.” Policies and procedures for identifying these contraventions are included in this section under the
headings:
• Allow violent, quarrelsome, riotous, or disorderly conduct, and
• Allow unlawful activities or conduct

heading: 16.1 Allowing violent, quarrelsome, riotous or dsorderly conduct
text:
Violent, quarrelsome, riotous, or disorderly conduct present serious safety concerns for staff, patrons, and the
surrounding community. These types of activities also impact a licensee/permittee’s ability to manage and control
the establishment/event site. Licensees/permittees must take positive action to prevent these activities and stop
them if they occur.

The Security Services Act requires the licensing of staff or contractors providing security guard services
(including door security) in licensed establishments as well as security guard services at special events where
liquor is sold or served. Full details on the licensing requirements for security guards under the Security Services
Act are available at the Ministry of Public Safety and solicitor General website at
http://www.pssg.gov.bc.ca/securityindustry/.
Under the legislation, security guards are eligible to obtain advanced training which authorizes them to carry and
use metal chain link handcuffs.

heading: 16.2 Prohibition against allowing violent, quarrelsome, riotous or disorderly conduct
text:
A licensee must not allow in the licensed establishment or event site:
• violent conduct,
• quarrelsome conduct,
• riotous conduct, or
• disorderly conduct.

16.3 Responsibility to notify police of violent, quarrelsome, riotous or disorderly conduct
If a licensee/permittee knows or suspects that violent, quarrelsome, riotous, or disorderly conduct is occurring or
may occur in the licensed establishment/event site, the licensee/permittee must notify the police immediately.

[Licensee/Permittee Terms and Conditions Handbooks]

text:

heading: 17.0 Introduction
text:
Policies and procedures for identifying each of these contraventions are outlined in this section under the
following headings:
• Sell or serve liquor to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of intoxication,
• Allow a person in a service area to become intoxicated, and
• Allow an intoxicated person to enter or remain in a service area

17.1 Sell or serve liquor to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of intoxication
The licensee/permittee is responsible for managing and controlling the establishment/event site so that it does not
negatively affect patrons or the community. Intoxication is a serious public safety issue. Intoxicated patrons may
be a danger to themselves or the public. Intoxication can be a factor in many crimes, including domestic violence,
drug offences, assault and driving violations. Intoxication is also associated with behaviour that has a negative
impact on communities, including late night noise, vandalism, and unsanitary behaviour.

An intoxicated patron’s reasoning is inhibited by the alcohol and the patron may not be able to exercise sufficient
judgment to stop consuming liquor. As well, the inability to reason or act in a normal capacity creates a risk that
the patron will harm themselves or others.
Providing liquor to a person who is already intoxicated increases this
risk.

17.2 Prohibition against selling or serving liquor to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of
intoxication
A person must not sell or serve liquor to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of intoxication.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.61(2)(a)]

heading: 17.3 Determining the state of intoxication
text:
The Act does not define “intoxication,” nor does the Regulation.

Intoxication is a state in which a person's normal capacity to act or reason is inhibited by alcohol or drugs.

Unlike the legal definition of impairment for the purpose of operating a motor vehicle or boat, there is no one
scientific measure that determines whether a person is intoxicated. Consuming liquor or drugs affects a person’s
physical and mental faculties.

Determining whether a person is intoxicated requires:
• observing a person’s mental and physical state, and
• comparing the person’s mental and physical state and the expected behaviour from an ordinarily prudent
individual in like conditions.

Signs of Intoxication:
Appearance:
Liquor - red or bloodshot eyes, glassy eyed, unable to focus, drooping eye lids; lack of eye contact, body tremors,
dishevelled, unkempt, a flushed or red face, unusual sweating, an odour of liquor, nauseous or vomiting,
sleepiness, head bobbing or requiring support, comatose.
Cannabis - red eyes, odour of cannabis, anxiety, delusional, depressed, suspicious

Diminished motor skills:
Liquor - unsteady on their feet, staggering, long, exaggerated or lurching steps, extreme and needless care in
walking, bumping into objects and people, unable to find the chair when sitting down, missing the table or chair

when leaning onto it, requiring an object for support (e.g.: a person or a wall), swaying from side to side, slowness
of breath, unable to handle small objects, e.g.: wallet, keys, bank cards, money or cell phone.
Cannabis - impaired cognition and perception, sleepiness, i

heading: 17.3 Determining the state of intoxication
text:
mpaired judgement

Atypical speech patterns: unable to get out the words, whispering unnecessarily, slurring, slow and deliberate
speech, poor or overstated enunciation, sudden bursts of unconnected or delayed speech (e.g.: cheering when the
goal was some time past), sudden variations in volume,

Misjudging distances: spilling a drink, missing the mouth when drinking, exaggerated care when setting down a
drink, fumbling with small objects (e.g.: keys, money, a cell phone), tripping downstairs,

Reduced Inhibitions: boasting, crude behaviour, unwarranted or unwelcome personal advances, aggressive verbal
intrusions, overstated and unruly interactions with others, persistence despite rejection or negative responses,
forgetful (e.g.: about drink orders or a recent conversation), belligerent or randomly rude, random kindness and
generosity to strangers (e.g.: buying a round for the house), sharing personal matters with strangers.

Irrational behaviour: reckless spending, unrestrained physical behaviour showing a disregard for others, openly
consuming drugs, urinating in public, disrobing, public or aggressive sexuality, picking fights, demanding
attention, ignoring the concerns of others.

The Assessment:
Each of the above behaviours may have a valid if not common explanation so while each of the above is a
symptom or sign of intoxication there may also be an alternate reason for the behaviour.

heading: 17.3 Determining the state of intoxication
text:
However, a combination
of the above behaviours will reinforce an assessment of intoxication and weaken alternate explanations.

The inspector or police officer must document and be able to describe enough signs of intoxication with a level of
detail so that a reasonable person would - sometime later - make the same assessment as the inspector at the time
in question. And the combination of indicators must be adequate to exclude on the balance of probabilities
alternate justification for the activity described.

heading: 17.8 Allow an Intoxicated Person to Enter or Remain in a Service Area
text:
To avoid the possibility of further liquor consumption and avoid any harm to other patrons or staff, a
licensee/permittee must not allow a person who is intoxicated or showing signs of intoxication to enter or remain
in the part of the establishment/event site where liquor is served. To ensure their safety, intoxicated persons may
remain in unlicensed areas of an establishment/event site while waiting for assistance or a ride home.

17.9 Prohibition against allowing an intoxicated person to enter or remain in a service area
A licensee/permittee must not allow an intoxicated person, or a person showing signs of intoxication to enter or
remain in that part of the establishment/event site where liquor is sold, served, or otherwise supplied.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.61(2)(b)(ii)]

21. what, if anything, the licensee/permittee, or staff did to remove the person from the establishment/event site,
and
4. Based on the evidence gathered, if the inspector forms the opinion that a contravention occurred, the inspector
will issue an electronic notification of noncompliance alleging a contravention of either:
• Allow an intoxicated person to enter or remain in a service area, s.61(2)(b)(ii) LCLA
(Licensee/Permittee)

heading: 18.0 Introduction
text:
Under section 61(4)(c) of the Act, it is an offence for a person to possess a knife or weapon without lawful excuse
in a licensed establishment or event site. Licensees and permittees must make sure people with weapons do not
enter or remain in their establishments or event sites. Policies and procedures for identifying this contravention
are outlined in this section under the heading:
• Allow a person with a knife or weapon to enter or remain an establishment or event site

18.1 Allow a person with a knife or weapon to enter or remain in an establishment or event site
The consumption of liquor affects behaviour and judgment. It reduces natural inhibitions. There is a greater
likelihood of a volatile and dangerous situation occurring when a patron has been consuming liquor and is in
possession of a weapon. A licensee/permittee must manage and control the behaviour of patrons to ensure the
safety of staff, patrons, and the community. Allowing a person with a knife or weapon to enter a licensed
establishment or event site is a serious public safety concern.
A licensee/permittee must not allow a person with a knife, firearm, or weapon to enter or remain in a licensed
establishment/event site if the licensee/permittee knows that the person has the weapon in their possession without
a lawful excuse.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.61(2)(b)(v)]
If a licensee or permittee knows or suspects that a person has a knife or weapon, the licensee/permittee should
notify the police immediately.

[Licensee Terms and Conditions Handbook]
[Special Event Permit Terms and Conditions Handbook]
“Weapon” means anything used, designed to be used, or intended for use:
• in causing death or injury to any person, or for the purpose of threatening or intimidating any person.
[Criminal Code of Canada, s.2]

heading: 18.5 Possession of a weapon for self-protection
text:
Self-protection is not a lawful excuse for possession of a weapon in a licensed establishment, event area or special
event area.

18.6 Elements of contravention: “allow a person with a knife weapon to enter or remain an establishment or
event site”
To allege the contravention of allow a person with a knife or weapon to enter an establishment or event site, an
inspector must gather evidence to demonstrate that:
• the person had a knife or weapon in their possession,
• the person did not have lawful excuse to possess the knife or weapon,
• the person was allowed to enter the licensed establishment or event site with the knife or weapon,
• the person was allowed to remain in the licensed establishment or event site with the weapon.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector knows or suspects that a person in a licensed establishment or event site has a knife or weapon,
the inspector will contact the police immediately. If there is potential for harm to the inspector or a volatile
situation, the inspector will leave the establishment or event site,

2. The inspector will document that he/she observed a person in possession of a knife or weapon and if safe to do
so will notify the licensee,
3. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention.

text:
The inspector may:
• interview staff,
• interview the licensee/permittee,
• if it is safe to do so, interview other patrons and obtain names and contact information,
• interview and obtain notes from any police officers in attendance, and/or
• obtain any surveillance videos from the licensee/permittee.

heading: SECTION 19: DISTURBANCE OF PERSONS IN THE VICINITY
text:
19.0 Introduction
Section 51(1)(c) of the Act allows the general manager to take enforcement action against a licensee or permittee
who contravenes the term and condition by failing to take reasonable measures to ensure that the operation of
their establishment or event site does not disturb persons in the vicinity of the establishment or event site.
Procedures for identifying this contravention are outlined in this section under the heading:
• Fail to comply with term and condition that requires licensee or permittee to take reasonable measures to
ensure that operation of the establishment or event site does not disturb persons in the vicinity

19.1 Fail to comply with term and condition that requires licensee or permittee to take reasonable measures to
ensure that operation of the establishment or event site does not disturb persons in the vicinity
Noise emanating from a licensed establishment/event site or from patrons entering or exiting the
establishment/event site may disturb neighbouring businesses and residents. Indecent or illegal behaviour by
patrons entering or exiting the establishment/event site may result in property damage and/or public safety
concerns.

Regard for community standards is one of the two operating principles that guide the branch’s regulation of
liquor. While it is not the intention of the branch to make licensees/permittees responsible for policing the streets
around their establishments or event sites.
The operational practices of licensees/permittees influence whether an
establishment/event site has a negative or positive effect on the surrounding community. Licensees/permittees
cannot prevent every incident occurring around establishments/event sites, but they do have an influence over the
number and severity of incidents and their effect on people in the vicinity.

heading: 19.2 Action against licensee or permittee
text:
The general manager may take action against a licensee/permittee who fails to take reasonable measures to ensure
that the operation of the establishment/event site is not contrary to the public interest and does not disturb persons
in the vicinity of the establishment/event site. In order for this contravention to be enforced, it must be established
within the applicable Terms and Conditions Handbooks.

[Licensee/Permittee Terms and Conditions Handbooks]

19.3 Elements of contravention: “fail to comply with term and condition that requires licensee or permittee to
take reasonable measures to ensure that operation of the establishment or event site does not disturb persons in the
vicinity”
• the licence or special event permit term and condition requires taking of reasonable measures against
disturbance of persons in the vicinity,
• the licensee or permittee did not take reasonable measures against disturbance of persons in the vicinity of
the establishment or event site,
• the operation of the establishment or event site resulted in disturbance to persons in the vicinity

In order to form the opinion that a licensee/permittee has committed a contravention, the inspector must identify a
pattern of disturbances which can be linked to a particular establishment/event site. In general, the inspector will
not issue an electronic notification of noncompliance for isolated or occasional incidents.

heading: 19.2 Action against licensee or permittee
text:
Where there is more
than one establishment/event site in the same area, the inspector will need to collect evidence to establish which
establishment/event site is responsible for the disturbance such as:
• the licensee/permittee is operating the establishment/event site without reasonable measures to prevent
disturbance to persons in the vicinity,
• the operation of the establishment/event site has resulted in disturbance to persons in the vicinity of the
establishment,
• the branch has informed the licensee/permittee of the disturbances and reasonable measures that should be
taken to prevent the disturbances,
• the licensee/permittee has not implemented the reasonable measures within a specified time period, and

• persons in the vicinity of the establishment/event site continue to be disturbed.

19.4 Determining whether the licensee/permittee is operating the establishment or event site without taking
reasonable measures to prevent disturbance to persons in the vicinity
When determining whether a licensee/permittee is operating an establishment or event site without taking
reasonable measures to prevent disturbances to persons in the vicinity, the inspector will consider the number and
severity of incidents and/or contraventions that have happened both inside and outside of the establishment or
event site.

heading: 19.2 Action against licensee or permittee
text:
Incidents and/or contraventions that may indicate that a licensee/permittee is operating the
establishment/event site without taking reasonable measures to prevent disturbance to persons in the vicinity
include:
• violent, quarrelsome, riotous, or disorderly conduct,
• unlawful activities or conduct,
• excessive noise that results in complaints,
• in the case of a Food Primary establishment operating outside its licence purpose, particularly a food-primary
operating as a liquor-primary establishment,
• patrons urinating or defecating in the vicinity,
• patrons vomiting or passing out in the vicinity,
• excessive littering in the vicinity that can be attributed to patrons of the establishment, and/or
• nuisance complaints from the surrounding properties that require police response.

heading: 19.5 Determining the vicinity of the establishment/event site
text:
A two to three block radius, or its equivalent, will generally be considered the vicinity of the establishment/event
site.

19.6 Determining whether the measures taken by a licensee or permittee to prevent disturbances are reasonable
Reasonable measures are those measures that are:
• reasonable in the circumstances, and
• reasonably within the capacity of the licensee/permittee to effect.

Reasonable measures are steps or strategies that licensees/permittees take to ensure their establishments/event
sites are run in a safe and considerate manner. The reasonableness of measures may vary from
establishment/event site to establishment/event site depending on the circumstances. For example, if the
establishment/event site has never had complaints or problems relating to noise, it may not be reasonable to
expect security staff to stop all exiting patrons and instruct them on respectful behaviour in the adjacent parking
lot.

heading: 19.5 Determining the vicinity of the establishment/event site
text:
However, if an establishment/event site has experienced problems and complaints, this may be a reasonable
measure for the licensee/permittee to employ to ensure the operation of the establishment/event site does not
disturb persons in the vicinity.

heading: 20.0 Introduction
text:
A liquor licence sets out either the maximum number of patrons permitted within the areas where liquor may be
consumed (patron capacity) or the maximum number of persons allowed in the establishment, including both
patrons and staff (person capacity).

All licences issued after December 2, 2002, set out a maximum person capacity and this capacity is equal to the
occupant load for the establishment. Licences issued prior to December 2, 2002, may state either a person or
patron capacity. This capacity may be less than the occupant load.
The penalty schedule includes two contraventions for overcrowding in a licensed establishment:
• exceeding the person or patron capacity in service area but occupant load not exceeded, and
• exceeding the person or patron capacity and occupant load in service area the number of persons is greater
than the occupant load.

Overcrowding that exceeds the occupant load presents a greater risk to public safety than overcrowding that does
not exceed the occupant load, and this is reflected in the penalty schedule. However, policies and procedures for
identifying these contraventions are the same and are grouped together in this section under the following
heading:
• Overcrowding

heading: 20.1 Overcrowding
text:
Licensees that exceed their capacity by overcrowding are operating contrary to the public interest. Specifically,
they are operating contrary to the principles of public safety and community standards.
The issue of public safety is most apparent when the overcrowding exceeds the occupant load. Getting out of a
building safely during a fire or other threat is difficult in a place where liquor is served, music is loud, and lighting
is dim. The risk of death or severe injury is greater when the building is overcrowded.

The public interest in community standards is also relevant to the contravention of overcrowding. The maximum
capacity established for a liquor-primary licence is the result of community input during the licensing process.
The maximums are set so as to reduce the risk of negative impacts on neighbourhoods and communities. These
negative impacts include late night disturbances, parking problems and traffic flow problems. Allowing licensees
to exceed their approved capacity effectively negates this community input.
Patron capacity means the maximum number of patrons that may be in the service area of the establishment. The
service area is designated by the general manager under section 73 of the Act as the area where liquor may be
sold, served, and consumed.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.73]
Person capacity means the maximum number of persons allowed in the establishment by the general manager.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.72]

heading: 20.4 Definition of occupant load
text:
Occupant load means the lesser of the following:
• A maximum number of persons allowed in the service area or at the event site under building regulations as
defined in section 1 of the Building Act,
• The maximum number of persons allowed in the service area or at the event site under the British Columbia
Fire Code adopted under the British Columbia Fire Code Regulation, and

• The maximum number of persons allowed in the service area or at the event site under any other safety
requirements enacted, made, or established by the local government or First Nation or treaty first nation for the
area in which the establishment or event site is located.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.145]

20.5 Prohibition against overcrowding beyond person capacity for licences issued or amended after December 2,
The number of people in an establishment must not exceed the person capacity set by the general manager if the
licence is a:
• food-primary licence,
• liquor-primary licence,
• a temporary use area endorsement endorsed on a liquor primary or food primary licence; or
a lounge, special event area or picnic endorsement, endorsed on manufacturer licence and
• issued after December 2, 2002, or amended in accordance with section 72 of the regulation.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.72]

20.6 Prohibition against overcrowding beyond person or patron capacity for licences issued before December 2,
The person or patron capacity of a licence issued before December 2, 2002, remains in effect as a term and
condition of the licence until rescinded or amended by the general
manager.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.73(2)]
[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 20.7 Taking person or patron counts
text:
Whenever an inspector inspects an establishment and believes it may be overcrowded, the inspector will, after
considering any safety concerns, count the number of patrons or persons present. The inspector will not factor a
margin of error into the count.

The inspector will conduct at least two counts, unless after conducting the first count the inspector determines it
necessary to leave the establishment for reasons of personal safety. Prior to conducting a count, the inspector
must:
• test their mechanical counters to a count of at least 50 to ensure they are operating correctly and note the date
and time the counter was tested,
• when taking a patron count, to count all the persons in the establishment and then (after confirming with the
licensee, manager, or supervisor the number of establishment employees on duty), subtract that number from
the total person count to determine the actual patron count, and
• at the inspector’s discretion, he/she may confirm with the licensee, manager, or supervisor the number of
establishment employees on duty before or after the conduct of count and or requesting the licensee, manager
or supervisor conduct a count.)

The inspector will record the results of both counts, whether or not they are the same.

heading: 20.8 Consistent process of the count
text:
Procedure:
Inspectors when conducting the count will:
In the case of a lone inspector:
1. in the case of a patron count, confirm with the licensee, manager or supervisor, the number of establishment
employees on duty (this may occur before or after the count at the inspector’s discretion),

2. conduct at minimum two separate counts both in a consistent process of execution (i.e.: from a vantage point
to observe the entire service area, or left to right across service area, or walking from one side of the service
area to the other, etc.), and
3. should enlist the establishment licensee, manager, or supervisor to also conduct at least two separate counts.
(this may be at the inspector’s discretion and before, after or simultaneous to the inspector’s initial count).
In the case of two or more inspectors:
4. in the case of a patron count, confirm with the licensee, manager or supervisor, the number of establishment
employees on duty,
5. the inspectors should determine the best strategy for conducting a count of that particular establishment. This
should include the same number of counts (i.e.: each inspector conducts a minimum of two counts), and
6. for constancy, each inspector is to conduct each of their individual counts in a consistent process of execution
and document the method of the count (i.e.: mechanical counter) etc.

heading: 20.9 Licensee procedures to prevent overcrowding
text:
A responsible licensee will implement procedures to ensure that overcrowding does not occur. Procedures may
include:
• having one or more security door staff,
• monitoring back entrances,
• ensuring all security door staff have counters,
• ensuring all staff are clearly aware of the licensed capacity of the establishment, and/or
• ensuring that, in establishments with multiple points of entry, procedures are in place to monitor the number
of patrons entering and exiting.

The general manager may impose procedures to prevent overcrowding as terms and conditions on a licence. The
terms and conditions may include any or all of the procedures described above.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.15]

heading: 20.10 Elements of contraventions related to: “overcrowding”
text:
To allege contraventions related to overcrowding beyond the person or patron capacity, an inspector must gather
evidence that:
• the number of patrons or persons in the establishment exceeded the licensed person or patron capacity but not
the occupant load, or
• the number of patrons or persons in the establishment exceeded the licensed person capacity and the occupant
load.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector suspects that an establishment may be overcrowded, the inspector will observe and document
the activities of security door staff, or other staff members, before notifying the licensee of their concerns,
2. In accordance with “Taking person or patron counts”, the inspector will take an initial count. Prior to taking
the count the inspector will review the licence and floor plan to verify the patron or person capacity, the layout
of the areas, area capacities and, if available, the occupant load,
3. If, after taking the initial count, the inspector concludes that an establishment may be over its licensed
capacity, the inspector will gather further evidence for each element of the contravention. The inspector may:
• take a count of the total patrons in the establishment or a specific area to determine if the establishment or
area is over its patron capacity.

heading: 20.10 Elements of contraventions related to: “overcrowding”
text:
The inspector may ask the licensee to identify staff members, so they can be
subtracted from the total person count,
• take a count of all persons in the establishment or a specific area to determine if the establishment or area is
over its person capacity,
• ask the licensee, manager, or supervisor to take a count,
• interview door staff and ask to see the numbers recorded on their counters,
• ask a police officer to take a count of the patrons and staff in the establishment if a police officer is present,

• interview the licensee and ask for a copy of the documentation from the local government authority that
certifies the current occupant load,
• contact headquarters licensing department to confirm the patron or person capacity and determine whether
or not the licensee has applied for an increase in capacity, and/or
• contact the appropriate local government authority to determine the occupant load of the establishment,
whether the licensee has applied to increase the occupant load of the establishment and the status of any
application,

Note: If due to the combination of the number of patrons, the insufficient lighting or loud music, the inspector is
not able to make an accurate count, he/she may ask the licensee to turn off the music and turn up the lights. If this
request is made and not granted, the inspector will note this in the inspector’s notebook.

6.
If the establishment is overcrowded, the inspector will tell the licensee to reduce the number of people in the
establishment.

heading: 21.0 Introduction
text:
Unlawful liquor is any liquor that has not been purchased, kept, prepared, served, or sold in compliance with the
Act, regulation or terms and conditions of a licence. Unlawful liquor includes:
• liquor purchased “over the counter” from a government liquor store by a licensee without identifying as a
licensee,
• liquor which has been smuggled from other provinces or other countries,
• liquor provided as an inducement by a manufacturer,
• adulterated or watered-down liquor,
• illegally manufactured (illicit) liquor including UBrew or UVin products and home distilled or home
fermented liquor,
• medicinal, confectionery, or culinary preparations used as a beverage or in mixed drinks,
• stolen liquor,
• diverted liquor products intended for export only, and
• non-duty paid liquor products.

Unlawful liquor is a public safety priority for the branch. It has many negative social and financial consequences
that result in a financial burden on taxpayers and lost government revenue.

Unlawful liquor:
• may contain contaminants that can cause illness or death,
• contributes to job loss and unfair competition, and
• undermines the integrity of the province’s liquor control system and therefore threatens the safeguards that
protect communities from the negative aspects of liquor consumption.

A number of provisions in the LCLA deal with the issue of unlawful liquor or relate procedurally to inspections
for unlawful liquor.

heading: 21.0 Introduction
text:
The regulation also prescribes certain practical measures to ensure that liquor purchases are
from appropriate sources and that those purchases are properly accounted for.

Schedule 2 to the LCLR identifies six contraventions under the category of “Unlawful Sale and Purchase of
Liquor.” Procedures for identifying these contraventions are included in this section under the following
headings:
• Unlawful sale of liquor,
• Unlawful purchase of liquor,
• Improper or unauthorized liquor storage,
• Sell or serve unauthorized liquor
• Sell or serve liquor purchased under another licence or permit,
• Fail to keep register of liquor purchases,
• Purchase liquor without recording the purchase against the licence number,
• Sell or serve liquor purchased under the authority of another licence or permit, and
• Dilute or adulterate liquor or refill or add to the bottle or container

heading: 21.1 Unlawful sale of liquor
text:
The unauthorized sale of liquor or the sale of liquor that has not been purchased from the Liquor Distribution
Branch is an extremely serious contravention that incurs the highest minimum penalty ranges outlined in Schedule
2. Illegally manufactured liquor or home fermented, or distilled products are unregulated and may pose a serious
threat to the health and safety of patrons who consume them.

The sale of liquor that has been:
• purchased from other jurisdictions,
• received as samples or gifts from manufacturers,

• smuggled, or
• stolen, and
• results in revenue loss to government and unfair competition in the legitimate liquor industry.

Licensees and permittees are responsible for the liquor sold or kept for sale at their establishments or event sites.
If a licensee purchases an establishment, including the liquor stock, it is their responsibility to ensure that the
stock only contains liquor purchased from the Liquor Distribution Branch.
A licensee/permittee must not:
• keep liquor for sale
• sell liquor,
• give liquor for other consideration, or
• take liquor for other consideration
except as provided under the LCLA or the Liquor Distribution Act

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.8(2)(a)]

heading: 21.3 Presumption that liquor found in licensed establishment/event site is kept for sale
text:
In an enforcement hearing, the general manager may presume that a licensee/permittee has sold, kept for sale or
given liquor contrary to the LCLA and Regulation based on:
• the kind and quantity of liquor found in the licensed establishment, event site or any storage areas, and/or
• the circumstances under which it is kept.

Unless the licensee/permittee presents convincing evidence to the contrary, the branch considers that liquor
located in liquor service or storage areas is kept for sale to patrons.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.8(2)(a)]
Liquor kept for culinary purposes must stay in the kitchen area away from liquor kept for sale.
To allege the contravention of unlawful sale of liquor, an inspector must gather evidence that:
• the licensee/permittee kept liquor for sale or sold liquor,
• the liquor kept for sale or sold by the licensee/permittee was not kept for sale or sold in accordance with the
Act the regulations or the terms and conditions of the licence or special event permit.
The general manager has established terms and conditions respecting the storage of liquor:
• private liquor belonging to a licensee, employee or patron must not be kept at a licensed establishment or in
storage areas associated with the establishment,
• requirements for storage of product by liquor manufacturers and UBrew/UVin licensees and permittees

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 21.7 Elements of contravention: “improper/unauthorized liquor storage”
text:
To allege the contravention of improperly storing liquor, an inspector must gather evidence that:
• the licensee/permittee kept liquor at the establishment/event site, and
• the liquor was stored contrary to the terms and conditions of the licence or permit

Procedure:

1. If an inspector suspects that a licensee/permittee is unlawfully selling liquor or is improperly storing liquor,
the inspector may:

2. The inspector will gather evidence of each element of the contravention.

heading: 21.8 Dilute or adulterate liquor
text:
To ensure product safety and fair value to patrons, section 144(1) of the Regulation prohibits licensees/permittees
from watering down, adding to, or otherwise diluting or adulterating liquor, except when filling a customer’s
drink order. A licensee or permittee must not dilute or adulterate liquor or keep for sale, sell, or serve liquor that
has been diluted or adulterated.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.144(1)(a) & (b)]
A licensee may pre-mix drinks in a suitable container in anticipation of a patron ordering a drink. A licensee may
not circulate trays of pre-mixed or pre-poured drinks that have not been ordered by patrons.

[Licensee Terms and Conditions Handbook]
A licensee/permittee must not dilute, or adulterate liquor purchased from the Liquor Distribution Branch for any
purpose other than upon the request of a customer ordering a drink or in anticipation of a patron ordering a drink.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.144(1)]

heading: 21.11 Elements of contravention: “dilute or adulterate liquor”
text:
To allege the contravention of diluting or adulterating liquor, an inspector must gather enough evidence to prove
each of the following elements on a balance of probabilities:
• the licensee or permittee has diluted or adulterated liquor, and
• the licensee or permittee kept for sale, sold, or served liquor that had been diluted or adulterated,
• the dilution or adulteration was not done at the request of a person ordering a drink

heading: 21.12 Prohibition against refilling or adding to bottles or containers
text:
A licensee/permittee must not refill a bottle or container or add to the contents of a bottle or container purchased
from the Liquor Distribution Branch. For these reasons, a licensee/permittee cannot produce what is commonly
known as barrel oaked or aged liquor (not aged in its original container) or infused liquor in which substances
(e.g.: herbs, spices, or fruit) are added to the liquor to create customized spirits.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.144(3)(a)]

heading: 21.13 Elements of contravention: “refill or add to bottle or container”
text:
To allege the contravention of refill or add to bottle or container, an inspector must gather enough evidence to
prove that:
• the licensee/permittee purchased a bottle or container of liquor,
• the licensee/permittee added to or refilled the bottle or container.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes a licensee/permittee or staff member diluting or adulterating liquor or refilling a
bottle or container, the inspector will observe and document the actions of the licensee/permittee or staff
member before alerting the licensee/permittee to their concerns,
2. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention.

heading: 21.14 Unlawful purchase of liquor
text:
As with the contravention of unlawfully selling liquor, branch concerns with respect to the purchase of liquor
other than through the Liquor Distribution Branch or another designated outlet include:
• health and safety concerns associated with liquor products that are not regulated or inspected,
• revenue loss to government,
• unfair competition in the legitimate liquor industry, and
• undermining the integrity of the liquor control system.

A licensee who purchases liquor from other than a Liquor Distribution Branch outlet or another designated outlet
commits the contravention “Unlawful Purchase of Liquor.”
A person must not purchase liquor or take liquor for other consideration from another person except as provided
in the Act, the Liquor Distribution Act or the regulations made under either of those Acts.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.8(2)(e)]
In addition to government liquor stores, the Liquor Distribution Branch may specifically designate outlets where
licensees/permittees may purchase liquor. Currently, designated outlets include the following:
• rural licensee retail stores,
• on-site agency stores at licensed wineries, breweries, and distilleries,
• independent wine stores, and
• Brewers' Distributors Ltd.

heading: 21.17 Elements of contravention: “unlawful purchase of liquor”
text:
To allege the contravention of unlawful purchase of liquor, an inspector must gather evident to demonstrate that:
• the licensee/permittee purchased liquor, and

conditions of the licence or special event permit.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector suspects that a licensee/permittee has unlawfully purchased liquor, the inspector may gather
evidence of the contravention during the course of a regular inspection,
2. The inspector will gather evidence of each element of the contravention identified.
