heading: 21.18 Failing to keep a register of liquor purchases
text:
While it is not a contravention relating to the purchase or sale of unlawful liquor, the failure to maintain a register
of all liquor purchased and received under a licence may be an indicator that a licensee is purchasing or selling
unlawful liquor. The liquor register is a useful tool both for licensees and inspectors to reconcile the liquor in the
establishment with liquor purchases made through the Liquor Distribution Branch or a designated outlet.
Although inspectors may also obtain this information directly from the Liquor Distribution Branch, licensees are
expected to keep a register of liquor purchases and have it available for inspection so that inspectors are able to
immediately identify any unlawful liquor in an establishment.

heading: 21.19 Licensee must keep a register of liquor purchases
text:
A licensee must keep a register (receipts, invoices) of all liquor purchased and received under the licence as well
as any and transfers for a period of at least six years from the making of each entry. The liquor register must be a
chronological filing of an establishment’s documentation that the licensee signs and receives when picking up
orders from the Liquor Distribution Branch or designated outlet. The licensee also must keep this information
separate from receipts for non-liquor items.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulations, s.80(4)]

heading: 21.20 System of accounting for spoilage or breakage is part of liquor register
text:
The licensee must be able to account for liquor that was lost due to spoilage or breakage. This may be
accomplished by keeping a written record in a logbook or by making a notation on the receipt or invoice for the
liquor in questions. The system or records used to account for the replacement of faulty kegs by credit from a
brewer’s agent are considered to be part of a licensee’s liquor register.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]
21.21 Elements of contravention: “fail to keep register of liquor purchases”
• the licensee failed to prepare and keep a register of liquor purchases,
• the licensee failed to keep the register for a period of at least 6 years from making of each entry

21.22 Failing to keep a record of liquor spoilage and breakage or replacement of faulty kegs as part of liquor
register
The general manager has established terms and conditions respecting the keeping of records for liquor spillage
and breakage and replacement of faulty kegs from a brewer's agent.

21.23 Elements of contravention: “failing to keep a record of liquor spoilage and breakage or replacement of
faulty kegs as part of liquor register”
• the licensee had to keep records of liquor spillage and breakage as part of the liquor register,
• they did not keep a record of replacement of faulty kegs from a brewer's agent, or
• the licensee was not able to produce a record of the spillage and breakage, or
• the licensee was not able to produce a record of replacement of faulty kegs from a brewer's agent

heading: 21.24 Failing to have liquor register available at the time of inspection
text:
The general manager has established terms and conditions respecting the keeping of a liquor register. Licensees
must keep a liquor register, and it must be available for inspection at all times. Liquor registers may be hardcopy
or digital. A licensee must keep the register for a period of at least 6 years from the making of each entry.

21.25 Elements of contravention: “fail to have liquor register available at the time of inspection”
• the licensee is required to have the liquor register available for inspection at all times,
• the licensee failed to have the liquor register available at the time of the inspection

Procedure:

1. If a licensee is unable to produce an accurate and complete liquor register for the establishment, the inspector
will document the evidence of the contravention, including:
• the number of times the inspector asked to see the liquor register,
• the circumstances surrounding the requests,
• any explanation provided by the licensee for the lack of a liquor register,
• the time period the licensee was given to produce the liquor register, and/or
• a description and copies of any records produced
2. Based on the evidence gathered, if the inspector forms the opinion that a contravention occurred, the inspector
will issue an electronic notification of noncompliance to the licensee alleging:
• Fail to keep a register of liquor purchases, s.
80(4) LCLR (Licensee), or
• Fail to have liquor register available at time of inspection, T&C (Licensee), or
• Fail to keep a record of liquor spoilage and breakage or replacement of faulty kegs as part of liquor
register, T&C (Licensee)

heading: 21.26 Purchase liquor without recording the purchase against the licence number
text:
To ensure accurate records of liquor purchases, licensees must purchase liquor from authorized Liquor
Distribution outlets and provide their licence number with every purchase. Accurate liquor purchase records help
the branch identify unlawful liquor and are used to calculate annual licence fees based on the value of a licensee’s
liquor purchases.

21.27 Prohibition against purchasing liquor without recording the purchase against the licence number
A licensee must purchase liquor for the licensed establishment only:
• from a government liquor store designated in writing by the general manager or other outlet designated by the
Liquor Distribution Branch, and
• after identifying themselves as a licensee and providing their licence number for the purchase.

[Licensee Terms and Conditions Handbook]

21.28 Elements of contravention: “purchase liquor without recording the purchase against the licence number”
To allege the contravention of purchase liquor without recording the purchase against the licence number, an
inspector must gather evidence to show that:
• the licensee has purchased liquor for sale in their licensed establishment,
• the licensee did not record the purchase against their licence number.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector suspects that a licensee has purchased liquor without recording the purchase against their
licence number, the inspector will gather evidence of either element of the contravention.

heading: 21.29 Selling or serving liquor purchased under the authority of another licence or permit
text:
Unless authorized by the general manager, a licensee/permittee may only sell or serve liquor that has been
purchased under that establishments licence or special event permit. It is necessary to accurately account for all
liquor purchased and sold under a licence/permit because of the potential impact on liquor licence/permit fees or
other revenue related fees and taxes.

21.30 Prohibition against selling or serving liquor that was purchased under the authority of another
licence or permit
A licensee must not sell or provide liquor that was purchased under the authority of another licence/permit, unless
otherwise authorized by the general manager.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.140]

heading: 21.31 Multiple establishments within the same facility and under the same ownership
text:
A licensee who owns more than one licensed establishment within the same facility may sell liquor in one
establishment that has been purchased under the licence of another establishment within the facility, so long as
neither establishment is a licensee retail store. For example, a licensee who owns a hotel with both a liquor-
primary and food-primary licence may purchase liquor for both establishments under the liquor-primary licence.

SECTION 22: LIQUOR SERVICE

heading: 22.0 Introduction
text:
Items 21 through 28 of the Penalty Schedule outline a number of contraventions to do with liquor service. Laws
and policies regarding liquor service are directed at preventing over-service and intoxication, maintaining the
support of communities, and avoiding disturbances. Procedures for these contraventions are outlined in this
section under the following headings:
• Operate establishment or event site without prescribed training program or re-certification,
• Allow a person to sell or serve liquor without prescribed training program or re-certification,
• Allow a person to supervise the sale or service of liquor without prescribed training program or re-
certification,
• Fail to clear patrons within ½ hour after the end of the hours of liquor service,
• Fail to take liquor from patrons within ½ hour after the end of the hours of liquor service,
• Allow a person to consume liquor more than half an hour after liquor service ends,
• Allow a person to consume liquor in a service area after ½ hour after the end of hours of liquor service,
• Licensee or permittee consume liquor while working,
• Permit liquor not sold or served by licensee or permittee to be consumed,
• Allow liquor to be taken from the service area, and
• Liquor quantities, pricing, and sales strategies

22.1 Operate establishment or event site without prescribed training program or re-certification
Serving It Right: The Responsible Beverage Service Program is a correspondence course that: educates licensees,
permittees, supervisors, managers, and servers about their legal responsibilities when serving liquor.

heading: 22.0 Introduction
text:
It provides
effective techniques to prevent problems related to over-service, service to minors and service to intoxicated
patrons.

Note: A Serving It Right certificate is required for permittees, supervisors, and managers for events with 500 or
more attendees. Special Event Server training is required for all permittees, supervisors, and managers for events
with fewer than 500 attendees. All event servers (paid or unpaid), regardless of the size of the event, must
complete Special Event Server training.

heading: 22.0 Introduction
text:
If a person has a valid Serving It Right certificate, they are not required to
complete Special Event Server training as well.

The following table shows who is required to complete Serving It Right (SIR) or Special Event Server (SES)
training:

attendees

22.2 Licensee/permittee must complete prescribed training program or recertification prior to operating
establishment or event site
Subject to sub-section 22.6, the prescribed training program or re-certification must be completed by:
• all licensees of liquor primary, liquor primary club, food primary, licensee retail store and rural licensee retail
store establishments,
• all licensees of winery, cidery, brewery, and distillery establishments with sampling rooms and wineries with
endorsements,
• all special event permittees, and training must be completed prior to operating an event site

If the licensee/Permittee is a private or public corporation, the prescribed training program or re-certification must
be completed by a director, officer, or employee of the corporation responsible for controlling the sale of liquor in
the establishment or at the event site.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.60]

22.3 Elements of contravention: “operate establishment or event site without prescribed training program or re-
certification”
To allege the contravention of failing operate establishment or event site without the prescribed training program
or re-certification, an inspector

heading: 22.0 Introduction
text:
must gather evidence that:
• the person holds a liquor licence to operate an establishment, and
• the person operated the establishment under the liquor licence without completing the prescribed training
program or re-certification as required by the regulations,
or
• the person is a special event permittee, and
• the person held a special event without the prescribed training or re-certification as required by the
regulations
Licensees and permittees must ensure all sellers and servers in a licensed establishment or at an event site as well
as those who supervise the sale and service of liquor must complete the prescribed training program or
recertification.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.60(1)]
[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.184 to s.190]
(Licensee/Permittee Terms and Conditions Handbook]
Effective 30, September 2020, there is no longer a grace period for completion of the prescribed training program
or recertification.

heading: 22.6 Responsible beverage service training programs from other Canadian jurisdictions
text:
Servers in all types of establishments relocating to British Columbia from other Canadian jurisdictions that have a
certificate showing proof of completion of one of the following responsible beverage service training programs:
• Pro-serve Program (Alberta),

• Serve it Right (Saskatchewan),
• It’s Good Business (Manitoba),
• Smart Serve (Ontario),
• Service in Action (Quebec),
• It’s Good Business: Responsible Service of Alcohol (New Brunswick),
• It’s Good Business (Nova Scotia),
• It’s Our Business (Prince Edward Island),
• It’s Good Business: Responsible Service of Alcohol (Newfoundland and Labrador), and

Licensees are responsible for ensuring that servers and supervisors who have completed responsible beverage
service training in other jurisdictions are informed about relevant BC legislation, such as the legal drinking age
and any relevant operating terms and conditions that apply to their establishments.

22.7 Licensee must verify completion of the prescribed training program or re-certification
A licensee must verify that a person has successfully completed the prescribed training program or re-certification
before allowing the person to sell or serve liquor or supervise the sale or service of liquor in an establishment.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 22.8 Evidence of completion of prescribed training program or re-certification
text:
The regulation establishes that a licensee must keep records respecting employees who sell or serve liquor as
follows:
• The employee’s name,
• The number of the employee’s certificate of completion for the SIR program, and expiry date, that date, and
• If the employee meets the training requirements under section 60(2) of the LCLA by successful completion
of a liquor service training program offered by another province and if the certificate shows a date, that date.

The Terms and Conditions mandates that the licensee must produce upon request of an inspector or peace officer,
those records.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.80(k)]
[Licensee Terms and Conditions Handbook]

certification”
To allege the contravention of allow a person to sell or serve liquor without the prescribed training program or re-
certification, an inspector must gather evidence that:
• the licensee's employee or the permittee's staff sold or served liquor, and
• the employee or staff who sold or served the liquor did not possess the prescribed training program or re-
certification at the time of the sale or service.

training program or re-certification”

• the person did not hold the prescribed training program or re-certification at the time the employee of the

The hours when a liquor-primary licensed establishment is allowed to sell liquor are determined, in part, by

heading: 22.12 LP Licensee must clear patrons within ½ hour after the end of liquor service
text:
Unless otherwise authorized by the general manager, a liquor-primary, liquor-primary club or manufacturer
licensee with a lounge or special event area or picnic area endorsement must ensure that patrons leave the
establishment within half an hour after the licensed hours of liquor service end. In some communities, the general
manager has authorized patrons to remain in the establishment up to one hour after the licensed hours of liquor
service ends.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.89(a)&(b)]

22.13 Elements of contravention: “fail to clear patrons within ½ hour after the end of the hours of liquor service”
To allege the contravention of fail to clear patrons within ½ hour after the end of the hours of liquor service, an
inspector must gather evidence that:
• it is more than 1/2 hour after the end of the established hours of liquor service,
• there are still patrons in the service area of the licensed establishment, lounge or special event area or picnic
area endorsement

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes people in an establishment more than half an hour after licensed liquor service ended,
the inspector will observe and document the activities of the people and staff,
2. If it appears that the people are patrons, the inspector will gather further evidence for each element of the
contravention.

22.14 Fail to take liquor from patrons within ½ hour after the end of hours of liquor Service
The hours when a licensed establishment may sell liquor are determined, in part, by community standards. In
particular, hours of liquor sale affect the surrounding residents and businesses in the community. If a licensee fails
to take liquor from patrons in a food-primary licensed establishment, patrons may continue to consume liquor
while the restaurant remains open, even though the hours of liquor service have ended. This can result in the
establishment shifting its primary focus.

22.15 Liquor must be taken from patrons within ½ hour after the end of the hours of liquor service
Food-primary licensees must ensure that liquor is taken from patrons within one-half an hour after the licensed
hours of liquor service end, unless:
• otherwise authorized by the general manager, or
• the liquor is a bottle of wine that is unfinished by a patron and re-sealed by the licensee in accordance with
section 141(4)(a) LCLR.
As well, Caterer licensees and Food-Primary and Liquor-Primary licensees or a licensee who holds a Temporary
Use Area Authorization must ensure that liquor is taken from patrons within one-half an hour after the licensed
hours of liquor service end.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.90(1)(a)(b) & (c)]

heading: 22.16 Determining whether fluid is liquor or an alcoholic beverage
text:
To allege this contravention, an inspector does not need to prove that the contents of a glass or bottle are liquor or
an alcoholic beverage. Evidence such as:
• liquor bottles containing fluid, or
• glasses containing fluid of the appropriate colour and form, e.g.: amber clear liquor in a glass beside a beer
bottle support the conclusion that the licensee has failed to take liquor from patrons within the time legally
allowed. An inspector may take samples of liquor in order to support the inspector's conclusion that the fluid
in question is liquor.

22.17 Elements of contravention: “fail to take liquor from patrons within 1/2 hour after the end of the hours of
liquor service”
To allege the contravention of fail to take liquor from patrons within 1/2 hour after the end of the hours of liquor
service, an inspector must gather evidence that:
• it is more than 1/2 hour after the end of the established liquor service hours,
• there are still "patrons" in the service area of the establishment,
• the patrons are in possession of liquor

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes patrons with liquor more than half an hour after licensed liquor service ended, the
inspector will observe and document the activities of patrons and staff before notifying the licensee of their
concerns,
2. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention.

22.18 Allow a person to consume liquor in a service area after 1/2 hour after end of hours of liquor service
The hours when a licensed establishment may sell liquor are determined, in part, by community standards. Patrons
who consume liquor and leave an establishment after the licensed hours of liquor service may disturb nearby
residents and businesses. Selling liquor after hours also leads to unfair competition with other licensed
establishments.

22.19 Licensee must not allow a person to consume liquor more than ½ hour after liquor service ends
Unless otherwise authorized by the general manager, licensees must not allow a person to consume liquor
• in the licensed establishment, or
• in an area licensed under a temporary change to a licence
more than half an hour after the hours of liquor service indicated on the licence or change approval end.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.91(1) & (2)]
Licensees may serve liquor until 4:00 am on January 1, unless prohibited by local government bylaws or the
general manager has directed otherwise, so long as food is available to patrons.
On the night of a time change (i.e., the first Sunday in April and the last Sunday in October) licensees must
operate according to the hours in effect at the start of the Saturday business day and wait to change their clocks
until after liquor service has ended for that business day.

heading: 22.24 Licensee or permittee consuming liquor while working
text:
The licensee must manage and control the behaviour of patrons to ensure the safety of staff, patrons, and the
community. When the licensee or employees drink liquor while working, their judgment and ability to manage
and control the establishment are impaired. This creates a public safety risk for other staff, patrons, and the
community.

22.25 Licensees and employees and permittees and staff must not consume liquor while working
The licensee and employees of the licensee as well as permittee and staff of the permittee, including those
employees who provide entertainment, must not consume liquor in the licensed establishment or event site:

• while working, or
• during their lunch or other breaks, including breaks taken between shifts on the same day.
The licensee/permittee and employees/staff may consume liquor in the licensed establishment or at an event site
when they are not working if they are treated as regular patrons of the licensed establishment or event.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.142]
[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 22.26 Entertainers may consume liquor while working
text:
Adult, professional entertainers may consume liquor while in the establishment; however, employees who provide
entertainment (such as a house DJ or house band) may not do so during working hours. As with patrons, it is the
responsibility of the licensee to ensure that professional entertainers do not become intoxicated. If an entertainer
becomes intoxicated, they must be refused service, removed from the establishment/event site and the licensee
must see that they depart safely from the establishment. An intoxicated entertainer must not be allowed into the
licensed establishment.

heading: 22.27 Elements of contravention: “licensee or permittee consume liquor while working”
text:
To allege the contravention of consume liquor while working, an inspector must gather evidence that:
• the licensee/permittee or employee/staff consumed liquor, and
• the licensee/permittee or employee/staff was working at the time the liquor was consumed.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector suspects a licensee/permittee employee/staff consumed liquor while working, the inspector will
observe and document the activities of the licensee/permittee or employee/staff,
2. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention. The inspector may:
• examine products to determine if they are liquor,
• interview staff,
• interview the licensee/permittee/employee/staff,
• interview the employee/staff,
• obtain payroll records or work schedules,
• obtain a copy of the person’s job description or employment contract to determine whether the person is an
employee or a contractor, and/or
• seize liquor samples for testing and analysis,

heading: 22.28 Permitting liquor not sold or served by the licensee to be consumed
text:
Customers may not bring in their own bottles of liquor to consume in an establishment. This rule is part of the
larger regulatory scheme that, among other things, requires a licensee to purchase liquor from the Liquor
Distribution Branch and have those sales recorded on their licence. As with that rule, the purpose of prohibiting
the consumption of liquor not purchased in the establishment is to ensure the quality of liquor and prevent over-
consumption in licensed establishments. Over-consumption of liquor has an impact on public safety and
community standards and may impair the ability of the licensee to manage and control the establishment.

22.29 Prohibition against permitting consumption of liquor not purchased or served by licensee
A licensee must not allow people in the establishment to consume liquor that was not purchased from, or served
by, the licensee.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.141(2)]

22.30 Elements of contravention: “permit liquor not sold or served by licensee to be consumed”
To allege the contravention of permit liquor not sold or served by licensee to be consumed, an inspector must
gather evidence to demonstrate that:
• it was liquor that was being consumed, and
• the liquor had not been purchased from, or served by, the licensee.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes a person consuming liquor that does not appear to have been purchased or served in
the establishment, the inspector will observe and document the activities of the person and staff before
notifying the licensee of their concerns,
2.

heading: 22.31 Allowing liquor to be taken from the Ssrvice area
text:
To ensure that the licensee is able to monitor the consumption of liquor sold in the establishment, the situations in
which patrons may take liquor outside of the establishment or the red-lined area are restricted. In order to
minimize the risk of tampering with unattended drinks, patrons are permitted to take drinks into washrooms, so
long as licensees have procedures in place to supervise activities occurring there.

heading: 22.32 Prohibition against allowing liquor to be taken from the service area
text:
A licensee must not allow liquor sold or served in a licensed establishment to be taken from the service area, other
than:
• an unfinished bottle of wine that is sealed by the licensee, or
• liquor that is sold for consumption off premises in accordance with the Act, regulation and terms and
conditions of the licence, or
• As exempted by regulation

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.141(4)]

heading: 22.33 Elements of contravention: “allow liquor to be taken from the service area”
text:
To allege the contravention of allow liquor to be taken from the service area, an inspector must gather evidence
that:
• the person removed from the service area, liquor that was sold or served by the licensee or permittee,
• the removal was not authorized by the Act, regulation or terms and conditions of the licence or special event
permit,
• the licensee or permittee knew or ought to have known the removal of the liquor

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes a person removing liquor from the establishment or with liquor outside the
establishment, the inspector will observe and document the activities of the person and staff before notifying
the licensee of their concerns,
2. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention.

heading: 22.33 Elements of contravention: “allow liquor to be taken from the service area”
text:
The inspector may:
• review the terms and conditions of the licence,
• examine products to determine if they are liquor,

heading: 22.34 Liquor quantities, pricing and sales strategies
text:
Control of liquor prices is directed at preventing over-service, over-consumption, and loss of control within a
licensed establishment. In general, the price of liquor must not be so low that it is likely to lead to over-
consumption. The purpose of control of liquor pricing is to prevent destructive competition and its spillover
effects. These concepts are explained in section 2“Operating Environment”.

22.35 Prohibition against providing unlimited or unspecified quantities of liquor for a single price
A licensee must not provide unlimited or unspecified quantities of liquor for a single price. Licensees may offer
an all-inclusive package that includes liquor in the price, but the amount of liquor provided must be specified and
not unlimited.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.82(1)(a) and s.118(a)]

22.36 Prohibition against using a sales strategy that is likely to promote or encourage intoxication
A licensee must not use a sales strategy that is likely to promote or encourage intoxication. Prohibited sales
strategies include:
• selling drinks “two for one,”
• cheap drink or free drink nights, or
• serving drinks that are larger than the maximum drink sizes.

Maximum drink sizes per person are:
• three ounces (85 ml) of distilled liquor,

• single servings of no more than 24 oz (682 ml) or smaller servings of multiple brands, provided the total
served at one time is no more than 24 oz (680 ml) of draught beer.

heading: 22.34 Liquor quantities, pricing and sales strategies
text:
(A Canadian pint is 568 ml.) Pitchers or
other multiple serving containers shared by two or more patrons may contain no more than 1.5 litres of
draught beer,
• two standard sized bottles or one large sized bottle of beer (up to 24 oz or 680 ml), or
• wine in single servings of 10 oz (284 ml), or in smaller servings of multiple brands, provided the total served
at one time is no more than 10 oz (284 ml); wine may also be served by the standard 750 ml bottle if it is to
be consumed by at least 2 people and with food. Wine may be served by the bottle, in non-refillable
containers of .75 litre to 1.5 litres, or in refillable containers of no more than 1.5 litres, if the container has
been approved by the Public Health Protection Branch, subject to these serving size rules

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.82(1)(b) and s.118(b)]
A licensee may alter prices during the day such as for “happy hour” but must not sell drinks below the minimum
pricing. A licensee may occasionally treat customers to a free drink but may not give away multiple drinks that
may cause over-consumption.

heading: 22.38 Advertising and promoting liquor prices
text:
A licensee must have a price list available to customers showing the quantities in which liquor is sold and the
price at which each quantity is sold. A licensee must not advertise or promote in a way that:
• suggests patrons may be provided free liquor,
• suggests patrons may be provided unlimited or unspecified quantities of liquor for a single price,
• suggests patrons may be provided liquor priced at less than the Liquor Distribution Branch purchase price, or
• uses a sales strategy that promotes or encourages intoxication, e.g.: two for one special.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.82(1) and s.118]

22.39 Elements of contravention: “using a sales strategy that is likely to promote or encourage intoxication
To allege the contravention of using a sales strategy that is likely to promote or encourage intoxication, an
inspector must gather evidence that:
• the licensee used a sales strategy to sell liquor,
• the sales strategy is likely to promote or encourage intoxication

Procedure:
1. If an inspector suspects that a licensee has committed a contravention relating to liquor pricing, the inspector
will gather evidence of the identified contravention.

Under item 29 of the penalty schedule, a licensee or permittee who refuses to produce records, liquor, or other
things, or allow liquor sampling, commits a contravention. Procedures for identifying this contravention are
outlined in this section under the heading:
• Failure to produce a record, liquor, or other thing

heading: 23.1 Failure to produce a record, liquor, or other thing
text:
Authorities under both Acts as well as procedures for requesting production of records, liquor and other things
and taking liquor samples are outlined in “Seizures and Evidence.” The failure to produce records and other
things and the refusal to allow liquor sampling are serious contraventions that undermine the Compliance and
Enforcement Program. Without access to records, liquor samples and other things associated with the operation of
the establishment or event site, the branch may be unable to identify serious contraventions, such as the sale of
unlawful liquor, and deal with them effectively. An inspector may request records, liquor, or other things through
issuance of a “Notice to Produce.”
A licensee or permittee must cooperate with the general manager by promptly producing and allowing inspection
and removal of the records, liquor samples and things the general manager is entitled to inspect or remove under
s.42 of the Act. Lack of cooperation from the licensee or permittee is considered a contravention of the Act.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.43]

heading: 23.3 Elements of contravention: “fail to produce a record, liquor or other thing”
text:
To allege the contravention of failing to produce a record, liquor or other thing, an inspector must gather evidence
that:
• the licensee or permittee was subjected to an inspection,
• the licensee or permittee was requested to produce and allow inspection and removal of records, liquor
samples or things pursuant to the inspection authority,
• the licensee or permittee did not promptly comply with the request.

Procedure:
1. If a licensee or permittee refuses or neglects to produce a record or other thing or allow liquor sampling, the
inspector will gather evidence of the contravention, including:
• description of the item requested,
• the relevance of the record, liquor sample, or other thing,
• how many times the inspector requested the item,
• the circumstances surrounding the requests,
• any explanation provided by the licensee/permittee for failing to produce the requested item,
• copies of any written requests including the Notice to Produce,
• the time period the licensee/permittee was given to produce the item, and/or
• a description and copies of any items produced, and
2. Based on the evidence gathered, if the inspector forms the opinion that a contravention occurred, the
inspector will issue an electronic notification of noncompliance alleging a contravention of:
• Failure to produce a record, liquor, or other thing, s.43(a)(iii) LCLA (Licensee/Permittee)

heading: 24.0 Introduction
text:
The LCLR penalty schedule specifies penalties for the contravention related to advertising as specified at section
64 Act. In addition, the general manager has established terms and conditions respecting the advertising of liquor.
Therefore, policies and procedures applicable to advertising are addressed under the heading:
• Unauthorized advertising or signs

There are specific advertising rules that apply to UBrew and UVin establishments. Those rules are outlined in
Section 28 UBrews and UVins.

heading: 24.1 Unauthorized advertising or signs
text:
Branch policy regarding signs and other forms of advertising is primarily directed at public safety concerns
associated with advertising that targets minors or promotes irresponsible drinking behaviour. To ensure that
members of the public are aware that adult entertainment may be occurring before entering a licensed
establishment, licensees must post signs informing the public of the nature of the entertainment.

heading: 24.2 Definition of advertise
text:
Advertise means to exhibit or display, or permit to be exhibited or displayed, a notice respecting liquor:
• by an electric, illuminated, or other sign, contrivance, or device, or
• on a building, signboard, billboard, vehicle, or other place in public view.

Advertise means to publish, broadcast, distribute or display a sign, notice, circular, letter, poster, handbill, card,
price list or information in any format that:
• names, represents, describes, or refers to liquor, or to the qualities or quantities of liquor,
• gives the name or address of a person manufacturing or dealing in liquor, or
• states or indicates where liquor may be obtained or purchased.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.64]
[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulations, s.168 to s.174]

heading: 24.3 Content of advertisements
text:
Unless otherwise restricted by the terms and conditions of a licence, licensee advertisements may specify:
• the kind, type, or class of liquor available for sale,
• particular liquor brands and manufacturers,
• licensed establishments and liquor stores where a particular product is available for sale,
• hours of sale,
• entertainment or food featured at the establishment, and
• liquor prices.

Advertisements must comply with the Code for Broadcast Advertising of Alcoholic Beverages published by the
CRTC. Advertisements must not:
• encourage people to drink liquor or drink irresponsibly,
• show a person drinking liquor,
• show a person with liquor but without food,
• show a person who is intoxicated, behaving irresponsibly, or behaving illegally,
• associate liquor with driving,
• use pictures of minors or personalities, images or activities that may appeal to minors,
• be directed at minors or placed in locations used or visited mostly by minors,
• depict liquor as one of life’s necessities, key to social acceptance or personal success, central to the
enjoyment of an activity or a status symbol,

• promote contests and tournaments involving wet t-shirts or wet jockey shorts, bare-as-you-dare or similar
themes or activities,
• refer to liquor products that are not listed or approved for sale by the Liquor Distribution Branch, or
• depict packaging or labelling that has not been approved under the Liquor Distribution Act.

heading: 24.4 Licensee retail store, rural licensee retail store and wine store names
text:
The following conditions apply to signage and advertising for LRS/RLRS:
• the words “British Columbia liquor store,” or “government liquor store,” may not be used to avoid confusion
with the names used by the Liquor Distribution Branch; and
• signs and advertisements may not use pictures of minors, personalities, images, or activities that may appeal
to minors.

In signage and advertising for wine stores, the following conditions apply:
• the words “B.C.,” “British Columbia” or “government,” may not be used to avoid confusion with the names
used by the Liquor Distribution Branch,
• signs and advertisements may not use pictures of minors, personalities, images, or activities that may appeal
to minors, and
• sacramental wine stores are permitted to advertise to members of the clergy or ministers of religion and are
prohibited from advertising to the public.
All indoor and outdoor signs must be approved by the general manager and must comply with local government
bylaws.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]
A licensed establishment that offers adult entertainment must post, at the entrance to the establishment, a sign to
inform the public of the nature of the entertainment.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

1. If an inspector observes advertising or signs that do not comply with the Act, regulation or terms and

heading: 25.0 Introduction
text:
The penalty schedule outlines minimum penalty levels for two contraventions under the heading of
“Entertainment:”
• Fail to comply with term and condition dealing with adult entertainment, and
• Fail to comply with term and condition dealing with entertainment that is not adult entertainment.

Minimum penalties for contraventions involving adult entertainment are higher than those involving
entertainment that is not adult entertainment.

heading: 25.1 Entertainment
text:
The licensee is responsible for managing and controlling the behaviour of patrons and ensuring the safety of staff,
patrons, and the community. Entertainment is a factor that may affect the licensee’s ability to maintain effective
management and control of the establishment. If the entertainment uses part of the licensed area, overcrowding
may impact the ability of staff to observe and control patron conduct. As a result, the branch authorizes the size
and location of performance areas.

Adult entertainment such as an exotic performance may present safety concerns for staff, performers, and patrons.
As a result, the branch prohibits certain types of performances such as simulated sex acts or acts with animals.

Entertainment in an establishment may also generate noise, nuisance and other negative impacts on nearby
residents and businesses. To ensure minors are not exposed to adult entertainment, performances by exotic
dancers and other adult-oriented entertainers are prohibited in establishments frequented by minors. The general
manager has imposed restrictions on the types of games and entertainment available in food-primary
establishments to maintain the primary focus on the service of food.
Licensees may only provide games and entertainment that are authorized by the general manager. The general
manager may impose terms and conditions on a licence that approve, prohibit, restrict, or limit any type or form
of game or entertainment in a licensed establishment.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.15]
A local government or First Nation may restrict or prohibit any type of entertainment or games allowed in a
licensed establishment.
A licensee must not offer or condone entertainment or games that may jeopardize patron or public safety.

heading: 25.5 Entertainment permitted in liquor primary establishments
text:
Unless otherwise restricted by the general manager, the following types of games and entertainment are permitted
in liquor-primary establishments:
• live or recorded music,
• radio or television,
• movies, so long as the primary focus of the establishment does not shift to that of a movie theatre and all
movies are shown in accordance with the Motion Picture Act and regulations,
• dancing,
• adult-oriented presentations,
• games of skill and games of chance so long as they do not offer a payoff or prize,
• contests and tournaments, so long as:

- there is no entry fee for contests,
- any tournament fees are donated to a recognized charity,
- everyone who enters the establishment is entitled to enter the contest,
- patrons may enter the contest without buying a drink,
- liquor is not a prize,
- winners do not need to be present to collect a prize,
- the event does not involve consumption of liquor, and
- the event does not involve physical contact between patrons.

Liquor-primary licensees may offer contact sports events with the approval of the general manager so long as the
sports do not involve patrons, and the licensee takes steps to protect both patrons and staff.

heading: 25.6 Entertainment permitted in food primary establishments
text:
Entertainment and games provided in a food-primary establishment must not result in the operation of the
establishment in a manner that is contrary to its primary purpose. The following types of games and entertainment
are permitted in food-primary establishments, unless restricted by the general manager:
• television, movies, recorded music, and live radio broadcasts. Movies must be appropriate for all age groups,
• computers that offer internet access, card games, board games, and games such as cribbage, and
• games of chance, including card games, which do not involve payoffs or prizes of any kind.

The following types of games and entertainment are prohibited in food-primary establishments:
• games that require the patron to get up from the food service area and which are likely to shift the primary
focus of the establishment away from the service of food, e.g.: darts, shuffleboard, foosball, billiards, pool,
video arcade style games, basketball, ice, or roller hockey, curling and bowling,
• performances by exotic dancers, and
• other adult-oriented performances.

heading: 25.7 Entertainment permitted in food primary establishments by authority on the licence
text:
The general manager may approve dine and dance and other forms of patron participation entertainment on a
food-primary licence. Patron participation entertainment must end by 12:00 midnight, unless the general manager
has approved longer entertainment hours.

The general manager may approve stage entertainment and other forms of patron non-participation entertainment
to a food-primary licence. Patron non-participation entertainment must end by 1:00 am, unless the general
manager has approved longer entertainment hours.

heading: 25.8 Entertainment permitted at special permit events and catered events
text:
Entertainment offered at events must not interfere with the licensee’s ability to maintain effective management
and control of the event and participants, not negatively affect the health and physical safety of the public, staff,
performers, and patrons, not impose noise, nuisance and other negative impacts on nearby residents and
businesses and comply with local bylaws.

Entertainment generally permitted at events includes:
• live radio and television broadcasts.
• recorded music, radio, and television broadcasts,
• recorded music, including presentations by DJ,
• patron-participation dancing,
• patron-participation sports where the physical safety of performers and patrons is not at risk, such as darts,
shuffleboard, foosball, billiards, pool, video arcade style games, basketball, ice or roller hockey, curling, and
bowling,
• prizefighting, kick-boxing, and other contact sports when there is no patron participation, and where the
licensee can demonstrate that adequate safeguards are in place to protect patrons, staff, and the public,

• computers that offer internet access, and
• board or card games such as cribbage

Minors are not permitted to attend events where adult oriented entertainment or gambling is taking place.

heading: 25.9 Factors that may indicate entertainment is affecting order in the establishment
text:
Entertainment must not adversely affect order in the establishment. Factors that may indicate that the order in the
establishment is being adversely affected include:
• the noise level,
• the general atmosphere, e.g.: chaotic,
• whether patrons remain in their seats,
• whether patrons crowd around the performance area in a manner that impairs the ability of staff to observe
and control patron conduct, and/or
• the nature of the entertainment, i.e., whether it seeks to provoke a response from the audience or encourage
participation in any form that affects the ability of the licensee to control the establishment.

heading: 25.10 Definition of adult entertainment
text:
• Adult entertainment includes exotic dancers, adult-oriented performer, or adult oriented activities. An exotic
dancer is an entertainer who removes clothing during a performance and/or performs in a sexually suggestive
manner.
• Adult-oriented performers are entertainers who present performances not suitable for minors (nudity, sexual
content, violence, obscene language).
• Adult-oriented activities are activities not suitable for minors (full or partial nudity, sexual content, violence,
degradation, or abuse).
• Dancers known as “belly dancers” are not considered exotic dancers.

25.11 Audience participation in performances by strippers, exotic dancers or other adult-oriented performers
The audience must not participate in performances by strippers, exotic dancers, or other adult-oriented
performers. Exotic dancers and other adult-oriented performers must not:
• engage in real or simulated sex acts, or in any acts involving coercion or violence, either simulated or real,
• insert any object into, or extract any object from the vagina or anus,
• urinate or defecate while performing,
• touch, or share food and beverages, or pass objects to members of the audience or to other performers,
• dance/perform on tabletops or other areas outside of approved areas,
• deliberately engage a patron in an adult-oriented performance or activity, or
• perform while intoxicated

Tipping and the distribution of promotional material are permitted provided there is no physical contact between
the performers and each other or with an audience member.

heading: 25.12 Terms and conditions of a licensee offering adult entertainment
text:
• the adult oriented performers/entertainers must be at least 19 and must wear appropriate clothing while
walking through the audience before and after performances. This clothing may be part of their stage
costume; however, the clothing must provide coverage of the entertainer’s breasts and genitalia,
• if the licensee has approval to allow minors, they must not offer adult entertainment during hours when
minors are permitted, or must post appropriate signage prohibiting minors during the event,
• performances must be confined to the stage or other approved areas. No performing is allowed in the
audience area,
• animals cannot be part of a performance and are not permitted as entertainment, except as approved by the
general manager,
• licensees must ensure that adult-oriented performers, exotic dancers, and adult-oriented activities cannot be
viewed from outside the service area. Dividers or other separation must prevent a line of sight into the area,

• exotic dancers and adult-oriented performers cannot act as servers or hold any other employment position in
the establishment while working in their role as entertainers. However, when individuals are not working in
their role as an entertainer, they may be employed as servers or hold positions of employment in the
establishment and may occur during the same shift, and
• where an entertainer holds another employment position in the establishment, they must change out of their
entertainer clothing and into clothing typical for the position they are tasked with prior to starting that
position.

heading: 25.12 Terms and conditions of a licensee offering adult entertainment
text:
exotic dancing/adult entertainment must not be combined with serving or any other employment
position.

25.13 Elements of contravention: “fail to comply with term and condition dealing with adult entertainment”
To allege the contravention of “fail to comply with term and condition dealing with adult entertainment,” an
inspector must gather evidence that:
• the licence or permit has terms and conditions on adult entertainment,
• adult entertainment was occurring within the licensed premises or special event was contrary to a specified
licence or permit term or condition

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes entertainment in a licensed establishment/event site that may contrary to a term or
condition of the licence/permit, the inspector will observe and document the activities of the entertainers,
patrons, and staff before notifying the licensee/permittee of their concerns,
2. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention.

heading: 25.12 Terms and conditions of a licensee offering adult entertainment
text:
The inspector may:
• review the terms and conditions of the licence/permit,
• contact the local government to determine whether the entertainment is restricted by bylaw,
• interview the entertainers and obtain names and contact information,
• interview staff,
• interview the licensee/permittee, and/or
• obtain copies of any advertisements for the entertainment/event site,

heading: 25.12 Terms and conditions of a licensee offering adult entertainment
text:
Based on the evidence gathered, if the inspector forms the opinion that a contravention occurred, the inspector
will issue an electronic notification of noncompliance alleging contravention of either:

• Fail to comply with term and condition dealing with adult entertainment, T&C (Licensee/Permittee), or
• Fail to comply with term and condition dealing with entertainment that is not adult entertainment, T&C
(Licensee/Permittee), or
• Allow a patron participation entertainment outside authorized hours, T&C (Food-Primary Licensee), or
• Allow unauthorized patron participation entertainment, T&C (Food-Primary Licensee), or
• Allow games and entertainment, T&C (Wine Store and Special Wine Store Licensee), or
• Fail to comply with requirements for games or entertainment, T&C (LRS Licensee), or
• Fail to comply with requirements for games, tournaments, contests, draws or other entertainment
activities, T&C (Licensee/Permittee)

heading: 26.0 Introduction
text:
Licensing contraventions are outlined in items 33 to 38 and items 42 and 43 of the Penalty Schedule. While, in
many cases, the investigation of licensing contraventions will involve the participation of the licensing division of
the branch, inspectors and investigators are responsible for ensuring compliance with and enforcement of the
licensing related provisions of the Act and regulations whenever they suspect a contravention. Procedures for
these contraventions are outlined in this section under the headings:
• Provide false or misleading information,
• Sell or serve liquor at a catered event without catering authorization,
• Sell or serve liquor at a market without market authorization,
• Sell or serve liquor at a food or beverage festival without temporary off-site sale authorization,
• Sell or serve liquor without temporary use area authorization,
• Unauthorized transfer of shares,
• Make a structural alteration to service area without amending licence to allow for the change,
• Make a structural change to a non-service area that will affect the operation of the establishment,
• Fail to comply with licence dormancy requirements.

Expired Licences:
Below are the contraventions associated with licensees continuing to operate with an expired licence:
1. Unlawful sale of liquor (s. 8 (2)(a) LCLA); or
2. Unlawful sale of cannabis (s. 15 CLCA).

After the first of every month, the Programs team will check Dynamics for expired licences and provide a
monthly report on expired licences to the Area Supervisors.

heading: 26.0 Introduction
text:
Area Supervisors will assign Liquor and Cannabis
Inspector to verify if certain expired licences are still operating and selling liquor or cannabis with an expired
licence. These assigned inspections will be risk assessed and completed during the less busier consumption times
(i.e., not during Friday or Saturday evening/night or during key event public safety inspections). This will ensure
that the licensing issues are addressed when the establishment in question is less busy for operational efficiency.

If during an inspection a Liquor and Cannabis Inspector identifies that a licensee is selling liquor or cannabis
while their associated licence is expired, the inspector will
a) Mark that checklist item as non-compliant,
b) Record the contravention,
c) Outcome the inspection as a ‘Contravention Identified’,
d) Include in notes that the contravention is for selling or serving with an expired licence, and
e) Complete the electronic notification process.

Depending on the number of days elapsed since the licence in question expired and the date of the inspection and
subsequent electronic notice of contravention, the Liquor and Cannabis Inspector shall consider and implement
one of the following approaches:

A. If the licence in question has only been expired for less than 30 days, the inspector will inform the
licensee to immediately renew their licence online (approximately 10 minute process). The inspector will
then check in Dynamics if the licence has been renewed within a one or two days. Subsequently:
i.

heading: 26.0 Introduction
text:
If the licence was renewed in Dynamics, the inspector shall hold a compliance meeting with the
licensee within one week to verify and confirm with the licensee that the licence was indeed renewed,
and then issue a No Enforcement Action Required (NEAR); or
ii. If the licence was NOT renewed in Dynamics, the inspector shall conduct another inspection as soon
as possible to observe the elements of the contravention of unlawful sale of liquor or cannabis and
issue a Notice of Enforcement Action (NOEA) for the contravention.

B. If the licence in question has been expired for more than 30 days, and the licensee is selling liquor or
cannabis, the inspector shall issue a Notice of Enforcement Action (NOEA) and inform the licensee that
they are not permitted to sell any liquor or cannabis without a proper licence. In the case of a cannabis
retail licence, the inspector will discuss the potential seizure of cannabis products in the establishment.

Subsequent non-compliance in continuing to operate and sell liquor or cannabis may result in more progressive
enforcement action.
The ability of the general manager to supervise the conduct and operation of licensed establishments depends to a
large extent on the honesty, integrity and dependability of the applicant or licensee personally. Providing false
information required as part of the licensing process may call into question whether the applicant or licensee is a
fit and proper person to hold a liquor licence.

heading: 26.2 Prohibition against providing false or misleading information
text:
A person applying for the issue, renewal, transfer, or amendment of a licence must not provide false or misleading
information in the application.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.57(1)(c)]

A person applying for a catering authorization must disclose all material facts required by the catering
authorization application and must not make any false or misleading statements in the catering authorization
application.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.96 and s.97]
Information includes whether the applicant or licensee:
• holds, or has previously held, an interest in a liquor licence,
• has a relationship with any liquor manufacturer or agent,
• has ever been charged with, or convicted of, a criminal offence,
• has a valid interest in the establishment property at the time of application, and
• intends to allow a third party to use the licence.

heading: 26.4 Elements of contravention: “provide false or misleading information”
text:
To allege the contravention of provide false or misleading information, an inspector must gather evidence either
that:
• the licensee, permittee or authorization holder made an application for a licence, permit or authorization,
• the application provided false or misleading information, OR
• the licensee, permittee or authorization holder made a report, or was required to make a report as specified,
• the report provided false or misleading information

heading: 26.5 Sell or serve liquor at a catered event without catering authorization
text:
The general manager has the statutory duty to supervise the conduct and operation of licensed establishments and
depends to a large extent on the voluntary compliance of the applicants and licensees. Selling or serving liquor at
a catered event without first having been issued a catering authorization through the Catering Authorization
process may call into question whether the applicant or licensee is a fit and proper person to hold a liquor licence.
The Catering Authorization also allows inspectors to assess the risk of each event and help maintain public safety.

heading: 26.6 Eligibility and authorities
text:
A catering authorization may be issued to a caterer who holds a catering licence, a liquor primary licence
endorsed with a catering endorsement and a food primary licence endorsed with a catering endorsement. The
catering authorization authorizes the licensee to sell and serve to the host and patrons at a catered event drinks
containing liquor in the service area under the authorization and the host and patrons at a catered event to
consume the drinks containing liquor in the service area under the authorization.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.94 and s.95]
26.7 Elements of contravention: “sell or serve liquor at a catered event without a catering authorization”
To allege the contravention of sell or serve liquor at a catered event without a catering authorization, an inspector
must gather evidence that:
• the catering licensee sold or served liquor,
• the catering licensee sold or served the liquor at a catering event,
• the catering licensee sold or served the liquor without a catering authorization at the time of the sale or
service of the liquor
A caterer may sell or serve liquor at a residence or premises that is not a licensed establishment. For this to occur
the liquor is sold or served at a residential event or a catered event in relation to which the caterer has been issued
a catering authorization by the general manager.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.95]

heading: 26.9 Requirement to apply for a catering authorization
text:
In order to sell liquor at a catered event, a licensed caterer is required to apply for a catering authorization. The
application must be submitted by the online form laid out by LCRB and must contain the required information in
order to assess the application. The general manager may require additional records or documents to further assess
the application.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.96 and s.97]

heading: 26.10 Cancellation of a catering authorization
text:
The general manager may cancel the catering authorization if in the general manager’s opinion, the circumstances
on the basis of which the catering authorization was issued have changed and no longer meet the requirements of
the Act or if the catering authorization was issued in error.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.50]

heading: 26.11 Sell or serve liquor at a market without a market authorization
text:
The general manager has the statutory duty to supervise the conduct and operation of licensed establishments and
depends to a large extent on the voluntary compliance of the applicants and licensees. Selling or serving liquor at
a market event without having been issued a market authorization through the authorization process may call into
question whether the applicant or licensee is a fit and proper person to hold a liquor licence. The market
authorization also allows inspectors to assess the risk of each event and help maintain public safety.
A market authorization may be issued to a licensee who holds a manufacturer licence with an on-site store
endorsement and authorizes the licensee to sell or serve liquor at the market event and for patrons to consume
samples of liquor in the service area under the authorization.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.102 and s.103]

text:

to further assess the application.

26.16 Sell or serve liquor at a food or beverage festival without temporary off-site sale authorization
The general manager has the statutory duty to supervise the conduct and operation of licensed establishments and
depends to a large extent on the voluntary compliance of the applicants and licensees. Selling or serving liquor at
a food or beverage festival without having been issued temporary off-site sales authorization may call into
question whether the applicant or licensee is a fit and proper person to hold a liquor licence. The temporary off-
site sales authorization also allows inspectors to assess the risk of each event and help maintain public safety.

heading: 26.17 Temporary off-site sales authorization
text:
A temporary off-site sales authorization authorizes licensed retail stores, wine stores and special wine stores to
sell liquor in unopened containers to patrons in the service area under the authorization at a food or beverage
festival for which a special event permit has been issued.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.106 and s.107]

liquor

heading: 26.21 Sell or serve liquor without a temporary use area authorization
text:
The general manager has the statutory duty to supervise the conduct and operation of licensed establishments and
depends to a large extent on the voluntary compliance of the applicants and licensees. Selling or serving liquor
without having been issued a temporary use area authorization through the authorization process may call into
question whether the applicant or licensee is a fit and proper person to hold a liquor licence. The temporary use
area authorization also allows inspectors to assess the risk of each event and help maintain public safety.

heading: 26.22 Temporary use area authorization
text:
A temporary use area authorization may be issued to a liquor primary or food primary licence holder endorsed
with a temporary use area endorsement. The temporary use area endorsement authorizes the licensee to sell drinks
containing liquor to patrons in the service area under the authorization and a patron to consume the drinks
containing liquor in the service area under the authorization.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.98 and s.99]

text:
In order to sell liquor in unopened containers to patrons in the service area a licensee is required to apply for a
temporary use area authorization. The application must be submitted in the form laid out by LCRB and must
contain the required information (date, time and location of the event that is proposed to be the subject of the
temporary use area authorization; description of the event; an estimate of the maximum number of people who
will be at the event site at one time) in order to properly assess the application. The general manager may require
additional records or documents to further assess the application.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.100]

heading: 26.26 Unauthorized transfer of shares
text:
A licensee must report an internal transfer of shares respecting the licence or the licensee, other than:
• the removal of shareholders, or
• the redemption or dissolution of shares
Unless:
• the licensee has been identified as having an association with another licence (a tied house), or
• the removal of the shareholder or redemption or dissolution of shares results in any of the remaining
shareholders moving from owning less than 10% of voting shares to owning 10% or more of voting shares in
the licensee.

Therefore, situations involving new owners or new shareholders with 10% or more voting shares require the
general manager to assess the suitability of these individuals, just as was done at the time of the original
application. A transfer of shares without approval may result in an establishment being operated by a person who
is not fit and proper to hold a liquor licence.
A private corporation that holds a licence must receive the approval of the general manager before completing a
transfer of shares of its capital stock, either externally to new shareholders or internally between current
shareholders that results in a new are existing shareholder acquiring more than 10% of the voting shares.

[Licensee Terms and conditions Handbook]

26.29 Making structural alteration to a service area without amending licence to allow for the change
The physical characteristics of an establishment affect the ability of licensees and their staff to manage areas
licensed for the sale and consumption of liquor. Specifically, problems of over-service, over-consumption, and
loss of control within a licensed establishment are related, in part, to the extent to which the physical dimensions
and layout of the establishment help or hinder staff in effectively managing the licensed area.

heading: 26.28 Elements of contravention: “unauthorized transfer of shares”
text:
Structural
alterations or other changes to the establishment including the size or location of the service area may
significantly affect the conduct and operation of the establishment as a whole, and therefore, requires prior
approval of the general manager.

26.30 Prohibition against making structural alteration to service area without amending licence to allow for the
change
Except for UBrews, UVins, and catering business locations, a licensee must not:
• make a structural alteration to a service area,
• change the size or location of a service area,
• make a structural alteration to any area of a licensed establishment that is not a service area that, in the
opinion of the general manager, will affect the operation of a service area, or
• make a change to the location or the size of the area of the manufacturing facility or the storage area in an
establishment under a manufacturer licence
without amending the licence.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.79(1)]

heading: 26.31 Definition of structural alteration
text:
A structural alteration is an alteration to existing construction resulting in a change to the free space within a
licensed area, including:

• a change in the position of a wall, floor or ceiling surrounding a licensed area
• a change in position, addition, or removal of fixed articles such as planters, partial height divider walls,
columns, pillars, ornamental displays, food and liquor service bars, stages, and dance floors
• a change in the position of access and exit points leading to or from a licensed area, including any opening
through which liquor is intended to pass,
• the addition of a lounge area in a food-primary establishment,
• a change to permitted fencing surrounding an outdoor patio, and
• such other construction, alterations or changes the general manager considers may affect patron routing,
capacity, or the line of sight between a staff control point and the licensed area of the establishment.

26.32 Make a structural change to a non-service area that will affect the operation of the establishment
Licensees must receive approval from the general manager before undertaking structural changes to a service area
or other part of the establishment that will affect the operation of the service area or changes to the size or location
of a service area.

heading: 26.31 Definition of structural alteration
text:
The general manager may refuse to renew, transfer, or amend and may also suspend or cancel a
licence if the licensee fails to receive prior approval for structural changes.

the establishment”
To allege the contravention of making structural change to a non-service service area that will affect the operation
of the establishment, an inspector must gather evidence that:
• the licensee made a structural change to a non-service area of the establishment,
• the operation of the establishment is affected by the structural change

Procedure:
1. If an inspector suspects that a licensee has made a change to a non-service area that will affect the operation of
the establishment, the inspector will gather evidence of each element of the contravention.

heading: 26.35 Fail to comply with licence dormancy requirements
text:
A licence is dormant when a licensee is not operating the licensed establishment that is the subject of the
licensee's liquor licence. If an establishment has multiple service areas the licence is only considered dormant if
all areas are not operating. Exceptions to this are endorsements and manufacturer sampling areas; these are only
permitted to operate in conjunction with the active licence they are issued under.

Establishments that are licensed for seasonal use (e.g.: ski hills and motor vessels) are not considered dormant
when they are closed for off-season periods. Routine establishment closures (i.e.: always closed Mondays etc.) are
not considered periods of dormancy.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s. 49(5)]
[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s. 92]
[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.37(5)]
[Cannabis Licensing Regulation, s. 27]
[Terms and Conditions Handbooks]

heading: 26.36 Distinguishing dormant from operational establishments
text:
An operational establishment is one that is open for business and routinely engaged in the activities for which it is
licensed. The Branch recognizes many establishments have unique characteristics in how they operate. For this
reason, instead of prescribing minimum operating requirements, the Branch will apply a reasonableness test to
differentiate between dormant and operating establishments. A reasonableness test allows flexibility to
accommodate a range of different operational businesses and circumstances.

Licensees should generally be able to show how a reasonable person in the community is able to identify the
establishment is open for business. The licensee is responsible for satisfying the general manager that the
establishment is operating in good faith.

This is also applicable to seasonal establishments. A seasonal establishment is one that routinely operates a part of
a year, usually due to factors such as weather, tourism, location, and community.
When asked, a seasonal establishment must be able to provide evidence to show the typical operational period and
off-season. It is not sufficient for a licensee to assert their establishment is operational, without evidence to
support that assertion.

When preparing to re-open a dormant establishment, licensees should do so with the dormancy period time-limit
in mind. Working toward re-opening an establishment (i.e.: renovating, staffing, etc.), is not considered an
operational establishment.

heading: 26.37 Notification of dormancy - closing and reopening
text:
It is a term and condition of a licence that licensees must notify the Branch of establishment closures of 90 days or
longer, within 10 days of the establishment closure, or as soon as the licensee becomes aware that the closure will
last longer than 90 days. The dormancy period starts the day the establishment stopped operating, not the day the
Branch was notified. When an establishment is ready to be re-opened, licensees must notify the Branch in
advance so that the licence may be removed from dormant status prior to re-opening. Licensees operating
seasonal establishments are not required to report seasonal closures. Establishments that operate seasonally are
not considered dormant during normal seasonal closures.
A licence may remain dormant for up to two years, providing it remains compliant with the Act, the regulation,
and the terms and conditions of the licence, unless an extension to the dormancy period has been approved.

heading: 26.39 Licence terms and conditions during dormancy period
text:
If a licensed establishment ceases operation but continues to hold a liquor licence, it must continue to comply with
the Act and regulations, and the terms and conditions of that licence. This includes maintaining valid interest in
the property and payment of the annual licence renewal fee. It is also a term and condition that a licensee report
and/or apply for changes that affect the licence.

When making changes to an establishment and/or licence during the dormancy period, licensees making business
decisions should do so with the dormancy period time-limit in mind. Timelines related to change applications; in
particular relocation applications, do not have the effect of extending the dormancy period, and are not generally
relevant in considering a request to extend the dormancy period.

Liquor inspectors may conduct inquiries or inspections to verify the establishment is closed and determine if it is
in compliance with the Act, regulations, and terms and conditions of the licence. Failure to abide by the T&Cs of
the licence may result in the cancellation of a liquor licence by the general manager before the end of the
dormancy period.

heading: 26.40 Alternate use during dormancy period
text:
A dormant licensed establishment cannot operate as another business during dormancy, unless specifically
permitted by the licence terms and conditions. For example, if a LP licence is approved as ancillary to a primary

business (such as a bookstore or spa), the primary business is still permitted to operate if the liquor licence is
dormant. Similarly, if an FP licence is dormant, the licensee may still operate the restaurant unlicensed.

When an establishment ceases to offer liquor service, as in the case of the examples above, the liquor licence is
considered dormant, and notification of the dormancy is required under the terms and conditions of the licence.
Liquor-free events may be held at a dormant establishment, provided it continues to comply with the licence
terms and conditions. However, a dormant licence cannot be temporarily de-licenced for the purpose of holding a
public or private special event or a catered event. A Special Event Permit or catering authorization cannot be
issued at a location that is the subject of a dormant licence.
