PROMOTIONAL ACTIVITIES
The LCLR penalty schedule specifies penalties for the contravention related to tied house and inducements. In
addition, the general manager has established terms and conditions respecting tied houses and inducements as
well as promotional activities and are addressed under the headings:
• Tied House,
• Inducements,
• Promotional Activities

heading: 27.1 Tied House
text:
A tied house is an association between a liquor retailer or on-premises consumption establishment and a liquor
manufacturer or its agent that is likely to lead to that manufacturer’s products being favoured. The associated
offsite establishments may be any type of establishment (liquor primary, food primary, private liquor/wine store,
or the business location of a caterer).

A tied house relationship exists where:
1. A person who holds a manufacturers licence has amount of ownership interest in a liquor retailer or on-
premises consumption establishment (for example, a shareholder in a company that holds a manufacturer’s
licence also holds shares in a business that has a licensee retail store licence),
or
2. A manufacturer’s proposed third-party operator has any amount of ownership interest in a retail or on-premises
consumption establishment,
or
3. An immediate family member of a person who holds a manufacturer’s licence has any amount of ownership
interest in a retail or on-premises consumption establishment licence. Immediate family members include spouses,
parents, siblings, and children only.

If any of these circumstances exist, owner of the retail or on-premises consumption establishment is considered to
be in a tied house relationship and is prohibited from carrying or selling the manufacturer’s product in that
establishment.

heading: 27.2 Failing to disclose information relating to tied houses
text:
The Act prohibits a licensee from having a relationship with a liquor manufacturer such that the licensee may be
inclined to promote the liquor of that particular manufacturer, unless an exemption has been granted. The
rationale for the restrictions against “tied houses” is that such relationships encourage monopolization, discourage
the entry of new manufacturers into the market, restrict consumer choice and result in pressure on licensees to
encourage consumption.

27.3 Prohibition against activities or relationships between manufacturers and other licensees
A manufacturer cannot at any time:
• Offer or give any kind of money, reward or discount to licensees who carry the manufacturer’s products.
• Provide any items, products or services to other licensees that are necessary to the operation of their
businesses. This includes financial assistance as well as fixtures or furnishings.
• Pay any portion of a licensee's advertising costs, or advertise a licensee's entertainment lineup, drink specials
or menu items.

heading: 27.2 Failing to disclose information relating to tied houses
text:
With the licensee's permission, the manufacture can include the licensee's logo in the
manufacturer’s advertisements but cannot demand or receive financial compensation or other consideration
in return.
• Provide or pay for entertainment in an establishment.

[Manufacturer Terms and Conditions Handbook]

27.4 Exemption from prohibition against certain activities or relationships between manufacturers and other
licensees
• If a manufacturer is selling their own liquor products at their own manufacturing site or, if a winery, at an
offsite wine store that the manufacture owns.
• If a small or medium-volume manufacturer and are in a tied house relationship with an establishment that is
located elsewhere, the licensee of that establishment may apply to the branch to request approval to carry and
sell the manufacturer’s products in agreement with the manufacturer. A manufacturer may only have ties
with up to three offsite licensed establishments. If approved, the offsite licensed establishments may sell the
manufacturer’s products, but they must also sell products from other manufacturers in that product category.

[Manufacturer Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 27.5 Elements of contravention: “Tied House”
text:
It is a contravention to arrange or agree to arrange, with another person to sell the liquor of a manufacturer to the
exclusion of the liquor of another manufacturer. To allege the contravention of tied house, an inspector must
gather evidence that:
• the licensee, permittee, liquor manufacturer or agent has an arrangement or an agreement to arrange with
another person to sell a manufacturer’s liquor,
• the arrangement or agreement to arrange the sale of a manufacturer’s liquor is made to the exclusion of the
liquor of another manufacturer

heading: 27.6 Applicants and licensees must disclose information relating to tied houses
text:
If any of the relationships referred to in “Tied House” apply to a person applying for a licence or holding a licence
under the Act, the applicant or licensee must promptly disclose the condition to the general manager even if the
prohibition does not apply to that licensee.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.12 and s.62]
[Manufacturer, LRS, LP and, FP Terms and Conditions Handbooks]

heading: 27.8 Inducements
text:
Inducements are incentives given to licensees by manufacturers or their representatives in free liquor product,
rebates, cash, or other consideration, in order to establish exclusivity of product sales or to increase a product's
sales. Giving or accepting inducements for promoting liquor is a serious contravention that incurs the highest
minimum penalty ranges included in Schedule 2 of the regulation.

To avoid the possibility and appearance of inducement activity, the branch has developed a number of terms and
conditions that govern promotional activity between licensees and manufacturers and agents.
Giving or accepting inducements for promoting a particular brand or manufacturer of liquor is a serious
contravention that can lead to destructive competition and its spillover effects. These concepts are described in
section 2 “Operating Environment”.
Unless exempted by the general manager, a person must not:
• offer, give, demand, accept or receive, or
• agree to offer, give, accept, or receive money, gifts, reward, or remuneration, directly or indirectly, for
promoting, inducing, or furthering the sale of a particular kind, class, or brand of liquor.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.62 (2)]

heading: 27.12 Fail to comply with promotional activity requirements
text:
Promotional activities by manufacturers and agents are restricted by regulation and policy to ensure that
inducement activities do not occur, and a selection of liquor brands are available to the public. Policies
surrounding conduct of tasting events guard against over-consumption. Promotional items for licensees are
restricted to items of little value so that it does not appear that a manufacturer is inducing a licensee to carry or
highlight the manufacturer’s products. The general manager has established certain terms and conditions
respecting promotional activities for agents, licensees and manufactures.

heading: 27.13 Prohibition against promoting the sale of a particular kind of liquor
text:
Unless exempted by the general manager, a licensee or the licensee's employee must not induce, further or
promote the sale of a particular kind, class, or brand of liquor. This prohibition does not apply with respect to

liquor sold at a winery, brew pub, distillery, or brewery or at an establishment operated on the same site as a
winery or brew pub with respect to liquor manufactured on the premises.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.62]

heading: 27.14 Terms and conditions of exemptions
text:
If the general manager has granted an exemption from the prohibition of an inducement, the trade practices terms
and conditions form part of the terms and conditions of the licence of the liquor manufacturer, agent, or licensee
to whom an exemption was granted. Any promotional activity undertaken in reliance on the exemption must be
consistent with the trade practices terms and conditions and any other terms and conditions imposed on the
licence.

heading: 27.15 Terms and conditions of exemptions given to stadiums or concert halls
text:
If the general manager has granted an exemption from the prohibition of inducements to a licensee that arranges
with a manufacturer or agent to sell a designated category of liquor in a stadium or concert hall, the following
terms and conditions apply to the licence:
• the licensee must make available to patrons at least one other product that:
- belongs to that category,
- is reasonably priced,
- is not connected with, or manufactured by, that manufacturer or agent,
- is made known to patrons in a manner satisfactory to the general manager, and
- is available from a reasonable number of take-away bars throughout the stadium or concert hall
• the licensee must ensure that at least 10 percent of the sales of the designated category of liquor are sales of
this other product,
• the licensee must display messaging that is satisfactory to the general manager to promote the responsible
consumption of liquor, and
• any other terms and conditions the general manager consider advisable.

heading: 27.16 Prohibition against accepting items or services from a manufacturer or agent
text:
Licensees may purchase items from manufacturers and agents at fair market value. A licensee must not accept
from a manufacturer or agent any items, products or services that are necessary for the operation of the licensed
business, including:
• money,
• credit or other forms of financial assistance,
• fixtures,
• furnishings,
• liquor products other than product samples,
• repair and maintenance costs,
• draught lines,
• glassware, other than disposable glassware in stadiums,
• games,
• refrigerators,
• shelving, or
• permanent display structures.

Licensees must also not accept from manufacturers or agents:
• advertising or advertising costs,
• entertainment or entertainment costs other than inexpensive forms of entertainment during theme nights, or
• rental costs for unoccupied rooms.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.62 (2)]

heading: 27.17 Promotional items
text:
A manufacturer or agent may loan a licensee “promotional items” with the manufacturer’s name or brand such as:
• signs,
• patio umbrellas,
• ceramic draught beer towers,
• mirrors,
• menu boards, or
• temporary display structures.

A licensee may accept promotional clothing items with a manufacturer’s name or brand, so long as the items are
given free to customers. Licensees may purchase promotional items such as shirts, caps or key chains displaying a
manufacturer’s name or brand at fair market value from a manufacturer or agent for re-sale to customers or staff.

A licensee may also accept promotional items of a nominal value from manufacturers or agents, such as:
• tent cards,
• posters,
• coasters,
• product brochures,
• ceiling danglers,
• shelf talkers, or
• other similar brand or corporately identified items so long as their menu already lists the brand of liquor
identified in the promotional items and it does not appear that the licensee is promoting a particular liquor
product or the products of a particular manufacturer. This means that brand identified or corporately
identified items of a particular manufacturer must not predominate.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.62 (2)]

heading: 27.18 Value-added promotional items
text:
A manufacturer or agent may provide value-added promotional items to a retail store and the following terms and
conditions apply:
• the manufacturer or agent has received approval from the Liquor Distribution Branch to offer the same
items in government liquor stores,
• the licensee must keep a copy of the approval letter from the Liquor Distribution Branch on site,
• the promotion must meet the guidelines set out in the Liquor Distribution Branch publication, The
Beverage Alcohol Promotions Program for B.C. Liquor Stores,
• the value of items may not exceed 20 % of the retail price of the base product,
• the items must be liquor, liquor-related or branded,
• the items may include third party coupons, but the coupons must not be for a rebate or reduction on the
price of liquor, free liquor, or cash,
• leftover items may be sold by the licensee after the promotional period is over,
• items are not transferable to other licensees or establishments, and
• the manufacturer, agent or licensee may advertise the promotion.

A manufacturer or agent may provide a retail store with value-added promotional items that are not being
supplied to government liquor stores if the items do not contain liquor.
A licensee may request or receive information and ideas from a liquor manufacturer that will enable the licensee
to improve their establishment or operating methods. However, the information must be directly supplied by the
manufacturer and not through an outside consultant. A licensee may not request or receive advice from a
manufacturer or agent about borrowing money or locating financing.

heading: 27.20 Product samples
text:
As a way of introducing new liquor products, a licensee may receive the following volumes of product samples
from a liquor manufacturer or agent in a year:
• the smallest sized bottle of distilled spirits,
• the smallest sized bottle of wine per vintage, and
• one dozen of the smallest sized bottles or cans of beer, cider, and coolers.

Licensees must record all samples received in their liquor registers. Product samples are only for consumption by
the licensee and their staff outside of the licensed area. The product must not be purchased or consumed by
patrons of the establishment.

heading: 27.21 Consumer tastings
text:
Manufacturers and agents may conduct consumer tastings in food-primary establishments and the following terms
and conditions apply:
• food must be available, and the event must not shift the focus away from the service of food,
• the licensee, manufacturer or agent may advertise the event outside the establishment,
• the licensee may not charge the manufacturer or agent a fee for conducting the tasting,
• all liquor product used in the tasting must be purchased from the licensee at no less than the price the
licensee normally pays for the product and no more than the price the licensee normally charges patrons.

heading: 27.21 Consumer tastings
text:
At
the end of the tasting, the licensee must refund the manufacturer or agent for the cost of any unopened
product and return the product to the licensee’s stock,
• the licensee must give the manufacturer or agent a countersigned receipt for the dollar value of sampled
product and retain a copy of the receipt for audit purposes,
• the manufacturer or agent must provide all the point-of-purchase show material used to support the
consumer tasting,
• the manufacturer or agent must be present for the duration of the tasting,
• the licensee’s staff must dispense all liquor products,
• patrons may be served a maximum sample of 30 ml of wine, or 45 ml if more than one wine is featured,
• patrons may be served a maximum sample of 30 ml of beer, cider or cooler, or 45 ml if more than one
product is featured,
• patrons may be served a maximum sample of 10 ml of spirits, or 20 ml if more than one spirit is featured,
• the licensee must not leave open containers of liquor unattended, and
• the licensee must not serve drinks by the tray load.

Manufacturers and agents may conduct consumer tastings of products available for sale in retail stores and the
following terms and conditions apply:
• the licensee, manufacturer or agent may advertise the event,
• the licensee may not charge the manufacturer or agent a fee for the demonstration space,
• the tasting must end 30 minutes before the store closes,
• only one tasting event may take place at a time,
• all liquor product used in the tasting must be purchased from the licensee at no less than the price the
licensee normally pays for the pr

heading: 27.21 Consumer tastings
text:
oduct and no more than the price the licensee normally charges patrons,
• the licensee must give the manufacturer or agent a countersigned receipt for the dollar value of sampled
product and retain a copy of the receipt for audit purposes,
• the manufacturer or agent must provide all the promotional materials used to support the consumer tasting,
• the manufacturer or agent must serve or hire servers for the tasting,
• servers must be familiar with the rules governing consumer tastings at liquor stores,
• patrons may be served a maximum sample of 20 ml of wine, or 30 ml if more than one wine is featured,
• patrons may be served a maximum sample of 30 ml of beer, cider or cooler, or 45 ml if more than one
product is featured,
• servers must not leave open containers of liquor unattended, and
• at the end of the tasting, all poured samples and opened bottles must be destroyed.
A licensee may accept hospitality expenses not associated with an educational event from a manufacturer or
agent, at a rate of up to $1,000 per licensee location per year. The manufacturer or agent may also pay for any
legitimate in-province travel costs related to the event.

heading: 27.23 Joint promotions
text:
A liquor-primary or food-primary licensee may enter into a joint promotion with a manufacturer or agent to
feature a manufacturer’s product during a special event; such as a winemaker’s or brew master’s dinner and the
following terms and conditions apply:
• the licensee, manufacturer or agent may advertise the event,
• the event must include a full meal, and
• the licensee must purchase the liquor served at the event from a designated Liquor Distribution Branch
outlet.

heading: 27.24 Visits
text:
When a manufacturer or agent visits a licensed establishment, they may purchase drinks for patrons and the
following terms and conditions apply:
• mass treating or buying drinks for the house is not permitted,
• the liquor serving provided to each customer at one time may not be greater than the normal serving size for
the establishment,
• the manufacturer or agent must pay the liquor bill before they leave the establishment,
• drink prices must be the same as those normally charged to patrons,
• the manufacturer or agent may not treat more than one table at a time, unless the tables include a bona fide
sporting team or an arts or cultural club,
• the licensee must give the manufacturer or agent a countersigned receipt for the dollar value of product
purchased, and
• the manufacturer or agent may not bring products into the establishment for the purpose of sampling.

heading: 27.25 Product vouchers
text:
A licensee may enter into an agreement with a manufacturer or agent to honour their product certificates in a retail
store and the following terms and conditions apply:
• only the manufacturer or agent may distribute vouchers,
• vouchers may specify a quantity of liquor that is no more than:
- the smallest sized bottle of distilled spirits available,
- the smallest sized bottle of wine available, or
- one dozen of the smallest sized bottles or cans of beer, cider, and coolers available
• once a voucher is redeemed, the manufacturer or agent must pay the licensee the full retail price for the
quantity of liquor specified on the voucher, and
• the licensee may not ask for or accept an additional redemption fee for accepting a product voucher.

heading: 27.26 Contests
text:
A manufacturer or agent may hold a contest in a licensed establishment and the following terms and conditions
apply:
• if the contest is running in a government liquor store, the contest must be for the same period and with the
same promotional materials on display as in the government liquor store,
• if the contest is not running in a government liquor store, the contest must meet the guidelines set out in the
Liquor Distribution Branch publication, The Beverage Alcohol Promotions Program for B.C. Liquor Stores,
• the manufacturer or agent must conduct the contest, install promotional items, and remove promotional items
within 10 days of the end of the contest,
• the manufacturer or agent must record the name of anyone who wins a prize worth more than $100, and
• the licensee may include contest entry forms in print advertisements and may mention where entry forms are
available.

heading: 27.27 Manufacturer sponsorships
text:
A manufacturer may sponsor an event, activity, or organization using their corporate name or brand name of the
manufacturer’s product. Manufacturer-sponsored events are not generally permitted in licensed establishments
due to laws prohibiting tied houses and inducements. Manufacturer-sponsored events are permitted at catered
events because the sponsorship agreement is not between the caterer and the manufacturer, and the caterer does
not directly benefit from the relationship. Manufacturers are permitted to sponsor licensee-associated sports
teams, tournaments or events held offsite. The sponsored activity may be held at:
• unlicensed venues,
• licensed:
- sports stadiums,
- recreational centres (including ski hills, racquet clubs and bowling alleys),
- concert halls, or
- university or cultural centres, or
- associated establishments exempted from the tied house requirements; or
• catered events

Joint sponsorship at or with a licensed establishment is not permitted unless the following criteria are met:
• The sponsored activity must be time-limited and not part of an on-going relationship with the licensed
establishment or caterer; and
• The manufacturer or agent has notified the LCRB, in writing, at least 14 days before any sponsored activity
takes place.

Sponsorship by manufacturers of events, activities, and organizations in which the participants or audience consist
primarily of minors is generally prohibited, unless authorized by the general manager.

heading: 27.28 Licensed establishment sponsorships
text:
A licensed establishment may sponsor an event, activity, or organization using their corporate name or the name
of the licensed establishment. The sponsored event or activity may be held at the licensed establishment or offsite
at an unlicensed venue or at a catered event:
Joint sponsorship with a manufacturer is not permitted unless the following criteria are met:
• The sponsored activity must be time-limited and not part of an on-going relationship with the manufacturer or
caterer; and
• The manufacturer or agent has notified the LCRB, in writing, at least 14 days before any sponsored activity
takes place.

Sponsorship by licensed establishments of events, activities, and organizations in which the participants or
audience consist primarily of minors is generally prohibited, unless the establishment is a food primary or a liquor
primary where minors are generally permitted, or unless authorized by the general manager.

heading: 27.29 Educational events and activities
text:
A licensee may attend an educational event or activity conducted by a manufacturer or agent and the following
terms and conditions apply:
• the manufacturer or agent may pay the licensee for legitimate expenses associated with attendance at the
event or activity up to a maximum of $1,000 per year per licensee location, and
• where the licensee owns multiple licensed establishments, the manufacturer or agent may pay expenses of up
to $1,000 per person to a maximum of $3,000 per year for attendance at events or activities by head office
staff.

heading: 27.30 Theme nights
text:
A liquor-primary licensee may collaborate with a manufacturer or agent to promote the sale of a particular kind of
liquor at a theme night and the following terms and conditions apply:

• theme nights are not allowed on university or college campuses,
• food must be available to patrons for the duration of the theme night,
• the theme night must have an educational component,
• liquor prices must be the normal prices charged to patrons,
• the manufacturer or agent must purchase any samples provided from the licensee,
• samples must be offered by the manufacturer or agent and not the licensee’s staff,
• the licensee’s staff may dispense samples from the bar unless a special service area is set up for the event.

In

• patrons may be served a maximum sample of 30 ml of beer, cider or cooler, or 45 ml if more than one
product is featured,
• patrons may be served a maximum sample of 10 ml of spirits, or 20 ml if more than one spirit is featured,
• the licensee must give the manufacturer or agent a countersigned receipt for the dollar value of the total
amount of liquor and / or food purchased,
• the manufacturer or agent may provide inexpensive forms of entertainment, such as games, but must not pay

• the manufacturer or agent must record the name of anyone who wins a prize worth more than $100,
• unless the general manager directs otherwise, prizes may display a manufacturer’s brand or name,
• prizes may not be liquor or drinks containing liquor,
• patrons must not be required to buy or drink liquor in order to participate in a contest,
• the licensee, employees and immediate family members are not eligible to enter or win a contest,

To allege the contravention of fail to comply with promotional activity requirements, an inspector must gather

heading: 28.0 Introduction
text:
UBrew and UVin establishments are retail outlets that provide ingredients, equipment, and support for customers
to make beer or wine products for their own consumption. Because of the unique nature of their operations, the
penalty schedule outlines a number of contraventions specific to UBrews and UVins. There are four distinct types
of UBrews and UVins. Each type is described in the paragraphs that follow.

1. Kettle brew UBrew
In this type of establishment, the customer makes the wort by adding malt, grains, and hops to boiling water in a
kettle. The malt may either be commercially produced or ground and boiled by the customer.

2. UBrew with a wort licence
These licensees have a federal wort licence that allows them to make wort for customers. The customer’s only
role in the production process is to pitch the yeast. Wort will spoil, so the addition of yeast must be done by the
customer shortly after the wort has been prepared.

3. UBrew or UVin selling kits
These types of establishments sell kits that either:
• contain all the components of the wort for customers to combine and boil
• contain “wort in a bag” that the customer pours into a carboy and then adds water and pitches the yeast, or
• contain wine juice or concentrate and other ingredients that the customer pours into a carboy and then adds
water and pitches the yeast.

4. UVin using grapes or fresh juice
Some UVins allow customers to use fresh juice rather than kits. Grapes may be crushed on site.

heading: 28.0 Introduction
text:
In these
establishments, the customer adds the juice and other ingredients to the carboy, adds water and pitches the yeast.

Regulations and policy with respect to the role of the customer and the responsibilities of the licensee are the
same for all four types of UBrew and UVin establishments. Procedures for identifying contraventions at UBrews
and UVins are outlined in this section under the following headings:
• Failing to ensure the customer performs required tasks,
• Failing to comply with payment, acknowledgment, or invoice requirements,
• Failing to comply with liquor storage requirements for carboys,
• Allowing consumption at the establishment,
• Allowing someone other than the customer to bottle product,
• Failing to ensure that the customer removes product,
• Allow unauthorized minor to manufacture product,
• Fail to comply with advertising requirements,
• Sell liquor outside of hours of liquor service,
• Failing to keep records and copies as prescribed, and
• Prohibited sales.
UBrews and UVins are not licensed as liquor manufacturers and may not manufacture product for commercial
purposes. The customer must perform certain tasks to ensure that UBrew and UVin establishments do not act as
manufacturers or as retail outlets.

heading: 28.2 Role of the customer in the manufacturing process
text:
A licensee must ensure that the customer performs the following tasks to produce product at a UBrew or UVin:

• wine/cider/cooler kits: pouring the juice or concentrate into the fermentation vessel and adding water (if
required), yeast and any other necessary ingredients,
• juice barrels: adding yeast and any other necessary ingredients to the barrel,
• beer in kettles: adding the necessary ingredients (e.g.: hops and malt extract) to the water in the kettle, letting
it cook and adding yeast,
• pre-made wort under federal wort licence: adding yeast to the wort prepared by the licensee,
• commercially available pre-packaged wort kits: pouring the wort into the fermentation vessel and adding
water (if necessary), yeast and any other ingredients,
• bottle washing and sterilizing,
• removing or defacing labels,
• bottling product,
• labelling, corking, capping, or shrink-wrapping bottles, and
• removing product from the facility.

A licensee may assist a customer to perform these tasks, but each task must be primarily performed by the
customer. A licensee may offer a reasonable amount of assistance to a disabled customer who is unable to
perform these tasks alone.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.44]

heading: 28.3 Fortifying product
text:
A licensee may allow customers to add distilled liquor, such as brandy or vodka, to a port or sherry product being
made at the establishment provided the customer purchased the distilled liquor from the Liquor Distribution
Branch. A licensee must not provide distilled liquor to a customer. The customer must not leave the distilled
liquor on-site for the licensee or staff to add to the port or sherry.

[UBrew/UVin Terms and Conditions Handbook]
A customer may top up their own product with product made previously at a UVin or commercially produced
wine. A licensee may not add product to a wine barrel or customer’s carboys to “top-up” the barrel or carboys. A
licensee may top up a customer’s product with water or another non-alcoholic substance.

[UBrew/UVin Terms and Conditions Handbook]
If a group of people is splitting a single batch or making more than one batch, each member of the group must:
• be involved in adding the ingredients required to start the batch,
• sign a declaration, and
• have their names stated on the invoice.
• at least one member of the group must bottle the product.

[UBrew/UVin Terms and Conditions Handbook]

To allege the contravention of failing to ensure the customer performs the required tasks, an inspector must gather

heading: 28.7 Payment, acknowledgment or invoice requirements
text:
In order to track and account for all products being prepared at a UBrew or UVin and ensure that product is being
prepared by legitimate customers, licensees must receive payment and issue invoices to all customers prior to
production. To ensure that customers are aware of the fact that UBrew or UVin product may not be sold and may
not be used at a special occasion licensed event, licensees must ensure that customers sign an acknowledgment
prior to production.

heading: 28.8 Payment, acknowledgment and invoice required
text:
A licensee must ensure that a customer does not begin producing or manufacturing their product until the
customer:
• pays for the ingredients or pays for the facilities or services if the customer brings in their own ingredients,
and
• signs an acknowledgment that the product is being made for the customer’s own consumption or the
consumption by others at no charge.

Upon payment, the licensee must provide the customer with an invoice that sets out the following information:
• the name and phone number of the customer,
• the type and quantity of product to be made,
• the date and the amount of payment received from the customer, and
• the name, address, and phone number of the licensee.

The licensee must provide an invoice even when there is no charge for the production, such as production by an
employee or the licensee or free production given to a customer who was dissatisfied with a previous batch of
product.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.43]

heading: 28.11 Tagging carboys
text:
The licensee must ensure that each carboy is properly tagged with:
• the customer’s name, and
• the date any enzymes or yeast were added to the product.
Licensees and employees producing product at the establishment must label their product as belonging to the
licensee or employee. If more than one customer’s product is placed in a barrel for aging, the licensee must affix
to the barrel the carboy tags of every customer whose product is stored in the barrel.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.46(1)]

A licensee must not permit the consumption of liquor at the establishment, other than allowing a customer to taste

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.45]

To ensure that product is not left for the licensee or another person to sell or consume after bottling, licensees
must ensure customers must immediately remove product from the premises after it is bottled.

heading: 28.17 Removal of finished product required
text:
Unless the licensee is moving the product for fermentation and aging to a secondary storage site that has been
approved by the general manager, a licensee must not remove product or permit another person to remove the
customer's product before bottling. A licensee must ensure that customers remove product immediately after
bottling. A licensee may not remove or deliver the beer or wine product of a customer after bottling. The licensee
must not store product that has been bottled.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.44(1)(f)]

heading: 28.18 Unauthorized trading rack or conduct product exchange
text:
The licensee must not encourage trading of product among customers by:
• providing a “trading rack” where a customer leaves some of their product in the licensed establishment after
bottling and in exchange takes other customer’s product that has been left behind in the trading rack, or
• allowing notices to be posted regarding trading.

[UBrew/UVin Terms and Conditions Handbook]

gather evidence that:
• the customer did not immediately remove the bottled product from the establishment after bottling.

evidence of the contravention.

The prohibitions respecting unauthorized minors:
• producing product at or entering a UBrew or UVin are meant to guard against consumption of liquor by
minors.
• Public safety issues associated with consumption of liquor by minors are outlined in Section 15“Minors”.

heading: 28.21 Minors in UBrews and UVins
text:
A licensee must not employ a minor in the establishment unless the minor is under the direct and continual

To ensure that licensees are not representing their establishments as places where customers can purchase finished
product, the content of advertisements for UBrews and UVins is limited by the regulation.

heading: 28.24 Permitted advertising
text:
A licensee may only do the following in an advertisement for a UBrew or UVin:
• state that the establishment is licensed to provide goods, facilities, or services for customers to produce or
manufacture beer, wine, or cider,
• state the name of the establishment and its address and phone number,
• advertise the availability of specific types of ingredients for producing or manufacturing wine, beer, or cider,
and/or
• provide a list of the goods, facilities, and services available and their prices. The licensee must clearly state
that the advertised price represents the cost of producing and manufacturing product at the establishment and
not the cost of finished product.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.172]
A licensee may not provide customers with a sample of product that is, or may be, produced at the establishment.

[UBrew/UVin Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 28.26 Promotions and discounts
text:
A licensee may advertise products on sale but may not advertise volume discounts for making more than one

• discount programs for frequent users,
• “company money” that can be reimbursed against future purchases,
• volume discounts to individuals or groups who make more than one batch at a time, or
• contests with free product or free services as the prize.

[UBrew/UVin Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 28.28 Fail to keep records and copies as prescribed
text:
To ensure compliance with the Act, regulation and terms and conditions of the licence, UBrew and UVin
licensees are required to maintain a variety of records and have them available for inspection. he regulation also
requires UBrew and UVin licensees to submit semi-annual reports indicating the volume of product produced in
the establishment. The branch reviews these reports for any significant change in product volumes that may
indicate unlawful liquor production.

heading: 28.29 Record keeping and reporting requirements
text:
A licensee must maintain and have available for inspection, for at least three years, the following records:
• purchase records for all ingredients used in the production and manufacturing of product,
• copies of invoices given to customers,
• records of product manufactured by the licensee or employees for their own use, and
• records detailing the disposition of spoiled, spilled, unclaimed or returned product.

If a licensee has a wort licence for the establishment, the licensee must ensure the wort licence is available for
inspection at all times. licensee must submit an annual report to the general manager outlining the volume of
product manufactured or produced in the establishment.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.51]

heading: 29.0 Introduction
text:
Item 54 of the penalty schedule outlines minimum penalty ranges for any contravention of the Act, regulation or
terms and conditions of the licence that is not specifically referred to elsewhere in the Schedule. It would be
impossible to include detailed policies and procedures in this manual for the wide range of contraventions that are
included under this item. However, because of the specialized nature of their operations, this section outlines
policies and procedures for identifying a number of contraventions that apply exclusively to manufacturers.

heading: 29.1 Manufacturers
text:
The “manufacture” of liquor is defined by the regulations as including one or more activities related to the
brewing, distilling, and fermenting of liquor, and include packaging, blending, and flavouring. Accordingly,
anyone wanting to manufacture liquor containing more than 1% alcohol by volume for sale is required to have the
appropriate manufacturer licence.

Manufacturer licences are issued to:
• wineries for the manufacture of aperitif wine, dessert wine, flavoured wine, fruit wine, mead, Asian wine,
sake, ice wine, table wine, sparkling wine, cider, wine coolers (made by fermenting grapes or fruit or any
other agricultural product) and other similar products. This includes fortified wines (wine to which spirits are
added) such as port, sherry, mantilla, madeira, and vermouth,
• distilleries for the manufacture of spirits, including whisky, gin, rum, vodka, tequila, cachaca, Asian spirits,
spirit coolers, products such as brandy that are manufactured by distilling wine, armagnac, cognac, eau de
vie, liqueurs and other similar products, and
• breweries for the manufacture of malt liquor (beer).

A manufacturer must have facilities and equipment on the premises to manufacture a sizeable amount of their
registered products at their licensed manufacturing site. It is contrary to the intent of the licence to manufacture
only a token amount on site in order to maintain a retail or on-premise consumption endorsement.

The Act permits liquor consumption in designated areas of a manufacturing site for the purpose of promoting the
manufacturer’s products.

heading: 29.1 Manufacturers
text:
As with any other category of licence that sells liquor, the branch will monitor
manufacturers to ensure they comply with the Act, the regulation, and the terms and conditions of the licence.
This means, for example, manufacturers must not serve liquor to minors or allow intoxication or overcrowding at
their establishments.

The specific policies that regulate the consumption of liquor at manufacturing sites reflect the unique nature of
their operations. The total volume of product that a manufacturer can sell as samples to a person in one day is
restricted by regulation to ensure these licensees do not operate designated sampling areas as liquor-primary or
food-primary establishments. Policies respecting licensed picnicking areas are designed to ensure that
manufacturers are able to supervise consumption and maintain the informal nature of these areas. Picnicking areas
are not meant to be operated as liquor-primary or food-primary establishments.

The Act allows manufacturers to apply for special occasion licences in order to promote their products through
special events. Other licensees and the public at large may only use special occasion licences for non-profit events
or events held to raise funds for a charitable purpose. Manufacturers may also apply for a special event
endorsement that allows them to host special events in designated areas at the manufacturing site.
The branch has
designed policies regarding the use of special occasion licences for manufacturers to ensure that these
establishments are not able to act as food-primary establishments through the use of special occasion licences.
The establishment may offer samples for free or for a charge. he maximum total volume of product samples that
an establishment may sell to a person during a day is 150 ml for a winery, 375 ml for a brewery and 45 ml for a
distillery.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.70]

heading: 29.3 Picnicking area endorsement
text:
A manufacturer with a picnicking endorsement may operate an outdoor picnic area and the following terms and
conditions apply:
• patrons may only consume liquor in the picnicking area during daylight hours,
• the picnicking area must be the size approved by the general manager and defined by a clearly identifiable
boundary. Boundaries may be either natural or constructed and must allow picnickers to easily discern the
boundaries of the area where they may consume liquor,
• a manufacturer may not host special events in the picnicking area unless the host of the event has obtained a
special occasion licence for the event and the manufacturer has suspended their picnicking endorsement for
the duration of the event,
• minors are allowed in the picnicking area unless otherwise restricted,
• the manufacturer may not sell or serve liquor in the picnicking area. Customers must purchase liquor from
the licensee’s other endorsement areas and carry it to the picnicking area, and
• customers must not consume liquor in the picnicking area unless it was purchased from the licensee.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.34]

heading: 29.4 Special event endorsement
text:
A manufacturer with a special event endorsement may host special events in a designated indoor or outdoor special event
area at the manufacturing site.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.33]

Manufacturers may sell and serve wine, cider and wine coolers manufactured in BC in the special event area.
Breweries and distilleries may serve products manufactured under their licence. Minors are not allowed in the
special event area unless they are accompanied by a parent or guardian or are employed as entertainers.

[Licensee Terms and Conditions Handbook]
A manufacturer with a tour endorsement may serve or sell samples of its products in a designated indoor or
outdoor tour area to patrons who are touring the manufacturing site.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.37]

heading: 29.6 Special event area permits
text:
A manufacturer may obtain a special occasion licence in order to conduct a tasting to acquaint the public with its
products. Licensees may make some profit from these events, so long as the prime purpose of the event is to
promote their products. Where a special event at a manufacturing site is being hosted by a third party and is
primarily for a purpose other than to acquaint the public with that manufacturer’s products, that third party must
obtain the special occasion licence for the event.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.33]

heading: 29.7 Lounge endorsement
text:
A manufacturer may apply for a lounge endorsement to serve and sell liquor in a designated area. Wineries may
sell wine manufactured in BC and breweries and distilleries may sell the products produced under their licences
and registered to them under their Liquor Distribution Branch manufacturing agreements. Lounges must have
food available to patrons.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Regulation, s.33]

Note: Where there are multiple manufacturing licences on the same site with the same licensee the endorsement
areas may occupy the same area (i.e.: one lounge for both licensees) and the licensee may serve the products
permitted under both endorsements (for example, the product permitted in a winery lounge and the product
permitted in a distillery lounge).

heading: 29.8 Production and equipment requirements
text:
Although some movement of product between licensed manufacturers is permitted, a manufacturer must have
facilities and equipment on the premises to manufacture a sizeable amount of their registered products at their
licensed manufacturing site. It is contrary to the intent of the licence to manufacture only a token amount on site
in order to maintain retail or on-premise consumption endorsement.

Requirements for wineries are the most specific in this regard. To be licensed, a winery must hold valid interest in
(lease or own) on-site fermentation tanks or barrels, filtering equipment and facilities sufficient to meet the annual
minimum production requirements (4,500 litres per year on site) and have the intent to do so. Once the winery
licence has been issued, a licensee must manufacture (including fermentation) at least 4,500 litres of wine each
year on site.

1. If an inspector suspects that a contravention is occurring at a manufacturing site involving sampling, special

the activities of the licensee, patrons, and staff before notifying the licensee of their concerns,

heading: 30.0 Introduction
text:
Schedule 2 of the regulations “Penalty Schedule” identifies the enforcement actions that may be taken by the
general manager against licensees or permittees that contravene certain sections of the Act or regulations.
Procedures for identifying these contraventions are included in this section under the following headings:
• Permitting sale, service, or consumption of liquor while licence or endorsement is suspended, or a
catering authorization or off-site sale or market authorization is suspended or cancelled,
• Fail to co-operate with inspection or entry by inspector or peace officer, and
• Fail to comply with term and condition requiring compliance with agreement under section 5 of the
Liquor Distribution Act

30.1 Permitting sale, service or consumption of liquor while a licence or endorsement is suspended or a catering
authorization or off-site sale or market authorization is suspended or cancelled
A licensee who commits this contravention manifests a flagrant and utter disregard of the law. Disregarding the
general manager's decision to suspend a licence or catering endorsement, or suspend or cancel a catering, off-site
sale or market authorization undermines the branch enforcement structure.

heading: 30.0 Introduction
text:
For this reason, the general manager
will act quickly and conclusively when a licensee is permitting the sale, service, or consumption of liquor while
under suspension or cancelled.

30.2 Enforcement action if a licensee permits the sale, service or consumption of liquor while the licence or
endorsement is under suspension or catering, off-site sale or market authorization is suspended or cancelled
If a licensee permits the sale, service or consumption of liquor while the licence or endorsement is under
suspension or the catering, off-site sale or market authorization is suspended or cancelled, the general manager
may cancel the licence or endorsement, or suspend the licence for a period of time the general manager considers
appropriate or order the transfer of the licence.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.51 to s.53]

endorsement is under suspension or the catering, off-site sale or market authorization is suspended or cancelled”

under suspension or the catering, off-site sale or market authorization is suspended or cancelled, an inspector must
gather evidence that:

• the licence or endorsement was suspended, or the catering, off-site sale or market authorization is suspended
or cancelled.

heading: 30.4 Failing to cooperate with inspection or entry by inspector or peace officer
text:
Failing to allow an inspector or peace office to enter a licensed establishment undermines the branch enforcement
structure. A licensee who commits this contravention manifests a flagrant and utter disregard for the law. For
these reasons, the general manager will act quickly and conclusively when a licensee fails to permit entry to an
inspector or peace officer. The regulation sets out serious consequences for this contravention.

heading: 30.5 A licensee must immediately allow the general manager to enter and inspect
text:
Upon request, a person must immediately allow the general manager to enter and to inspect:
• all premises used for the storage of liquor including off-site premises, and
• the licensed establishment or event site,
• promptly produce and allow inspection and removal of the records, liquor samples and things the general
manager is entitled to inspect or remove under section 42 Act.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.43 (a)]
A person must not obstruct the general manager or withhold, destroy, conceal, or refuse to provide information or
produce a record, liquor sample or other thing that is required by the general manager or is otherwise related to
the inspection.

[Liquor Control and Licensing Act, s.43 (b)]

heading: 30.7 A licensee must admit a peace officer without warrant
text:
A person must immediately admit a peace officer who, on reasonable and probable grounds, believes that
conditions for obtaining a search warrant exist but has a reasonable belief that the delay necessary in obtaining a
search warrant would result in the loss or destruction of evidence

30.10 Failure to comply with term and condition requiring compliance with agreement under section 5 of the
Liquor Distribution Act
LDB has agreements with all BC manufacturers (under section 5 of the Liquor Distribution Act) authorizing them
to act as the agent of the LDB in the wholesaling of their liquor to licensees and other authorized private outlets.
As agents of LDB, LDB specifies terms and conditions under which they are authorized to conduct such sales,
including relating to the collection and deposit of sales proceeds and recycling fees and container deposits (where
applicable), and the records required to account for these sales.

When manufacturers fail to comply with the terms of the agreements, it is often difficult for the LDB to enforce
compliance because the Liquor Distribution Act does not provide for penalties. The LCLA system of
administrative penalties is an effective way to promote voluntary compliance with the LDB requirements.

heading: 30.12 Draw attention to a liquor Iispector, minor agent or police officer
text:
Drawing the attention of patrons to the fact that liquor inspectors, minor agents contracted to the branch, and/or
police are present in an establishment may put the safety of the liquor inspectors, minor agents contracted to the
branch, and police at risk.

Accordingly, licensee actions must not cause the attention or focus of patrons to shift towards liquor inspectors,
minor agents contracted to the branch, or police at any time, including at the time of entry, during an inspection,
or when exiting the establishment.

Actions such as announcing the arrival of liquor inspectors, raising or flashing lights, turning down music, playing
particular soundtracks (e.g.: "Bad Boys" or 'Hawaii Five O"), using spotlights, or any other similar actions are not
permitted.

Licensees or their staff may not take, save, or distribute photographs or video of liquor inspectors or minor agents
contracted to the branch in any manner (e.g.: on a staff bulletin board, print media, social media, or the internet).

heading: 31.0 Introduction
text:
One of the significant goals of the CCLA is to prevent minors from accessing cannabis due to the detrimental
effects that may be caused by childhood, adolescent and continued use of cannabis. As part of its responsibility to
administer and enforce the CCLA, the LCRB must protect minors from the negative effects and risks associated
with cannabis use through various strategies which are identified in the Compliance and Enforcement Program.

A minor is defined in the CCLA as any person under the age of 19 years. Sections 69 to 76 of the CCLA contain a
number of provisions designed to help keep cannabis and cannabis products out of the hands of minors. There are
also provisions that prevent cannabis from being marketed to minors and prevent minors from working in the
cannabis industry including in marketing.

The guiding principles of these provisions include the notion that cannabis use that begins early in adolescence, is
frequent, and continues over time is more likely to cause harm. These harms may have permanent effects over a
person’s lifetime. Therefore, it is reasonable to discourage and prevent cannabis use by minors.

heading: 31.0 Introduction
text:
Police Officers
and Inspectors are delegated authority under the CCLA to enforce these provisions to ensure licensees are in
compliance.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.38]

Police Officers and Inspectors also have authority, under the Offence Act, to issue violation tickets directly to
minors for violations of the CCLA.

[Offence Act, Violation Ticket Administration and Fines Regulation, Schedules 1 and 2]

The following violation tickets may be issued to minors:

This section outlines policies and procedures for identifying contraventions involving minors organized under the
following headings:
• Sell or supply cannabis or cannabis accessories to a minor
• Perm
itting minors in licensed cannabis retail store/producer retail store
• Identification requirements.
Selling or supplying cannabis or a cannabis accessory to a minor is considered a significant public safety
contravention due to the detrimental effects that may be caused by childhood, adolescent, and continued use. The
CCLA stipulates that a person (licensee) must not sell or supply cannabis or a cannabis accessory to a minor.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.69(1) and s.69(2)]
To allege the contravention of sell cannabis or cannabis accessories to a minor, an inspector must gather enough
evidence to prove each of the following elements on a balance of probabilities that:
• the licensee sold non-medical cannabis or cannabis accessory to the person,
• the person was a minor
To allege the contravention of supply cannabis or cannabis accessories to a minor, an inspector must gather
enough evidence to prove each of the following elements on a balance of probabilities that:
• the licensee supplied non-medical cannabis or cannabis accessory to the person,
• the person was a minor

heading: 31.4 Prohibition against allowing a minor to enter or be in a specified place
text:
To prevent minors from accessing cannabis or cannabis products, the CCLA also stipulates that a licensee or
employee of a licensee must not allow a minor to enter or remain in a place where the licensee conducts
authorized cannabis activities. As well, a person who works in a government cannabis store must also not allow a
minor to enter or remain in the store.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.70(2)(a) and s.70(3)]
To allege the contravention of permitting a minor to enter or be in a specified place where the licensee conducts
authorized cannabis activities, an inspector must gather enough evidence to prove each of the following elements
on a balance of probabilities that:
• the person was a minor, and
• the minor was in a place where the licensee conducts authorized cannabis activities.

heading: 31.6 Other prohibitions related to minors
text:
The following are other prohibitions related to minors:
• a licensee must not allow a minor to consume or possess cannabis in or at a place under the licensee’s
control,
• a licensee must not allow a minor to work in an office or other place associated with the authorized person's
cannabis business,
• a licensee must not display cannabis or cannabis accessories in view of minors,
• a person who markets, advertises, or promotes cannabis must not allow a minor to take part in those activities
and a minor must not market, advertise or promote cannabis,
• a person must not ask or allow a minor to purchase or attempt to purchase cannabis for the person,
• a minor must not possess, consume, produce, supply, sell, purchase, or attempt to purchase cannabis,
• a minor must not possess, make, supply, sell, purchase, or attempt to purchase a cannabis accessory, and

• a minor must not, for the purposes of obtaining cannabis or a cannabis accessory or of gaining access to a
place that a minor is prohibited under this Act from entering, present identification or another record to
establish the minor's age or identity if that identification or other record:
(a) has been altered to misrepresent the age or identity of the minor,
(b) was issued by the issuing agency to another person, or
(c) is forged or fraudulently made

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.70, s.71, s.72, s.73 and s.75]

heading: 31.7 Identification requirements
text:
The licensee and their employees are required to ask for two pieces of identification to verify that a person is 19
years of age or older. The primary piece of identification must be issued by a government agency; and must
include the holder’s name, date of birth and picture. The secondary piece of identification is used to verify the
authenticity of the first piece and must include the holder's name and signature OR picture.

Section 69(4) of the CCLA establishes a defense to the allegation of selling or supplying cannabis or a cannabis
accessory to a minor. If the person can demonstrate that they required the patron to produce the prescribed
identification, they examined it, have reason to believe it is authentic, and they came to the conclusion that the
person is not a minor, they are considered not to have contravened section 69(1), (2) or (3) Act.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.69(4)]

heading: 31.8 Verifying authenticity of identification
text:
A licensee may do one or more of the following to verify that identification is authentic:
• have the person provide a sample signature and compare the signature to the signature on the identification,
• ask for additional pieces of identification.
• ask the person what their zodiac sign is,
• ask the person for their middle name and how to spell that name, and/or
• ask the person for information that is on the identification such as address, postal code, etc.

Licensees have no legal authority to retain identification that is false. Inspectors will not accept or collect false
identification from licensees.

heading: 31.9 Sample types of identification
text:
An expired driver’s licence (or other expired government ID) may be accepted by the licensee as ID as long as it
can be read, and it is possible to recognize the person from the picture. This is because the purpose is to verify age
and not to verify the entitlement to drive and the fact it is expired does not affect the process of verifying the
person’s age.

ID cards issued by band councils (or the Nisga’a Lisims Government or a Treaty First Nation) may be accepted
by the licensee as a secondary piece of ID as long as it has the person’s name and picture or signature. As with
any type of ID, if there is a reasonable doubt about its authenticity it should not be accepted as proof of age.

An interim licence (the yellow paper) issued by ICBC may also be accepted as a secondary piece if it contains the
person’s name and signature. An interim licence is not acceptable as a first piece of ID since it does not include a
picture. In all cases, it is the responsibility of the licensee to verify age, and it is up to the licensee to determine on
a “case by case” basis where the identification presented verifies to the licensee’s satisfaction that the person
checked is not a minor.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.69(4)]
[Cannabis Licensing Regulation, s.37]

heading: 32.0 Introduction
text:
Violence, unlawful activity, or weapons in a Cannabis Retail Store/Producer Retail Store
Violent or disorderly conduct or unlawful activities and the presence of weapons present serious safety concerns
for staff, patrons and the surrounding community and would impact a licensee’s ability to manage and control the
establishment.

Licensees and employees must not allow violent or disorderly conduct or unlawful activities to take place in their
store. Licensees also must also ensure that weapons are not brought into their store. If a licensee believes this is
the case; they may ask the persons to leave or forbid the person from entering the establishment. Licensees should
also contact police for assistance at any time where there is a threat to public safety.

If there is an imminent threat to public safety, the general manager can suspend a cannabis retail licence for 24
hours and order the immediate removal of customers. In this situation, licensees are required to take all reasonable
steps to ensure that customers vacate the establishment immediately.

Licensee requirements and procedures for inspectors to identify these contraventions are included in this section
under the headings:
• Allow violent or disorderly conduct in establishment
• Allow unlawful activities or conduct in establishment
• Allow a person who has a weapon to enter or remain in an establishment.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.49(2)]

heading: 32.1 Allowing violent or disorderly conduct in establishment
text:
Violent or disorderly conduct presents serious safety concerns for staff, patrons, and the surrounding community.
These types of activities impact a licensee’s ability to manage and control the establishment. Licensees must take
actions to prevent these activities from occurring and stop them if they occur. This includes any behaviour that
might cause a reasonable person to believe their safety is threatened. If a licensee or employee knows or suspects
this kind of behaviour has taken place, is currently taking place, or may take place, they must notify police
immediately.

Section 49 of the CCLA specifies conduct in licensed establishments. It states that licensees must not allow
violent or disorderly conduct to take place in the licensed establishment. Therefore, licensees are expected to put
effective measures in place to prevent violent or disorderly behaviour; and should contact the police where
necessary.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.49(2)(c)]
[Terms & Conditions Handbook]

heading: 32.2 Elements of contravention: “allow violent or disorderly conduct in an establishment”
text:
If an inspector finds that the licensee has allowed violent or disorderly conduct to take place in the establishment,
the inspector should gather as much information as possible to support the finding.

To allege the contravention of allow violent or disorderly conduct, an inspector must gather evidence that:
• the conduct was violent or disorderly,
• the violent or disorderly conduct occurred in the establishment,
• the licensee allowed the behaviour to occur or continue,

Procedure:

1. If an inspector observes or suspects that violent or disorderly conduct may occur or is occurring in the
licensed cannabis store, the inspector will assess:
• the ability of the licensee to manage the situation, and
• the safety risk to the inspector, patrons, and staff,
2. If the inspector concludes that the licensee is unable to manage the situation and the situation is unsafe, the
inspector will contact the police and seek their attendance and assistance at the establishment,
3. The inspector may consider a suspension under section 36 of the CCLA,
4. If safe to do so, the inspector will attempt to gather evidence to satisfy the elements of the contravention
which are identified above. This may include:
35.

text:
observing and documenting the activities/conduct of the licensee, staff, and patrons,
• interviewing the licensee, staff members, and/or patrons,

Examples of the evidence that the inspector may gather for each element of the contravention are listed in the

heading: 32.3 Allow unlawful activities or conduct in establishment
text:
Illegal activities in a licensed establishment such as trafficking unlawful drugs or stolen property may present
safety concerns for staff, patrons, and the surrounding community. Licensees must take actions to prevent these
activities from occurring.

For the purposes of alleging a contravention under the CCLA, unlawful activities or conduct are any activities or
conduct occurring in a licensed establishment that are contrary to, prohibited by or unauthorized by law including,
but not limited to criminal acts.

Licensees must notify police immediately upon becoming aware of an unlawful activity or conduct occurring in
establishment.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.49(2)(d)]
[Terms & Conditions Handbook]

heading: 32.4 Elements of contravention: “allow unlawful activities or conduct in an establishment”
text:
If an inspector suspects the licensee has allowed unlawful activities or conduct to occur; he/she must collect as
much information/evidence as possible to support the finding.

To allege a contravention of these requirements an inspector must gather evidence of:
• The nature of the unlawful activity/conduct,
• The location of the incident (i.e., in the licensed establishment),
• the actions of licensee or their staff that would suggest they knew or ought to have known the behaviour or
incident was taking place; and
• that the licensee or their staff did not take any action or attempt to take any action to rectify or address the
situation.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes or suspects that unlawful activities or conduct has occurred in the establishment, the
inspector will assess:
• the safety risk to the inspector, patrons, and staff,
2. The inspector will contact the police and seek their attendance and assistance at the establishment,
3. The inspector may consider a suspension under section 36 of the CCLA,
4. If safe to do so, the inspector will attempt to gather evidence to satisfy the elements of the contravention which
are identified above. This may include:
36. observing and documenting the activities/conduct of the licensee, staff, and patrons,
• interviewing the licensee, staff members, and/or patrons (if safe to do so)
• obtaining surveillance videos from the licensee,

heading: 32.5 Allow a person who has a weapon to enter or remain in an establishment
text:
The consumption of liquor affects behaviour and judgment. It reduces natural inhibitions. There is a greater
likelihood of a volatile and dangerous situation occurring when a patron has been consuming liquor and is in
possession of a weapon.

A licensee must manage and control the behaviour of patrons to ensure the safety of staff, patrons, and the
community. Allowing a person with a weapon to enter a licensed establishment or event site is a serious public
safety concern.

32.6 Prohibition against allowing a person who has a weapon to enter or remain in an establishment
A licensee must not permit a person with a weapon to enter or remain in a licensed establishment if the licensee
knows that the person has the weapon in their possession without a lawful excuse.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.49 (2)(e)
If a licensee knows or suspects that a person has a weapon, the licensee should notify the police immediately.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]
“Weapon” means anything used, designed to be used, or intended for use:
• in causing death or injury to any person, or for the purpose of threatening or intimidating any person.

[Criminal Code of Canada, s.2]

heading: 32.9 Possession of a weapon for self-protection
text:
Self-protection is not a lawful excuse for possession of a weapon in a licensed establishment.

32.10 Elements of contravention: “allow a person who has a weapon to enter or remain in an establishment”
To allege the contravention of permitting a person who has a weapon to enter or remain an establishment, an
inspector must gather evidence to demonstrate that:
• the person had a weapon in their possession while in the licensed establishment,
• the person did not have a lawful excuse to possess the weapon,
• the actions of licensee or their staff that would suggest they knew or ought to have known the behaviour or
incident was taking place, and
• that the licensee or their staff did not take any action or attempt to take any action to rectify or address the
situation.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector knows or suspects that a person in a licensed establishment has a weapon, the inspector will
contact the police immediately. If there is potential for harm to the inspector or a volatile situation, the
inspector will leave the establishment or event site,
2. The inspector will document that he/she observed a person in possession of a weapon and if safe to do so will
notify the licensee,
3. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention.

heading: 33.0 Introduction
text:
The table found in Schedule 2 of the Cannabis Licensing Regulation contains two contraventions under the
heading of “Advertising or Branding”:
• failure to comply with term and condition of a licence restricting advertising, promoting, or displaying
cannabis or cannabis accessories (Item 21), and
• failure to comply with term and condition of a licence restricting advertising or branding of a non-medical
cannabis retail store (Item 22).

In addition, the general manager has imposed a number of terms and conditions related to advertising and
branding which are spelled out in the Cannabis Retail Store Terms and Conditions Handbook and Producer Retail
Store Terms and Conditions Handbook.

Licensee requirements and procedures for inspectors to identify these contraventions are included in this section
under the heading:
• Restrictions on associations with another businesses, and
• Unauthorized advertising or branding.

heading: 33.1 Restrictions on associations with another businesses
text:
A licensee must not sell non-medical cannabis as part of another business (co-location) other than a licensed non-
medical cannabis retail store). The LCRB does not consider or grant any intellectual property rights with respect
to the store name or other branding, including signage, proposed by the applicant as part of the application
process or licensee in a store/branding change application. It is the applicant’s or licensee’s responsibility to
satisfy itself with respect to all matters relating to the suitability of the name and any other branding for the
applicant’s or licensee’s purposes.

A licensee must not:
• Jointly advertise with another business,
• Offer discounts in the store based on purchases in another business, or
• Operate a patron loyalty program, whether or not it is in association with another business.

Under the CLR, a licensee must not sell non-medical cannabis as part of another business. The only business that
is authorized within the non-medical cannabis retail store is business related to cannabis, cannabis accessories,
bags of a class or type approved by the general manager, and/or prepaid purchase cards for use in the non-medical
cannabis retail store.

A licensed cannabis retail store must not include use of terms or signs that suggest the business is related to
medical cannabis.

heading: 33.1 Restrictions on associations with another businesses
text:
The Cannabis Retail Store Terms & Conditions Handbook provides that:
• A licensee must not use a name that implies that the non-medical cannabis retail store sells medical cannabis.
This includes using traditional or non-traditional spelling of words such as “pharmacy, apothecary or
dispensary,” and
• A licensee may not use graphics, such as a green cross, that imply medical cannabis.

33.2 Elements of contravention: “fail to comply with restrictions on associations with other businesses”
To allege the contravention of fail to comply with requirements restricting association with another business
(other than a licensed non-medical cannabis retail store), the inspector must gather evidence that the retail store
failed to comply with the requirements. Depending on the circumstances, this evidence may include:
• the licensee associated with another business,
• the association was contrary to the terms and conditions of the licence

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes any of the elements as described that indicate the retail store failed to comply with
requirements restricting association with another business (other than a licensed non-medical cannabis retail
store), the inspector will gather evidence of the contravention.

heading: 33.3 Advertising and promotions
text:
Advertise means to exhibit or display, or permit to be exhibited or displayed, a notice respecting cannabis:
• by an electric, illuminated, or other sign, contrivance, or device, or
• on a building, signboard, billboard, vehicle, or other place in public view.

Advertise means to publish, broadcast, distribute or display a sign, notice, circular, letter, poster, handbill, card,
price list or information in any format that:
• names, represents, describes, or refers to cannabis, or to the qualities or quantities of cannabis,

• gives the name or address of a person manufacturing or dealing in cannabis, or
• states or indicates where cannabis may be obtained or purchased.

All advertising and promotion by cannabis licensees must comply with the provincial Cannabis Control and
Licensing Act, Regulations and terms and conditions of the licence.

Note: Although not a mandate of the branch to enforce, licensees must also be in compliance with the advertising
and branding requirements of the federal Cannabis Act as well as local government and/or Indigenous nation
requirements for the area in which the store is located. Where Inspectors become aware of a possible
contravention of the federal Cannabis Act or local government and/or Indigenous nation requirements, the
inspector may bring the possible contravention to the attention of the appropriate authority.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]
The name of the business and exterior signage must comply with provincial requirements and be approved by the
branch. All business names and signage must comply with the advertising terms and conditions and cannot
mislead the public as to what type of business the licensee operates.

heading: 33.5 Signs
text:
All indoor and outdoor signs must be approved by the general manager. The licensee cannot advertise or brand
their store in a way that indicates that the store is associated with the government or is exercising a function of the
government; this includes the use of words, phrases, designs, domain names or other branding elements or indicia.

The following conditions apply to signage and advertising for a cannabis retail store:
• the words “British Columbia Cannabis Store,” or “government cannabis store,” may not be used to avoid
confusion with the names used by the LDB; and
• signs and advertisements may not use pictures of minors, personalities, images, or activities that may appeal
to minors.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 33.6 Elements of contravention: “unauthorized advertising, branding or signs”
text:
To allege the contravention of unauthorized advertising or signs, an inspector must gather evidence that the
advertising or sign does not comply with the CCLA, regulation or terms and conditions of the licence:
• the licensee advertised, branded the store, or used exterior signs,
• the advertising, branding or exterior signs were unauthorized.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector observes advertising, branding or signs that do not comply with the CCLA, regulation or terms
and conditions of the licence, the inspector will gather evidence of the contravention.
