heading: 34.0 Introduction
text:
Inspectors are tasked with administering and enforcing the Cannabis Control and Licensing Act. In order to
accomplish this, they must monitor licensees to ensure compliance. As part of this effort to confirm compliance
inspectors are required to conduct inspections, including inspection and examination of records and things within
the establishment.

The CCLA prescribes the authority for inspectors to conduct inspections and also prescribes the scope of these
inspections. Licensees are required to cooperate by allowing entry and inspection of their licensed establishment
and cooperating with the inspection requirements. A number of provisions in the CCLA speak to these
requirements and this section outlines those requirements. Specifically:
• Failure to cooperate during general manager inspection,
• Failure to produce records or things,
• Obstruct or attempt to obstruct a peace officer,
• Provide false or misleading information in inspection performed by general manager.

heading: 34.1 Authority to enter and inspect licensed establishments
text:
For the purposes of conducting an inspection to determine compliance with this Act and the regulations, the
general manager may enter a licensed establishment at any reasonable time for the purpose of conducting an
inspection.

When the general manager conducts an inspection, a licensee must allow the general manager to immediately
enter the licensee's establishment and facilitate the inspection.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.84 and s.85]

heading: 34.2 Failure to cooperate during general manager inspection
text:
Failure to cooperate or allow immediate entry or inspection is a serious violation and undermines the Branch’s
compliance and enforcement program. A licensee who commits this contravention manifests a flagrant and utter
disregard for the law. For these reasons, the general manager will act quickly and conclusively when a licensee
fails to permit entry to an inspector or peace officer. The regulation sets out serious consequences for this
contravention.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.85]

heading: 34.3 Elements of contravention: “fail to cooperate during general manager inspection”
text:
To allege the contravention of failing to permit entry or obstruction of an inspection; an inspector must gather
evidence that:
1. the establishment is licensed under the LCLA, and one of the following:
• the general manager attempted to enter or inspect the licensed establishment,
• the licensee neglected or refused to allow establishment to be immediately entered or inspected by the
general manager

Procedure for failure to cooperate during general manager inspection:
1. When requesting entry into an establishment, the inspector must first identify themselves and present LCRB
issued identification to the licensee or staff of the establishment,
2. Where entry to an establishment is not permitted, is obstructed or delayed in any manner the inspector(s) will
inform the licensee/staff or person of the requirement to permit entry pursuant to section 85 of the CCLA
[cooperation of licensee] and that any further delay or refusal to provide immediate entry may result in
enforcement action against the licensee,

37. If the licensee or staff does not permit immediate entry, the inspector(s) will withdraw and no longer attempt
to gain entry. For safety reasons, under no circumstances is the inspector to try to gain forceful or covert
entry into the establishment after being denied entry.
3. The inspector(s) will immediately document the circumstances,
38. The inspector may contact the police and ask them to attend at the establishment and request entry into the
establishment. Police will be contacted where there may be an immediate threat to public safety.

heading: 34.4 Production of records or things for inspection
text:
When an inspector enters the establishment for the purposes of conducting and inspection, the
inspector is entitled to the following:
1. inspect any records required under this Act or by the terms and conditions of a licence to be kept by the
licensee or other records found in the licensee's establishment,
2. remove the records referred to in paragraph (a) for the purposes of the inspection or making copies or
extracts,
3. require a licensee to provide information relating to the inspection,
4. require any person in the licensee's establishment, including patrons, to produce identification for the
purposes of inspection,
5. inspect the licensee's establishment and the operations carried on there,
6. open a receptacle or package found in the licensee's establishment,
7. examine any substance or thing found in the licensee's establishment, take a sample of any substance for the
purposes of testing and analysis, and remove any thing for inspection,
8. inspect or ascertain the chemical or physical properties of a substance found in the licensee's establishment,
9. if the general manager finds cannabis that, in the opinion of the general manager, is possessed in
contravention of this Act or the regulations, the general manager may seize and remove the cannabis and the
packages containing it; procedures for taking samples or seizing cannabis and cannabis accessories is
outlined in “Seizure, Samples and Evidence”, and
10.
make a record, including an audio or video record, of the licensee's establishment or of anything or person in
the licensee's establishment.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.84]

heading: 34.5 Failure to produce records or things for inspection
text:
Failure to cooperate with the inspection authority or failure to produce records or things which the general
manager is entitled to inspect constitutes a contravention. Licensee`s must cooperate and promptly produce any
record or thing which an inspector is entitled to inspect for the purpose of determining compliance with the
CCLA, regulation and terms and conditions of their licence.

When an inspector conducts an inspection, a licensee must not obstruct the general manager or withhold, destroy,
conceal, or refuse to provide or produce information or a record, cannabis or other thing required by the general
manager or is otherwise related to the inspection. The licensee must also not provide false or misleading
information.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.85(1)(b)]

heading: 34.6 Elements of contravention: “fail to produce records or things”
text:
To allege the contravention of fail to produce records or things; or that the licensee withheld, concealed, or
refused to provide information to the general manager; an inspector must gather evidence that:
• the general manager requested the licensee to promptly produce records and things for inspection,
• the licensee did not promptly produce records or things requested for inspection

Procedure:
1. The inspector will clearly request the record, information, or thing from the licensee. The request may be an
informal verbal request or a formal request through the issuance of a Notice to Produce Records,
2. The inspector will document the details surrounding the request and response or lack of response by the
licensee and/or staff,
3. The inspector will document any conduct by licensee or their staff which suggests the licensee, or their staff
have obscured information or things which have been requested for inspection,
4. If the licensee does not provide the information, record or thing, the inspector will complete and issue a
Notice to Produce Records (if one has not been issued already) outlining the information to be produced and
deadline for producing the information,

5. The Notice to Produce Records should be sent to the mailing address on record,
6.

heading: 34.6 Elements of contravention: “fail to produce records or things”
text:
Inspector may gather further evidence of the contravention as necessary by:
• interviewing the licensee, staff, and/or patrons, and
• observing and documenting the activities of the licensee, patrons, and staff when the request to inspect,

heading: 35.0 Introduction
text:
The LCRB aims to keep profits related to cannabis sales out of the hands of criminals and to protect public health
and safety by allowing adults to access safe and legal cannabis. The federal and provincial governments track
cannabis supply through the legislation and regulations which govern federally licensed producers and
provincially licensed retail stores.

The BC Liquor Distribution Branch (LDB) is the wholesale supplier of cannabis in BC and conducts their sales
through BC Cannabis Stores (BCCS) under the Cannabis Distribution Act. BCCS’s obtain cannabis supply from
federally licensed producers. Anyone other than the BCCS or a federally licensed producer, who sells cannabis in
BC, must be licensed under Cannabis Control & Licensing Act. This means all cannabis retail licensees can only
purchase and sell cannabis which is purchased from a BC Cannabis Store.

Unlawful cannabis is any cannabis that has not been purchased, kept for sale, or sold in compliance with the
legislation, regulation and terms and conditions associated with a Cannabis Retail Store licence.

Unlawful cannabis is a priority for the branch due to its negative social, financial, health and safety consequences
for the public.

heading: 35.0 Introduction
text:
It undermines the integrity of the federal and provincial regulatory system and therefore threatens
the safeguards that protect communities from the negative aspects of the unlawful sale and purchase of cannabis.

A number of provisions in the CCLA deal with the issue of unlawful cannabis or relate procedurally to
inspections for unlawful cannabis.

The unlawful sale and purchase of cannabis involves contraventions under the following headings:
• Unlawful possession, sale, or supply of cannabis,
• Failing to maintain a register of cannabis purchased and received.

heading: 35.1 Unlawful possession, sale or supply of cannabis
text:
The unauthorized sale of cannabis is an extremely serious contravention that incurs the highest minimum penalty
ranges prescribed in the regulation. Illegally produced, purchased and sold cannabis can pose a serious health and
safety risk to patrons who consume it and contribute to the unlawful trafficking /dealing of cannabis.

Licensees are responsible for the cannabis sold or kept for sale at their establishments. They are responsible for
complying with the provisions specified and must ensure that unlawful cannabis is not present in their store. It is
their responsibility to purchase cannabis from the authorized source. If a licensee purchases an establishment and
transfers a licence into their name, it is their responsibility to ensure that the stock contains cannabis legitimately
purchased from a BC Cannabis Store.

heading: 35.2 Prohibition against unlawful possession, sale or supply of cannabis
text:
Licensees must only purchase and sell cannabis which is registered under the Cannabis Distribution Act and
purchased from a BC Cannabis Store under their licence number.

Any cannabis obtained otherwise, will be considered illicit or unlawful and subject to seizure. This includes:
• cannabis obtained directly from licensed federal producers,
• obtained from another retail licensee,
• obtained from medical marijuana dispensaries,
• privately produced sources,
• samples left by licensed marketers,
• from illegal dealers/marketers,
• illicitly imported from any other province or country,
• intended for export,

• provided as an inducement by a manufacturer,
• adulterated cannabis,
• homegrown cannabis,
• any source which is not purchased under the correct license number,
• any personal cannabis stored in establishment, even if lawfully purchased.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.14 and s.15 (c)]
[Cannabis Retail Store Terms and Conditions Handbook]

35.3 Elements of contraventions related to: “unlawful possession, sale, purchase or supply of cannabis”
To allege the contravention of unlawful possession, sale, purchase or supply of cannabis, an inspector must gather
evidence that the licensee possessed, sold, purchased, or supplied cannabis that was not purchased from the
LDB/BCCS under their licence number.

For the purposes of the CCLA, "sell" includes: offering for sale, exposing for sale, and having in possession for
sale, exchanging and giving for any consideration, including for the purchase or transfer of something.

heading: 35.4 Maintaining a register of cannabis purchased and received
text:
The Branch must verify that licensees are in compliance with the purchase and sale requirements for cannabis to
prevent unlawful cannabis from entering the market/industry. In order to accomplish this, the terms and
conditions of a cannabis retail license require licensees to keep detailed records of their sales and purchases.

A cannabis register is a record of all a licensee’s purchases and sales (i.e.: receipts and invoices) of their cannabis
inventory. A licensee must keep a cannabis register, and the register must be available to inspect at all times.
Cannabis registers may be in the form of hardcopies or be digitally kept. The records must account for all
cannabis on site and be kept in a legible, orderly fashion so that an inspector can easily match the stock to the
records.

A licensee must also be able to account for any cannabis that was returned to the LDB or BC Cannabis Retail
Store disposed of due to spoilage or other reasons.

text:

heading: 36.0 Introduction
text:
Section 38 of the CCLA allows the general manager to take enforcement action against a licensee who
contravenes the term and condition by failing to take reasonable measures to ensure that the operation of their
establishment does not disturb persons in the vicinity of the establishment. Procedures for identifying this
contravention are outlined in this section under the heading:
• Failure to comply with term and condition that requires the licensee to take reasonable measures to ensure
that the operation of the establishment does not disturb persons in the vicinity

36.1 Failure to comply with term and condition that requires the licensee to take reasonable measures to ensure
that the operation of the establishment does not disturb persons in the vicinity
Noise emanating from a licensed establishment or from patrons entering or exiting the establishment may disturb
neighbouring businesses and residents. Indecent or illegal behaviour by patrons entering or exiting the
establishment may result in property damage and/or public safety concerns.

Regard for community standards is one of the two operating principles that guide the branch’s regulation of
cannabis. While it is not the intention of the branch to make licensees responsible for policing the streets around
their establishments, the operational practices of licensees influence whether an establishment has a negative or
positive effect on the surrounding community.
Licensees cannot prevent every incident occurring around
establishments, but they do have an influence over the number and severity of incidents and their effect on people
in the vicinity.

heading: 36.2 Action against licensee
text:
The general manager may take action against a licensee who fails to take reasonable measures to ensure that the
operation of the establishment is not contrary to the public interest and does not disturb persons in the vicinity of
the establishment.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

36.3 Elements of contravention: “Failure to comply with term and condition that requires the licensee to take
reasonable measures to ensure that the operation of the establishment does not disturb persons in the vicinity”
To allege the contravention of failure to comply with term and condition that requires the licensee to take
reasonable measures to ensure that the operation of the establishment does not disturb persons in the vicinity, an
inspector must gather evidence that:
• the operation of the establishment has resulted in disturbance to persons in the vicinity of the establishment,
• the branch has informed the licensee of the disturbances and reasonable measures that should be taken to
prevent the disturbances,
• the licensee has not implemented the reasonable measures within a specified time period,
• persons in the vicinity of the establishment continue to be disturbed

In order to form the opinion that a licensee has committed a contravention, the inspector must identify a pattern of
disturbances which can be linked to a particular establishment. In general, the inspector will not issue an
electronic notification of noncompliance for isolated or occasional incidents.

heading: 36.2 Action against licensee
text:
Where there is more than one
establishment in the same area, the inspector will need to collect evidence to establish which establishment is
responsible for the disturbance.

36.4 Determining whether the manner of operating the establishment is contrary to the public interest
When determining whether a licensee is operating an establishment in a manner that is contrary to the public
interest, the inspector will consider the number and severity of incidents and/or contraventions that have happened
both inside and outside of the establishment. Incidents and/or contraventions that may indicate that a licensee is
operating an establishment in a manner that is contrary to the public interest include:

• violent, or disorderly conduct,
• unlawful activities or conduct,
• excessive noise that results in complaints,
• Allowing consumption of cannabis or liquor in or around the vicinity of the establishment,
• excessive littering in the vicinity that can be attributed to patrons of the establishment, and/or
• nuisance complaints from the surrounding properties that require police response.

heading: 36.5 Determining the vicinity of the establishment
text:
A two to three block radius, or its equivalent, will generally be considered the vicinity of the establishment.

36.6 Determining whether the measures taken by a licensee to prevent disturbances are reasonable
“Reasonable measures” are those measures that are:
• reasonable in the circumstances, and
• reasonably within the capacity of the licensee to effect.

Reasonable measures are steps or strategies that licensees take to ensure their establishments are run in a safe and
considerate manner. The reasonableness of measures may vary from establishment to establishment depending on
the circumstances. For example, if the establishment has never had complaints or problems relating to noise, it
may not be reasonable to expect security staff to stop all exiting patrons and instruct them on respectful behaviour
in the adjacent parking lot.

heading: 37.0 Introduction
text:
Customers may not consume non-medical recreational cannabis or medical cannabis in a licensed Cannabis Retail
Store whether or not the non-medical recreational cannabis was purchased from the licensee or the medical
cannabis was purchased from an authorized seller or the person in possession of the medical cannabis has a legal
prescription to consume the medical cannabis.

This rule is part of the larger regulatory scheme that, among other things, requires a licensee to purchase cannabis
from the Liquor Distribution Branch and have those sales recorded on their licence. Additionally, the purpose of
prohibiting the consumption of cannabis in the establishment is consistent with the prohibition of the consumption
of tobacco in the workplace.

heading: 37.1 Allowing cannabis consmption in a retail store
text:
The prohibition on the consumption of cannabis in a licensed establishment ensures the protection from exposure
to harmful cannabis smoke to workers and the public. As well, as cannabis is a hallucinogenic product, the
consumption of cannabis has an impact on public safety and community standards and may impair the ability of
the licensee or cannabis retail workers to manage and control the establishment.

heading: 37.2 Prohibition against permitting consumption of cannabis in a cannabis retail store
text:
A licensee must not allow people in the establishment to consume liquor that was not purchased from, or served
by, the licensee.

[Cannabis Licensing Regulation, s.5(1)(i)]

37.3 Elements of contravention: “permitting consumption of cannabis in a cannabis retail store”
To allege the contravention of permitting consumption of cannabis in a cannabis retail store, an inspector must
gather evidence to demonstrate that:
• the product consumed was cannabis,
• the consumption occurred in the cannabis retail store

Procedure:

of the person and staff before notifying the licensee of their concerns,
2. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention. The inspector may:

• interview the licensee,
• if it is safe to do so, interview the person,

heading: 38.0 Introduction
text:
Intoxication can be a serious public safety issue. Intoxicated patrons may be a danger to themselves or the public.
Intoxication can be a factor in many crimes, including drug offences such as trafficking and possession of an
illegal substance, assaults and driving violations. As well, intoxication may be a factor in domestic violence.
Intoxication is also associated with behaviour that has a negative impact on communities, including late night
noise, vandalism, and unsanitary behaviour. LCRB aims to prevent and minimize these negative impacts through
education and enforcement of provisions surrounding the sale of cannabis to intoxicated patrons.

Policies and procedures for identifying each of these contraventions are outlined in this section under the
following headings:
• Determining level of intoxication,
• Sell cannabis to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of intoxication, and
• Allow an intoxicated person to enter or remain in an establishment.

heading: 38.1 Determining the level of intoxication
text:
The Act and regulation do not define “intoxication.” Intoxication is a state in which a person's normal capacity to
act or reason is inhibited by alcohol or drugs.

Determining whether a person is intoxicated by alcohol, cannabis or other drugs or a combination of substances
requires a contextual assessment that includes:
• observing a person’s mental and physical state, and
• comparing the person’s mental and physical state and the expected behaviour of a sober individual in like
conditions.

Signs and Symptoms of Intoxication:
Appearance: red or bloodshot eyes, glassy eyed, unable to focus, drooping eye lids; lack of eye contact,
dishevelled, unkempt, a flushed or red face, unusual sweating, an odour of liquor, nauseous or vomiting,
sleepiness, head bobbing or requiring support, body tremors, comatose.

Diminished motor skills: unsteady on their feet, staggering, long, exaggerated or lurching steps, extreme and
needless care in walking, bumping into objects and people, unable to find the chair when sitting down, missing
the table or chair when leaning onto it, requiring an object for support (e.g.: a person or a wall), swaying from side
to side, slowness of breath, unable to handle small objects, e.g.: wallet, keys, bank cards, money or cell phone.

Atypical speech patterns: unable to get out the words, whispering unnecessarily, slurring, slow and deliberate
speech, poor or overstated enunciation, sudden bursts of unconnected or delayed speech (e.g.: cheering when the
goal was some time past), sudden variations in volume.

Misjudging distances: spilling a drink, missing t

heading: 38.1 Determining the level of intoxication
text:
he mouth when drinking, exaggerated care when setting down a
drink, fumbling with small objects (e.g.: keys, money, a cell phone), tripping downstairs.

Reduced Inhibitions: boasting, crude behaviour, unwarranted or unwelcome personal advances, aggressive verbal
intrusions, overstated and unruly interactions with others, persistence despite rejection or negative responses,
forgetful (e.g.: about drink orders or a recent conversation), belligerent or randomly rude, random kindness and
generosity to strangers (e.g.: buying a round for the house), sharing personal matters with strangers.

Irrational behaviour: reckless spending, unrestrained physical behaviour showing a disregard for others, openly
consuming drugs, urinating in public, disrobing, public or aggressive sexuality, picking fights, demanding
attention, ignoring the concerns of others.

The Assessment
Each of the above behaviours may have a valid if not common explanation so while each of the above is a
symptom or sign of intoxication there may also be an alternate reason for the behaviour. However, a combination
of the above behaviours will reinforce an assessment of intoxication and weaken alternate explanations.

The inspector or police officer must document and be able to describe enough signs of intoxication with a level of
detail so that a reasonable person would - sometime later - make the same assessment as the inspector at the time
in question. And the combination of indicators must be adequate to exclude on the balance of probabilities
alternate justification for the activity described.

heading: 38.2 Selling cannabis to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of intoxication
text:
An intoxicated patron’s reasoning is inhibited by alcohol or drugs, including cannabis. The patron may not be able
to exercise sufficient judgment to stop consuming these substances. As well, the inability to reason or act in a
normal capacity creates a risk that the patron will contribute to the negative impacts noted above and possibly
harm themselves or others. Selling cannabis to a person who is already intoxicated or is showing signs of
intoxication increases this risk.

38.3 Prohibition against selling cannabis to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of intoxication
A person must not sell cannabis to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of intoxication.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.49(2)(a)]

38.4 Elements of contravention: “sell cannabis to an intoxicated person or a person showing signs of
intoxication”
To allege the contravention of selling cannabis to a person showing signs of intoxication, an inspector must gather
evidence that:
• the licensee sold cannabis to the person, and
• the person was intoxicated or was showing signs of intoxication at the time of the sale.

Procedure:
1. If an inspector receives a police or coroner’s report on a fatal or serious injury motor vehicle accident where
the driver was intoxicated and had been at a licensed establishment prior to the accident, the inspector will
forward the report to the Division’s Manager of Investigations for review who may proceed with an
investigation into whether the licensee sold cannabis to an intoxicated person or a person who appears to be
intoxicated,
2.

heading: 38.5 Allowing an intoxicated person to enter or remain in an establishment
text:
To avoid the possibility of harm to other patrons or staff, a licensee must not allow a person who is intoxicated or
appears to be intoxicated to enter or remain in the establishment.

38.6 Prohibition against allowing an intoxicated person to enter or remain in an establishment
A licensee must not allow an intoxicated person to enter or remain in that part of the establishment where
cannabis is sold.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.49(2)(b)]

38.7 Elements of contravention: “allow an intoxicated person to enter or remain in an establishment”

• the person was allowed to enter or remain in the establishment

2. The inspector will gather further evidence of each element of the contravention.

heading: 39.0 Introduction
text:
The application process involves extensive measures of assessment for applicant suitability which includes
security screening and financial integrity checks to ensure applicants are Fit & Proper status. These measures are
undertaken to help deter and eliminate criminal associations from entering the regulated non-medical retail
cannabis industry. The details an applicant provides at the time of licensing are critical factors taken into
consideration and are the basis for granting a cannabis retail license. Inability for the Branch to conduct an
assessment on an applicant may be detrimental to this purpose.

heading: 39.1 Requirement to report licence changes
text:
Once a license has been issued, licensees must inform the Branch of any changes that alter the original
information they provided to the Branch, including changes in any circumstance related to their license. Some
changes require the Branch’s prior approval, while others require the licensee to report the change within 10 days.
Failure to obtain approval or report changes is a licensing contravention and subject to enforcement action and/or
penalties.

heading: 39.3 Making structural alterations or changes
text:
The physical characteristics of an establishment are assessed at the time of licensing by requiring a licensee to
submit a floor plan. The floor plan must depict specific details regarding the proposed retail area and features
including the following:
• each room or area labeled with its intended use and dimensions,
• washrooms, stairs, and elevators,
• entrances and exits (including those used by staff only),
• storage areas, and
• identify the security system and other physical security features that secure the store.

The establishment is inspected and after confirmation that all licensing criteria are met, an area indicated on the
floor plan is approved as the retail area for the sale of cannabis to occur. Structural alterations or other changes to
the establishment, including the size or location of fixed structures require prior approval of the general manager
to ensure licensing criteria continue to be met.

heading: 39.4 Prohibition against making structural alterations or changes without amending licence
text:
A licensee must not make structural alterations to the establishment without prior application and approval.
Examples include:
• a structural alteration to a service area,
• change the size or location of a service area,
• an alteration to any area of a licensed establishment that is not a service area that, in the opinion of the
general manager, will affect the operation of a service area, or,
• a change to the location or the size of the storage area in an establishment without amending the licence.
[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 39.5 Definition of structural alteration
text:
A structural alteration is an alteration to existing construction resulting in a change to the free space within a
licensed area, including:
• a change in the position of a wall, floor or ceiling surrounding a licensed area,
• installing or removing a window,
• a change in the position of access and exit points leading to or from a licensed area, and
• such other construction, alterations or changes the general manager considers may affect patron routing,
capacity, or the line of sight between a staff control point and the licensed area of the establishment.

Note: Changes to the layout such as moving a display shelf, “point of sale” counter is very minor but likely high
frequency occurrences.

heading: 39.5 Definition of structural alteration
text:
Considering the low risk, the following changes are NOT to be considered as structural
changes requiring a structural alteration application:

• relocating fixed display cabinets or removing them entirely,
• adding or removing shelves,
• moving the point of sales location,
• adding or removing the reception area,
• moving secured storage from one room to another, and
• adding, moving, or removing security cameras

Historically, inspections of CRS establishments have identified no issues of risk or impact to compliance concerns
related to these types of changes.

• a change was made to the structural or layout of the retail store,

to allow for the change, the inspector will gather evidence of each element of the contravention.

heading: 40.0 Introduction
text:
The CCLA and CLR contain provisions which intend to mitigate the potential for federally licensed producer to
have dominance over the non-medical cannabis retail sector in BC.

The CCLA requires that the general manager must not issue, renew, transfer, or amend a licence, other than a
licence of a prescribed class, to or for:
• a person who has arranged, or agreed to arrange, with another person to sell the cannabis of a federal producer
to the exclusion of the cannabis of another federal producer,
• a federal producer or the federal producer's agent, or
• a person who is so associated with, connected with, or financially interested in a federal producer or federal
producer's agent that the person is, in the opinion of the general manager, likely to promote the sale of
cannabis of the federal producer.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.26.4 and s.50]

heading: 40.1 Tied House
text:
A tied house exists when there is an association between a cannabis retailer and a federally licensed cannabis
producer or its agent that is likely to lead to that manufacturer’s products being favoured.

The general manager will consider the following to determine if there is likelihood to promote a particular federal
licensed producer’s product:

1. The financial interconnectedness of a cannabis retailer and a federal cannabis licensed producer.
• Whether a federal licensed producer is a significant shareholder (control of 20% or more of the voting
shares) of a B.C. cannabis retailer or the federal licensed producer is a significant shareholder of a significant
shareholder of a B.C. cannabis retailer,
• Whether a B.C. cannabis retailer is a significant shareholder (control of 20% or more of the voting shares) of
a federal licensed producer or the B.C. cannabis retailer is a significant shareholder of a significant
shareholder of a federal licensed producer, and
• Whether a person, partnership or company is a significant shareholder (control of 20% or more of the voting
shares) in both a B.C. cannabis retailer and a federal licensed producer or a person, partnership or company is
a significant shareholder in a company that is a significant shareholder in both a federal licensed producer
and a B.C. cannabis retailer.
2. Whether an immediate family member of the licensee has any interest in a federal licensed producer.
Immediate family members include spouses, parents, siblings, children, sons-in-law, and daughters-in-law, and
3.

heading: 40.1 Tied House
text:
The general manager will also consider any other association, connection or financial interest between a B.C.
cannabis retail licensee and federal licensed producer. There may be a combination of factors that when taken
together lead to a reasonable conclusion there is likelihood to promote.

Where an association, connection or financial interest exists between an applicant and a federal licensee or the
licensee’s agent, the general manager may determine that it is necessary to restrict the person from selling any
products of the associated federal licensed producer. Doing so would eliminate the risk that the person would
promote the federal licensee’s cannabis, enabling the general manager to issue a licence. In such cases, the general
manager may issue a licence with term and condition stating the restriction.

[Cannabis Control and Licensing Act, s.26.4 and s.50]
To allege the contravention of tied house, an inspector should gather evidence that:

• the licensee has an arrangement or an agreement to arrange with another person to sell the cannabis of a
federal producer,
• the agreement or arrangement was to the exclusion of the cannabis of another federal producer

heading: 40.3 Disclosing information relating to tied house
text:
The terms and conditions of a Cannabis Retail licence require that the licensee obtain approval and report any
changes that alter the information provided to the branch at the time of application. In relation to tied houses, the
licensee must report the following to the Branch within 10 days of occurring:
• producer or marketer obtains a financial interest in the retail licence, or
• a person with a financial interest in the licensee obtains a financial interest in a producer, or
• an immediate family member of the retail licence holder obtains a financial interest in a producer.

Failure to obtain approval or report changes is a licensing contravention and subject to penalty.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 40.5 Inducements
text:
Inducements are incentives given to licensees by producers or their marketers such as gifts, rewards, rebates,
money, or other remuneration, in order to establish exclusivity of product sales or to increase a product's sales.
Giving or accepting inducements for promoting a particular producer`s cannabis or particular type of cannabis can
lead to destructive competition and market domination.

In order to encourage a fair and balanced market and prevent domination of any producer in the retail industry, the
terms and conditions for Cannabis Retail Licensees specify rules surrounding promotional activities between
provincial licensees and federal producers.

Federally licensed producers and their marketers may hire employees or contract with a person to promote and
market the producer’s cannabis products that the marketer is authorised to represent. The marketer must provide
their employees with identification establishing them as a marketing representative for the federal producer and
they must carry out their marketing activities in accordance with their marketer licence terms and conditions.

Giving or accepting inducements for promoting a particular producer`s brand or type of cannabis product is a
contravention that can lead to destructive competition and its spillover effects. These concepts are described in
“Operating Environment.”
To allege the contravention of inducements, an inspector should gather evidence that:
• the licensee offered, gave, requested, accepted, or agreed to offer, give, or accept money, gifts, a reward or
remuneration, directly or indirectly,
• the offer was to promote, induce or further the sale of a particular class or brand of cannabis

heading: 40.7 Prohibition against giving or accepting gifts for promoting cannabis
text:
Licensees are not permitted to ask for or receive financial or other benefits from a federally licensed producer or
marketer in exchange for selling or promoting their products. As well, the CCLA prohibits a licensee from
arranging, or agreeing to sell the cannabis of a federal producer to the exclusion of the cannabis of another federal
producer.

Licensees and their employees may not request or accept money, gifts, rewards or remuneration to promote,
induce or further the sale of a particular brand of cannabis. For example, a licensee must not:
• Pay money or provide other benefits to secure their ability to purchase a federal producer’s products,
• Request money or other benefits from a federal producer or their marketer in return for buying their products
from the LDB,
• Accept money or other benefits in exchange for agreeing not to stock a competitor’s product, or
• Make agreements that give them exclusive access to a producer’s product, or product line.

Various types of activities which constitute an inducement are specified in the Licensee Terms and Conditions
and include but are not limited to the following:
1. Licensees are prohibited from accepting any items, products or services from a federal producer or marketer
that are necessary for the operation of their business. This includes financial assistance as well as permanent
fixtures, furnishings, or display structures,
2. Federal producers/marketers cannot buy shelf space, offer weight discounts, or offer discounted product in
exchange for marketing benefits,
3.

heading: 40.7 Prohibition against giving or accepting gifts for promoting cannabis
text:
Licensee may hire and pay for their own outside consultant or financial advisor, or they may accept
information and ideas to help improve their business directly from a producer or marketer, however, the
producer or marketer cannot pay for an outside consultant or financial advisor to help a licensee,
4. A licensee may not accept product samples for themselves or their employees from a federal producer,
marketer, or any other person,
5. Licensees must pay for their own advertising. A cannabis producer or marketer may not pay for a licensee’s
advertising costs (or vice versa), and joint marketing plans are not permitted. With permission from a
producer or marketer, a licensee can include the producer's logo in ads, but they cannot demand or receive
any kind of compensation in return,
6. Licensee may not accept product vouchers for cannabis or cannabis accessories (i.e.: certificates for a
specific quantity of cannabis or a cannabis accessory that customers redeem for no charge), and
7. Licensees, employees, or both may attend educational events or activities hosted by a federal producer or
marketer and may accept payment from the federal producer or marketer for legitimate travel, meals, and
accommodation and entertainment expenses associated with the educational event, up to $1,500 per licensee
location per year.

heading: 40.7 Prohibition against giving or accepting gifts for promoting cannabis
text:
If a licensee has multiple licensed stores (i.e.: a chain of cannabis stores), they may also
accept expenses of $1,500 per person to a maximum of $4,500 per head office per year.

[Cannabis Control & Licensing Act, s.50]
[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 41.0 Introduction
text:
Schedule 2 of the CLR “Penalty Schedule” identifies the enforcement actions that may be taken by the general
manager against licensees that contravene certain sections of the CCLA or regulation. Procedures for identifying
these contraventions are included in this section under the following headings:
• Fail to comply with online sales requirements,
• Altering or adding substance to cannabis,
• Cannabis pricing,
• Use sales strategy likely to promote or encourage the excessive, irresponsible, or dangerous use of cannabis,
• Requirements for prescribed training program or re-certification.

heading: 41.1 Fail to comply with online sales requirements
text:
Licensees may post information inside their store and on an online system about:
• Non-medical cannabis available for purchase from the licensee,
• Cannabis accessories,
• Prices for non-medical cannabis available for purchase and cannabis accessories, and
• Gift cards.

Licensees may offer reservations or sales of non-medical cannabis, cannabis accessories, gift cards and shopping
bags to customers through an online system, or by telephone.
The online system must:
• be administered or operated, in whole or in part, by the licensee, or a third party on behalf of the licensee,
• comply with all laws, rules and requirements that apply to the licensee, and
• the online system must have an age verification tool that restricts entry to adults only.

Non-medical cannabis reserved or purchased online, or by telephone, must be picked up in the establishment
during the establishment’s hours of sale.

[Terms and Conditions Handbook]

heading: 41.2 Elements of contravention: “fail to comply with online sales requirements”
text:
To allege the contravention of failure to comply with online sales requirements the inspector must gather evidence

heading: 41.5 Cannabis pricing
text:
Control of cannabis prices is directed at preventing over-service, over-consumption, and loss of control by the
consuming public. In general, the price of cannabis must not be so low that it is likely to lead to over-consumption
or resale for profit. The purpose of control of cannabis pricing is to prevent destructive competition and its
spillover effects. These concepts are explained in “Operating Environment.”
Licensees are prohibited from selling cannabis below minimum pricing.

heading: 41.13 Draw attention to a cannabis inspector, minor agent or police
text:
Drawing the attention of patrons to the fact that cannabis inspectors, minor agents contracted to the branch, and/or
police are present in an establishment may put the safety of the cannabis inspectors, minor agents contracted to
the branch, and police at risk.

Accordingly, licensee actions must not cause the attention or focus of patrons to shift towards cannabis inspectors,
minor agents contracted to the branch, or police at any time; including at the time of entry, during an inspection,
or when exiting the establishment.

Actions such as announcing the arrival of cannabis inspectors, raising, or flashing lights, turning down music,
playing particular soundtracks (e.g.: "Bad Boys" or 'Hawaii Five O"), using spotlights, or any other similar actions
are not permitted.

Licensees or their staff may not take, save, or distribute photographs or video of cannabis inspectors or minor
agents contracted to the branch in any manner (e.g.: on a staff bulletin board, print media, social media, or the
internet).

heading: 41.15 Fail to complete the prescribed training program or re-certification
text:
Selling It Right: is a mandatory self-study course the provides education for non-medical cannabis licensees and
employees on applicable laws and how to sell cannabis in a socially responsible manner.

The establishment of the Selling It Right training program supports the Branch’s mission of promoting safe
establishments and safe communities, minimizing the health and social harms of liquor and cannabis, and helping
licensees succeed.

Providing training for everyone responsible for the sale and promotion of non-medical cannabis also aligns with
government’s priorities of protecting children and youth and promoting health and safety.

The Selling It Right training certificate is valid for two years.

cannabis,
